articles.title: Malaysia to work towards Myanmar's full reintegration into ASEAN, PM says - Yahoo News Singapore
articles.summary: Malaysia to work towards Myanmar's full reintegration into ASEAN, PM says  Yahoo News Singapore
articles.full_text:
By Rozanna Latiff and Hasnoor Hussain
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Malaysia hosted Myanmar's junta chief-turned-President Min Aung Hlaing on Thursday, saying it aimed to reintegrate the country with Southeast Asian bloc ASEAN, but made clear the visit did not amount to recognition for the military-backed government.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim pledged to continue working with Myanmar on tasks such as the repatriation of thousands of its nationals, a move criticised by the United Nations and rights groups concerned about the risks stemming from civil war.
"Malaysia will do whatever is possible to make sure that we ... ultimately, take Myanmar as part of our community of nations, without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN," Anwar told media after meeting Min Aung Hlaing.
The Myanmar leader's two-day visit aims to build greater international legitimacy after Min Aung Hlaing became president in April following an election criticised as a sham by rights groups and Western nations.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since 2021, when Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup against a democratically elected government, unleashing armed conflict across much of the country.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations barred Min Aung Hlaing and senior Myanmar officials from its summits for not adhering to an ASEAN-brokered peace plan after the coup.
But some member nations, such as Cambodia, Laos, Thailandand Vietnam, have sought to re-establish ties.
Anwar acknowledged concerns about Myanmar's democratic processes but called for differences to be respected, adding that Min Aung Hlaing had shown willingness to be collaborative.
Malaysian government spokesperson Fahmi Fadzil denied that Min Aung Hlaing's visit amounted to recognition of Myanmar's government, however, state news agency Bernama said.
"This meeting does not mean we recognise the Myanmar government," Fahmi, who is communications minister, was quoted as saying. "It is intended to find a solution to the long-standing issue of Myanmar refugees in our country."
MYANMAR TO SEND MORE NAVY SHIPS TO REPATRIATE ITS CITIZENS
Anwar also expressed appreciation to Min Aung Hlaing for accepting the return home of 10,493 Myanmar nationals from Malaysia.
Malaysia has said it can no longer take in refugees from Myanmar, citing the financial burden and security risk. As it is not a party to the UN refugee convention, Malaysia treats asylum-seekers as illegal migrants.
Last month it sent back about 1,500 people on Myanmar naval ships, part of a wider repatriation effort to deport as many as 5,000.
Myanmar citizens held in Malaysian immigration centres would be taken home as soon as possible, Min Aung Hlaing said.
"Because the current weather is favourable, I will dispatch navy ships to repatriate them," he told Thursday's briefing,
adding that he would invite Anwar to visit when the time was right.
The leaders did not say if their talks covered repatriation plans for Rohingya Muslim refugees, many of whom fled Myanmar after a brutal 2017 military crackdown in western Rakhine state.
Muslim-majority Malaysia widely criticised the crackdown at the time. But public sentiment has turned in recent years, with increasing harassment and scrutiny of Rohingya in Malaysia amid a surge of online hate speech and misinformation.
Anwar has said he would push for Myanmar to accept Rohingya refugees. Malaysia was hosting about 193,000 refugees and asylum seekers from Myanmar as of February, about 65% of them Rohingya, UN data shows.
Buddhist-majority Myanmar does not recognise the Rohingya as one of its official ethnic groups and denies citizenship to most.
ASEAN URGED NOT TO LEGITIMISE MYANMAR LEADER
Myanmar's pro-democracy activists and resistance groups have repeatedly urged ASEAN to refrain from conferring political legitimacy on Min Aung Hlaing's presidency.
"His legitimacy is a nightmare for the whole nation, for the people who have ... sacrificed their homes," Swam Saung, a member of the Myanmar Affairs Alliance, told a gathering in Kuala Lumpur, the capital.
He also expressed fear for those repatriated, saying they could face forced conscription in the military conflict with ethnic armed groups.
Malaysia has traditionally upheld principles of humanitarian values, democracy, and human rights during engagements on Myanmar within ASEAN, an umbrella group of Myanmar armed ethnic groups and democratic bodies said.
"Hosting of Min Aung Hlaing at the head-of-state level stands in direct contradiction to these established principles,"
the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union, added in a statement.
(Reporting by Rozanna Latiff and Reuters staff; Additional reporting by Hasnoor Hussain and Ahmad Luqman Ismail; Editing by Kate Mayberry, Raju Gopalakrishnan and Clarence Fernandez)

articles.title: Head of the Import-Export Department explains 3 reasons for the high increase in electronics imports. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Head of the Import-Export Department explains 3 reasons for the high increase in electronics imports.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Representatives from the Import-Export Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade) provided information and explanations on some of the reasons for the recent surge in electronics imports, along with solutions for directing and managing exports to further promote exports and control the trade deficit.
Three main reasons for the surge in electronics imports.
At the Ministry of Industry and Trade 's regular press conference for the third quarter of 2026, held on the afternoon of October 7, 2026, the import-export situation and the trade deficit were of great interest to many journalists.
Regarding the recent surge in imports, particularly of electronics, computers, components, and equipment, Ms. Trinh Thi Thu Hien, Deputy Director of the Import-Export Department, provided information and explanations on several contributing factors.
Khám phá thêm
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch
Khám phá ĐNA
Firstly, this is due to rising global raw material prices. Ms. Hien stated that some chips or SSD storage drives have increased by 300 to 500%, so with the same import volume as the previous year, but due to the 300 to 500% price increase, the import value has increased many times over.
The second reason related to the increase in imports is the issue of inventory and stockpiling. Recently, as the development of artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly focused and preparations for producing AI-related products have been underway, shortages and even "stockouts" have arisen for certain materials used in AI production.
Given this situation, some factories and companies are tending to build up inventory. Some manufacturers have now increased their inventory holding period from 6 weeks to 12 weeks, or increased the value of their inventory from $100 million to $700 million.
The third reason related to the increase in import figures at electronics and semiconductor exporting companies, according to Ms. Hien, lies in the expansion of production. For example , Samsung's factory in Thai Nguyen increased its investment to $1.5 billion; Intel moved its factory from Costa Rica to Vietnam; or BYD's factory in Phu Tho also expanded and upgraded its investment...
" These factors have contributed to the high import figures in the recent period ," said the Deputy Director of the Import-Export Department.
You may also like
Focus on four groups of solutions to boost exports and control the trade deficit.
Regarding solutions to promote exports and control the trade deficit, Ms. Trinh Thi Thu Hien stated that, in implementing Notice No. 443/TB-VPCP of the Government Office dated August 20, 2026, on the conclusions of the Standing Deputy Prime Minister at the meeting on promoting exports and controlling the trade deficit, as well as Notice No. 481/TB-VPCP of the Government Office dated September 14, 2026, on the conclusions of the Standing Deputy Prime Minister at the working session with the Vietnam Electronics Business Association and a number of large semiconductor import-export enterprises, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has several orientations related to groups of solutions for direction and management.
Firstly, there is a group of solutions related to mechanisms and policies.
Secondly, there is a group of solutions related to market issues.
Thirdly, the group of solutions relates to supporting and partnering with businesses.
Fourth, in the long term, the set of solutions relates to improving the capacity of businesses in Vietnam, as well as increasing the added value of products manufactured in Vietnam.
Regarding the target of keeping the trade deficit for the whole year of 2026 below $10 billion, Ms. Trinh Thi Thu Hien stated that from the beginning of the year, Government Resolution No. 01/NQ-CP set an export target of approximately 15-16% for 2026. Unless there are significant negative developments, exports will reach the target for the whole year, as the end of the year is the peak export season.
According to data released by the General Statistics Office on October 3rd, in September 2026, the total value of goods exports and imports reached US$117.69 billion, an increase of 7.3% compared to the previous month and a 42.4% increase compared to the same period last year. The trade balance for goods in September returned to a surplus after nine consecutive months of deficits, with a surplus of US$1.27 billion.
Overall, in the first nine months of 2026, total merchandise exports and imports reached US$888.02 billion, an increase of 30.4% compared to the same period last year, with exports increasing by 24.5% and imports increasing by 36.7%. The trade balance for the nine months showed a deficit of US$19.42 billion.

Regarding imports, the value of goods imported in September 2026 reached US$58.21 billion, an increase of 6.0% compared to the previous month. Of this, the domestic economic sector accounted for US$13.14 billion, an increase of 2.5%; and the foreign-invested sector accounted for US$45.07 billion, an increase of 7.1%. Compared to the same period last year, the value of goods imported in September increased by 45.8%, with the domestic economic sector increasing by 22.1% and the foreign-invested sector increasing by 54.6%.
In the third quarter of 2026, import turnover reached US$170.33 billion, an increase of 42.2% compared to the same period last year and an increase of 8.8% compared to the second quarter of 2026.
Overall, in the first nine months of 2026, merchandise imports reached US$453.72 billion, an increase of 36.7% compared to the same period last year. Of this, the domestic economic sector accounted for US$118.17 billion, an increase of 23.5%; and the foreign-invested sector accounted for US$335.55 billion, an increase of 42.0%.
Regarding the structure of import groups in the first nine months of 2026, the production materials group reached US$426.92 billion, accounting for 94.1%, of which machinery, equipment, tools and spare parts accounted for 58.3%; raw materials, fuels and materials accounted for 35.8%. The consumer goods group reached US$26.80 billion, accounting for 5.9%.

articles.title: South China Sea: Strengthening the rule of law, protecting connectivity, and promoting substantive cooperation. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: South China Sea: Strengthening the rule of law, protecting connectivity, and promoting substantive cooperation.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Managing differences based on international law, protecting vital shipping lanes and infrastructure, and promoting cooperation to meet common needs were the highlights of the 18th International Scientific Conference on the South China Sea, which recently concluded in Hanoi. Discussions emphasized the need to build an inclusive and stable regional maritime order linked to the shared responsibilities of all nations.
On the afternoon of October 8th, the 18th International Scientific Conference on the South China Sea, themed “Competition, Connectivity and Cooperation: The South China Sea and Regional Maritime Order,” organized by the Diplomatic Academy of Vietnam, concluded in Hanoi after two days of discussions.
The discussions focused on four main areas: managing disputes while upholding the rule of law and controlling crises; protecting connectivity, freedom of navigation, and infrastructure resilience; promoting substantive cooperation that promptly addresses common needs; and building and strengthening an inclusive and stable maritime order based on international law.
Managing competition and preventing escalation.
Most speakers assessed that, although no major conflict has occurred, the South China Sea is facing long-term strategic competition. Gray zone activities are gradually changing the situation on the ground and eroding trust between the parties. In this context, controlling actions that risk escalating tensions and seeking peaceful solutions to disputes are urgent requirements.
According to the speakers, competition management should be based on international law, particularly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), combined with enhanced dialogue and the development of appropriate management mechanisms. Proposals included establishing a Code of Conduct for Avoiding Unintended Encounters at Sea (CUES) for coast guard forces, enhancing maritime awareness (MDA), establishing hotlines, and improving information sharing.
Experts expect ASEAN and China to reach a substantive, effective, and efficient Code of Conduct in the South China Sea (COC) that is consistent with international law and UNCLOS, clearly defining the obligations of the parties and dangerous behaviors. However, opinions also note that the entire burden of managing tensions should not be placed on a single mechanism like the COC.
Many discussions suggest that great power competition will continue, but all parties still have a common interest in avoiding hot conflict and maintaining strategic stability. Great powers need to demonstrate greater responsibility in exercising self-restraint and avoiding coercive changes to the status quo.
Protecting maritime connectivity and critical infrastructure.
Discussions have shown that stability in the South China Sea needs to be viewed within a broader context, interconnected with strategic shipping lanes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Malacca Strait. A disruption at one point could impact the entire network; therefore, protecting connectivity requires a regional approach to maintaining safe and uninterrupted shipping lanes, while also preparing mechanisms and scenarios for crisis response.
Enhancing resilience has been identified as a crucial measure to ensure connectivity. Scholars propose diversifying supply sources, developing alternative energy sources and transportation routes, strengthening storage capacity, improving infrastructure capacity, and applying modern technology in monitoring and operation.
You may also like
Regarding critical infrastructure such as submarine cables, opinions emphasized the need to diversify cable routes and clarify the roles of each entity in ensuring security and enhancing resilience. Experience from many places shows that self-reliance, along with cooperation between countries, international and regional organizations, and between the public and private sectors, plays a crucial role in protecting submarine cable systems.
Collaboration stems from shared needs and overlapping interests.
To make regional cooperation more substantive, many opinions suggest prioritizing areas that meet common needs and intersecting interests, such as search and rescue, ensuring the safety of fishermen, disaster response, protecting underwater cables, marine scientific research, fisheries management, and environmental protection. Information sharing, infrastructure protection, human resource training, and enhancing maritime law enforcement capacity are also areas that can promote cooperation.
Science and technology are seen as driving forces for future cooperation. However, the application of new technologies must comply with international law, based on mechanisms that ensure transparency, data reliability, and the protection of national data sovereignty .
Speakers argued that priority should be given to improving the effectiveness of existing mechanisms rather than focusing on building new ones. Cooperation can develop gradually, from individual initiatives to shared processes, standards, and capabilities that can be sustained in the long term.
Fishery cooperation between Vietnam and China in the Gulf of Tonkin is cited by experts as a good practice in combining law, policy, and technology. Cooperation between Vietnam and the Philippines, through the signing of memoranda of understanding and the implementation of specific coordinated activities, including support for fishermen, is also considered a valuable lesson to learn.
Notably, there have been suggestions that ASEAN should gradually institutionalize feasible areas of cooperation, such as strategic infrastructure and submarine cables.
Strengthening an inclusive and stable maritime order.
Discussions view the South China Sea as a shared space, where many complex disputes exist, but which is also a vital link in the region's trade, energy, data, and ecosystem networks.
To ensure a stable and inclusive regional order, speakers emphasized the need to implement comprehensive measures that adhere to international law, with UNCLOS as the foundational framework. ASEAN and ASEAN-led mechanisms, such as the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) and the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting Plus (ADMM+), need to further enhance their central role.
ASEAN needs to be more proactive in building trust, protecting common interests, establishing norms, and connecting stakeholders through multilateral, bilateral, and sub-multilateral mechanisms. These mechanisms should complement each other, enhance information sharing, and avoid fragmentation or exclusion.
You may also like
An inclusive order also needs to ensure that small and medium-sized countries can participate in shaping norms, protecting their legitimate interests, and enhancing their response capabilities. Changes in maritime safety, infrastructure resilience, and benefits to the community will be measures of the effectiveness of regional cooperation.
Speaking at the closing session on the afternoon of October 8th, Dr. Nguyen Hung Son, Director of the Diplomatic Academy, summarized the overarching message of the discussions: the future of peace and stability in the South China Sea does not lie in the early resolution of disputes, but in countries building a system of rules, ensuring predictability, enhancing self-reliance, and promoting substantive cooperation.
Alongside the conference, activities such as the Southeast Asia Dialogue, the Southeast Asia-Pacific Dialogue, the Young Leaders Program, and the annual South China Sea Report were held, contributing to promoting dialogue, research, and policy exchanges on maritime issues.
This year's conference continues to focus on the next generation. The Young Leaders session listened to proposals and initiatives from young speakers from various countries aimed at strengthening regional maritime order and promoting substantive cooperation even amidst disagreements and strategic competition.

articles.title: Turning border advantages into a new export growth engine for Tuyen Quang. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Turning border advantages into a new export growth engine for Tuyen Quang.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
When trade promotion is linked to production, logistics, and the actual needs of the market, the advantage of being a border gateway will gradually be transformed into a growth driver for Tuyen Quang in the coming years.
From Shan Tuyet tea products, medicinal herbs, processed agricultural products to OCOP (One Commune One Product) products with distinctive mountainous characteristics, many of Tuyen Quang's key products are facing the opportunity to access the Chinese market more widely.
The Vietnam-China International Trade Fair ( Tuyen Quang ) in 2026, expected to attract around 300 booths, is not simply a place to display and introduce products, but is also expected to create more substantive connections between businesses of the two countries, expand export markets, and promote border trade.
In the context of Tuyen Quang's implementation of the Program to Reach International Markets for the period 2026-2030, this fair is even more significant as it becomes one of the concrete activities aimed at bringing local products beyond traditional markets and gradually participating more deeply in regional and international supply chains.
According to the program approved by the Provincial People's Committee, Tuyen Quang aims to achieve an average annual export growth rate of 11-12% by 2030; and to organize three Vietnam-China International Trade Fairs in 2026, 2028, and 2030.
Bringing local products closer to the market.
Khám phá thêm
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch
Khám phá ĐNA
In recent years, the product structure of Tuyen Quang has become increasingly diverse. From the Shan Tuyet tea growing region in the high mountains, fruit orchards, medicinal herb farms, to processed agricultural and forestry products and traditional handicrafts, many products have been standardized, branded, and participated in the OCOP program.
However, to transform product advantages into greater economic value, the challenge remains expanding the market, building stable distribution channels, and meeting the increasingly high standards of export markets.
The 2026 Vietnam-China International Trade Fair is being held in this context. According to the organizers, the fair is expected to have approximately 300 booths, showcasing characteristic products, OCOP products, typical rural industrial products, and many product groups from Vietnamese and Chinese businesses.
The event also included a Vietnam-China trade networking conference, and exchange activities with the trade offices of Zhou Wenshan, Yunnan Province and Baise City, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region (China).
Notably, Tuyen Quang does not view the trade fair as merely a temporary promotional activity. In its Program to Reach International Markets for the period 2026-2030, the province has identified product groups with strengths and export potential including high-quality tea, oranges and processed agricultural products, medicinal herbs, OCOP products, deeply processed forest products, and handicrafts.
You may also like
The province also aims to support 30-50 businesses and cooperatives to participate in programs, trade fairs, conferences, and trade delegations abroad; and to provide training and capacity building for at least 450 businesses and cooperatives in applying e-commerce and integrating into the international economy.
Tuyen Quang and Zhouwenshan have favorable conditions to strengthen these connections. At a meeting between the Department of Industry and Trade of Tuyen Quang province and the Zhouwenshan Trade Bureau in 2026, both sides agreed on many areas of cooperation, including facilitating the export of high-quality Vietnamese fruits to China, promoting investment in trade and logistics infrastructure at the border gate area, and expanding cooperation on several agricultural products.
Chau Van Son's side also agreed to coordinate the organization of a delegation of businesses and delegates to attend the Vietnam-China International Trade Fair in Tuyen Quang in the fourth quarter of 2026.
This provides a foundation for meetings at trade fairs to go beyond initial information exchange. For local businesses, the Chinese market is large and located right across the border, but for goods to reach a wider and more sustainable market, products must meet regulations regarding quality, traceability, quarantine, packaging, and stable supply. Therefore, trade fairs also offer businesses a clearer understanding of market demands, allowing them to adjust production starting from the raw material sourcing area.
From connecting trade fairs to cross-border trade flows.
The highlight of the 2026 Vietnam-China International Trade Fair lies not only in its scale of approximately 300 booths but also in the series of coordinated business networking activities.
According to Plan No. 381/KH-UBND dated October 5, 2026, of the People's Committee of Tuyen Quang province, two bilateral talks will take place on October 24 with the Commerce Bureau of Wenshan Prefecture, Yunnan Province, and the Commerce Bureau of Baise City, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region (China).
On the same day, the business networking conference is expected to gather approximately 200 delegates, with 20-30 exhibition booths for business networking. The program will include time to introduce potential and strengths, exchange cooperation opportunities, and organize the signing of contracts and memoranda of understanding as stipulated.
Combining bilateral talks with direct connections between businesses is expected to create more opportunities for Tuyen Quang's goods to access the Chinese market, while also promoting trade cooperation and import-export activities through border gates.
According to Mr. Hoang Anh Cuong, Director of the Department of Industry and Trade of Tuyen Quang province, this year's fair is organized with a focus on promoting products and connecting with genuine trade. Through business meetings, product introductions, and discussions, the province aims to expand cooperation with Chinese localities, creating conditions for businesses and cooperatives to find partners and develop markets, especially for products with strengths and export potential. At the same time, this is also an opportunity to promote border trade and gradually increase the value of local goods.
A major advantage for Tuyen Quang in developing its foreign trade is its border with China and its long-standing cooperative relationship with localities on the Chinese side. If this advantage is effectively exploited, the border region can become a gateway for goods from the province and other localities in the region to the Chinese market, while also expanding logistics, transportation, trade, and tourism services.
In fact, trade relations between Tuyen Quang and localities in China are being promoted in an increasingly substantive direction. During working sessions with Yunnan province in 2026, the leaders of Tuyen Quang province proposed that both sides continue to strengthen business connections, facilitate access to the Chinese market for Tuyen Quang's agricultural products and other strong goods, and coordinate the organization of the Vietnam-China International Trade Fair in 2026. Both sides also identified ample room for cooperation in trade, investment, and tourism.
You may also like
The 2026 Vietnam-China International Trade Fair can therefore be seen as a link in a longer-term strategy. From booths showcasing tea, medicinal herbs, agricultural products, and OCOP products to business networking tables, the ultimate goal remains to create more markets for goods and transform cooperative relations between localities of the two countries into concrete trade flows.
When market doors open wider, opportunities don't stop at individual businesses. Behind every product are raw material sources, cooperatives, and thousands of individual producers. A stable consumer market can motivate people to improve product quality, encourage businesses to invest more in processing, and enable localities to form more competitive value chains.
From a trade fair with around 300 booths to the goal of achieving an average export growth of 11-12% per year, it's been a long journey. But the connections forged in Tuyen Quang during this event could become the starting point for new contracts, new markets, and increasingly vibrant flows of goods across the Vietnam-China border.
When trade promotion is closely linked to production, logistics, and the actual needs of the market, the advantage of being a border gateway will gradually be transformed into a growth driver for Tuyen Quang in the coming years.

 With rising imports, we need to look at the quality of capital flows and resources.
 At the seminar "Improving the Quality of Import and Export Growth in the Process of Restructuring the Industry and Trade Sector" organized by the Industry and Trade Magazine, Ms. Trinh Thi Thu Hien, Deputy Director of the Import and Export Department, Ministry of Industry and Trade , stated that in the first nine months of 2026, the total import and export turnover of goods reached over 888 billion USD, an increase of 30.4% compared to the same period. Of this, exports reached over 434 billion USD, an increase of 24.5%; and imports reached over 453 billion USD, an increase of 36.7%.
 Notably, imports continued to focus primarily on production materials. This group of goods reached US$426.92 billion, accounting for 94.1% of total import turnover; of which machinery, equipment, tools, and spare parts accounted for 58.3%, and raw materials, fuels, and other materials accounted for 35.8%. 
|  | 
| Ms. Trinh Thi Thu Hien, Deputy Director of the Import-Export Department, Ministry of Industry and Trade | 
 This structure shows that imports are closely linked to production, investment, and exports. However, according to delegates, one should not only look at the increase in import figures to assess the health of the economy . What needs to be considered is the "hidden" aspect behind those figures: whether imports serve to expand capacity, innovate technology, and create new production capabilities; and how much value is created and retained domestically.
 The electronics industry is a case in point. According to Ms. Hien, the increase in imported raw materials and components can stem from various reasons such as rising input costs, businesses proactively increasing inventory, or expanding production. Therefore, an increase in import value does not necessarily mean a decline in domestic production capacity.
 Notably, some electronics companies have increased their raw material reserves to ensure production in the face of potential supply shortages. Simultaneously, several large corporations continue to expand their factories and invest in additional fixed assets in Vietnam, driving up demand for imported machinery, equipment, and raw materials.
 The bottleneck lies in the capacity of Vietnamese businesses.
 From the import story, a larger issue arises: the economy's ability to absorb and transform resources. This is also the crucial factor determining the amount of added value that Vietnam can retain. According to Mr. Phan Duc Hieu, a member of the 16th National Assembly and a member of the National Assembly's Economic and Financial Committee , to improve the quality of import and export growth, Vietnamese businesses must participate more deeply in global value chains, enhance the domestic supply of raw materials for manufacturing and export businesses, and increase their capacity to directly participate in domestic and international economic activities. 
|  | 
| Mr. Phan Duc Hieu, Member of the 16th National Assembly , Member of the National Assembly's Economic and Financial Committee. | 
 In reality, despite the rapid increase in export volume, domestic businesses still face limitations in technology, scale, management capacity, and the ability to meet supply chain standards. This has resulted in spillover effects from the FDI sector to the domestic business sector not meeting expectations.
 In Quang Ninh , Mr. Le Hong Giang, Deputy Director of the Department of Industry and Trade, said that in the first nine months of the year, the locality saw the addition of 1,300 businesses participating in import and export activities. However, the capacity of domestic businesses in terms of scale, technology, and supply capabilities remains limited, while the demands of the supply chain are increasingly high regarding quality, timeliness, traceability, environmental protection, and social responsibility.
 In particular, supporting industries have not adequately met the needs of FDI enterprises. Components, raw materials, packaging, logistics, and many products and services serving production still have to be imported. This is one of the reasons why the value created domestically does not match the scale of exports.
 According to Ms. Do Thi Thuy Huong, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Electronics Business Association, it is necessary to simultaneously improve technological capacity, develop supporting industries, increase linkages with FDI enterprises, and better meet international standards. Technology and innovation are key factors. Businesses need to increase investment in automation, digitalization, AI, product design, data management, quality control, and research and development. This is the way to transform imported machinery, equipment, and raw materials into productivity, new products, and added value, instead of just serving low-margin processing stages.
 Integrate import, production, and export into a single value chain.
 To improve the quality of import and export growth, experts emphasize that the solution is to simultaneously enhance production capacity, develop markets, improve supporting industries, and strengthen business linkages.
 According to Ms. Trinh Thi Thu Hien, in the long term, the focus must remain on domestic production. Imported production lines and equipment should not only serve processing purposes but also contribute to improving internal capacity, increasing self-reliance on products, and promoting the internal added value of Vietnam's manufacturing sector. 
|  | 
| Vietnamese businesses need to master technology. | 
 To achieve this goal, import and export development policies need to be implemented synchronously, encompassing market access, rules of origin, green standards, and business support. Leveraging FTAs also requires businesses to be more proactive in organizing production, ensuring the origin of goods, and meeting increasingly stringent requirements regarding the environment, sustainable development, and the circular economy.
 For the FDI sector, the issue is not just about attracting more projects, but more importantly, increasing the spillover effect. According to Ms. Do Thi Thuy Huong, FDI attraction policies need to be linked to domestic enterprise development policies, so that each FDI project can become a "nucleus" that draws in a network of Vietnamese businesses to participate in supplying, adopting standards, training human resources, and improving technological capabilities.
 In the long term, Mr. Phan Duc Hieu believes that high growth demand also presents an opportunity to enhance domestic production capacity. Initially, importing machinery, equipment, and production materials is necessary for expansion. However, in the long run, it is essential to gradually develop domestic production capacity, replacing inputs that Vietnamese businesses are capable of producing, while simultaneously forming value chains led by Vietnamese enterprises.
 From that perspective, the quality of import and export growth should not be measured solely by trade volume or trade surplus/deficit status. A more important measure is the ability to transform trade flows into domestic production capacity, technology, productivity, and added value.
 When imported machinery, raw materials, and components become inputs for new production capacity; production creates higher-value products; exports generate resources for reinvestment, and reinvestment further enhances technological capabilities, the economy will form a more sustainable growth cycle. This also forms the foundation for Vietnamese businesses to gradually move up the value chain, reduce dependence on inputs that can be produced domestically, and increase the value created and retained within the economy.

articles.title: The head of the Import-Export Department outlined four key solutions to further promote exports and control the trade deficit. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The head of the Import-Export Department outlined four key solutions to further promote exports and control the trade deficit.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Representatives from the Import-Export Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade) provided information and explanations on some of the reasons for the recent surge in electronics imports, along with key solutions to further promote exports and control the trade deficit.
Three main reasons have led to the recent surge in electronics imports.
At the Ministry of Industry and Trade 's regular press conference for the third quarter of 2026, held on the afternoon of October 7, 2026, the import and export situation attracted considerable attention from journalists.
Regarding the recent surge in imports, particularly of electronics, computers, components, and equipment, Ms. Trinh Thi Thu Hien, Deputy Director of the Import-Export Department, stated that the data shows that these imported goods and essential inputs reflect the need to expand production, increase investment, and prepare for future growth, not an increase in imports of non-essential consumer goods.
Firstly, raw material prices have surged: Contract prices for some high-end memory chips used in premium mobile phones and tablets have increased by more than 300% year-on-year due to a global shortage of mobile device memory chips driven by the surge in artificial intelligence infrastructure. While import volume may not have increased year-on-year, the 300% increase in value means the import figures reflect a significant trade deficit. Although the volume of raw material imports and finished product exports haven't changed much, the increase in import value indicates a decrease in the trade deficit or surplus.
Secondly, businesses are increasing inventory to prepare for production: Businesses are increasing inventory (some factories have increased it from 3-6 weeks to about 12 weeks) due to the continuous rise in import prices of raw materials for the electronics industry; in addition, some items are subject to control policies of the exporting country, so they need to be stockpiled.
Thirdly, factory expansion and capacity increase in Vietnam: Several investment projects to expand and shift technology in this field have been implemented. Many new investment projects, including those in chip testing and AI, have been launched (Samsung reinvested in a new factory in Thai Nguyen with an initial scale of $1.5 billion; Intel moved its chip production line from Costa Rica to Vietnam; BYD Vietnam Electronics Factory (Hong Kong, China ) increased investment in Phu Tho province; Accton (Intel's partner) increased investment in Phu Tho; LG, Quanta, and Foxconn also increased their investment capital...).
" These factors have contributed to the high import figures in the recent period ," said the Deputy Director of the Import-Export Department.

Focus on four key solution groups to boost exports and control the trade deficit.
In the context of a volatile global economy , the increasing trend of trade protection measures, and intensifying competition, maintaining export growth while controlling the trade deficit at a reasonable level remains a task that requires close monitoring and management.
Regarding solutions to boost exports and control the trade deficit, Ms. Trinh Thi Thu Hien stated that, in implementing Notice No. 443/TB-VPCP of the Government Office dated August 20, 2026, on the conclusions of the Standing Deputy Prime Minister at the meeting on promoting exports and controlling the trade deficit, as well as Notice No. 481/TB-VPCP of the Government Office dated September 14, 2026, on the conclusions of the Standing Deputy Prime Minister at the working session with the Vietnam Electronics Business Association and a number of large import-export enterprises in the semiconductor industry, the Ministry of Industry and Trade will focus on four key groups of solutions in the coming period.
Firstly , proactively manage imports in an efficient and sustainable manner.
Secondly , continue to drive export growth by exploring and expanding export markets.
Thirdly , we will continue to support businesses in enhancing their competitiveness. The Ministry will coordinate efforts to remove obstacles and effectively implement decentralization and delegation of authority in the import and export sector, thereby reducing costs, shortening processing times, and creating more favorable conditions for businesses' production and operations. We will also provide information on import market regulations, and offer early warnings of technical barriers and trade defense measures.
" Government Resolution No. 01/NQ-CP sets a target of approximately 15-16% growth in export turnover. Unless there are significant negative developments, exports will meet the annual target because the end of the year is the peak season for exports ," said Ms. Trinh Thi Thu Hien.
According to data released by the General Statistics Office on October 3rd, in September 2026, the total value of goods exports and imports reached US$117.69 billion, an increase of 7.3% compared to the previous month and a 42.4% increase compared to the same period last year. The trade balance for goods in September returned to a surplus after nine consecutive months of deficits, with a surplus of US$1.27 billion.
Overall, in the first nine months of 2026, total merchandise exports and imports reached US$888.02 billion, an increase of 30.4% compared to the same period last year, with exports increasing by 24.5% and imports increasing by 36.7%. The trade balance for the nine months showed a deficit of US$19.42 billion.

Regarding imports, the value of goods imported in September 2026 reached US$58.21 billion, an increase of 6.0% compared to the previous month. Of this, the domestic economic sector accounted for US$13.14 billion, an increase of 2.5%; and the foreign-invested sector accounted for US$45.07 billion, an increase of 7.1%. Compared to the same period last year, the value of goods imported in September increased by 45.8%, with the domestic economic sector increasing by 22.1% and the foreign-invested sector increasing by 54.6%.
In the third quarter of 2026, import turnover reached US$170.33 billion, an increase of 42.2% compared to the same period last year and an increase of 8.8% compared to the second quarter of 2026.
Overall, in the first nine months of 2026, merchandise imports reached US$453.72 billion, an increase of 36.7% compared to the same period last year. Of this, the domestic economic sector accounted for US$118.17 billion, an increase of 23.5%; and the foreign-invested sector accounted for US$335.55 billion, an increase of 42.0%.
Regarding the structure of import groups in the first nine months of 2026, the production materials group reached US$426.92 billion, accounting for 94.1%, of which machinery, equipment, tools and spare parts accounted for 58.3%; raw materials, fuels and materials accounted for 35.8%. articles.title: CHR urges stronger Asean action on Myanmar crisis - Inquirer.net
articles.summary: CHR urges stronger Asean action on Myanmar crisis  Inquirer.net
articles.full_text:
MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) is calling for stronger regional efforts to protect civilians and deliver humanitarian aid in Myanmar, with the Philippines serving as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) this year.
The appeal came as the Philippine rights body renewed its concern over the worsening humanitarian and human rights situation in Myanmar, more than five years after the military coup in February 2021.
The CHR said armed conflict, attacks affecting civilians, displacement and restrictions on fundamental freedoms continue to threaten communities in the country. It said the scale of casualties and displacement also points to the need for stronger measures to protect civilians and hold violators accountable.
Reports of restrictions on humanitarian assistance and attacks involving civilians and humanitarian responders have further complicated the situation, according to the commission.
“The CHR stresses that humanitarian assistance must reach affected communities safely and without undue obstruction,” it said.
READ: Myanmar marks bitter 5-year anniversary of 2021 coup
The commission also drew attention to the situation of workers in Myanmar, citing continuing concerns over freedom of association and forced labor.
It noted that the International Labour Conference adopted a resolution in June 2025 under Article 33 of the International Labour Organization Constitution concerning Myanmar’s compliance with the Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise Convention, 1948, and the Forced Labour Convention, 1930.
The CHR said the ILO has continued to call for an end to violence, arbitrary arrest, detention and torture while pressing for the protection of freedom of association and the elimination of forced labor.
Women and other vulnerable groups have also been disproportionately exposed to the consequences of the crisis, the commission said.
On Aug. 3, 2026, the CHR and civil society partners held a forum examining the humanitarian situation in Myanmar and regional accountability efforts through the Women, Peace and Security framework.
The discussions included the experiences of affected communities and risks faced by women, including gender-based and sexual violence.
The forum also emphasized the need for affected communities to have their experiences and perspectives reflected in regional responses to the crisis.
The CHR said Asean and its member states can play an important role in strengthening civilian protection, facilitating humanitarian assistance and supporting accountability as the crisis continues.
It also stressed the importance of credible and independent national human rights institutions in the region.
The commission noted that the South East Asia National Human Rights Institutions Forum is conducting a formal review of the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission’s continued eligibility for membership.
The review concerns its independence, effectiveness and institutional integrity under standards reflected in the Paris Principles.
“The CHR respects the integrity of this ongoing process and the opportunity afforded to MNHRC to respond before any determination is made,” the commission said.
“The CHR stresses that regional and international responses to the crisis in Myanmar must remain anchored in the protection of human rights, respect for international humanitarian law, accountability for serious violations, and the meaningful participation of affected communities,” it added.
Beyond regional mechanisms, the CHR also emphasized the need to continue gathering and verifying information on alleged human rights violations in Myanmar.
“Independent monitoring and documentation remain essential to establishing accountability and enabling victims and their families to pursue truth, justice, and effective remedies,” it said.
The commission also urged sustained international efforts to ensure that life-saving humanitarian assistance reaches people in need without obstruction.
It said cooperation among the United Nations, Asean, national human rights institutions, civil society organizations and other stakeholders should strengthen civilian protection and accountability.
For the CHR, responses to the Myanmar crisis should remain grounded in human rights, international humanitarian law and the participation of communities directly affected by the conflict.
“The CHR stands with the people of Myanmar in their aspiration for a future founded on human rights, peace, accountability, and democratic governance,” it said. /dm

articles.summary: Indonesia aims to boost manufacturing GDP share past 20 percent  ANTARA News
articles.full_text:
Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesian Industry Minister Muhammad Sarmuji aims to boost manufacturing's contribution to gross domestic product (GDP) to between 20 and 25 percent to drive national economic growth.
The statement came ahead of the two-year mark of the Prabowo Subianto–Gibran Rakabuming Raka administration on Oct. 20.
Speaking in Jakarta on Thursday, Sarmuji said the industrial sector must outpace overall economic growth, given its role as a key economic driver.
"The industrial sector should not lag behind or merely keep pace with our economic growth. We are actively looking for ways, truly looking for ways, to get this sector growing even faster," Sarmuji said.
He noted that industry currently contributes around 19 percent to GDP, with the government aiming to gradually raise that share past 20 percent toward a broader target of 21 to 25 percent.
The minister emphasized that raising this contribution is essential to ensure manufacturing continues driving national economic growth.
"We must not let our industry fade before reaching its peak. It's true that in developed countries, industry slows down and may decline," he said.
This occurs because mature economies shift focus, not because the sector itself is inherently weak, Sarmuji explained.
He noted that setting contribution targets requires evaluating the overall state of domestic manufacturing.
He stressed that the government plays a vital role in creating a supportive ecosystem that enables business players to run and expand operations.
Manufacturing growth has remained positive over the past three years, expanding 4.64 percent in 2023 and 4.43 percent in 2024, before climbing to 5.30 percent in 2025.
According to Statistics Indonesia (BPS), manufacturing was the largest single contributor to national GDP in 2025, accounting for 19.07 percent.

articles.title: Indonesia considers moratorium on semi-finished nickel smelters to curb global oversupply - streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.summary: Indonesia considers moratorium on semi-finished nickel smelters to curb global oversupply  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
Targeting the oversupply crisis
The Indonesian government is actively considering a moratorium on the construction of new smelters that produce semi-finished nickel products, a strategic move aimed at addressing a severe global oversupply that has depressed prices and threatened the profitability of the nation's downstreaming program. Coordinating Minister for Downstreaming and Energy Transition Bahlil Lahadalia confirmed that the administration is reviewing policies to limit the expansion of facilities producing nickel pig iron (NPI) and ferronickel, which are classified as class-2 nickel products.
Indonesia, the world's largest nickel producer, has aggressively expanded its smelting capacity over the past decade following a ban on the export of raw nickel ore. The policy was designed to force foreign and domestic investors to build processing facilities onshore, thereby capturing more value from the country's mineral resources. However, the rapid proliferation of these smelters, largely backed by foreign capital, has led to a glut in the global market for intermediate nickel products.
Shifting focus to EV battery materials
The proposed moratorium reflects a critical pivot in Jakarta's industrial strategy. While the initial phase of downstreaming successfully established Indonesia as a dominant player in the stainless steel supply chain, the government now views class-2 nickel as a low-value commodity with diminishing returns. The true economic prize lies in the electric vehicle (EV) battery supply chain, which requires class-1 nickel products such as nickel sulfate, mixed hydroxide precipitate (MHP), and high-pressure acid leach (HPAL) outputs.
By restricting new investments in semi-finished smelters, the government intends to redirect capital toward these higher-value processing facilities. Bahlil Lahadalia has emphasized that the current oversupply not only hurts Indonesian miners and smelters but also undermines the country's leverage in global trade negotiations. Stabilizing prices through controlled supply is seen as essential to maintaining the long-term viability of the nickel sector.
Environmental and resource constraints
Beyond market economics, the moratorium is also driven by concerns over the rapid depletion of Indonesia's high-grade nickel reserves and the environmental impact of unchecked smelter expansion. The proliferation of coal-powered captive power plants to feed the energy-intensive RKEF (Rotary Kiln Electric Furnace) smelters has drawn criticism from environmental groups and international trade partners, particularly the European Union and the United States, which are increasingly demanding low-carbon minerals for their green energy transitions.
State-owned enterprises, including the Indonesia Battery Corporation (IBC) and MIND ID, have echoed the call for a more measured approach to smelter licensing. Industry stakeholders argue that without a moratorium, the continued dumping of cheap Indonesian NPI into global markets could trigger further trade disputes and anti-dumping duties, isolating Indonesian products from key Western markets.
Investor reactions and regulatory certainty
The prospect of a moratorium has generated mixed reactions from the investment community. While established players in the EV battery supply chain welcome the shift toward higher-value products, investors who have already committed capital to RKEF smelter projects face significant regulatory uncertainty. The government has assured that existing projects under construction will likely be allowed to proceed, but new licensing for semi-finished facilities will be frozen pending a comprehensive review of national smelter capacity and global demand forecasts.
Legal experts note that implementing a formal moratorium requires careful coordination across multiple ministries, including the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources, the Ministry of Industry, and the Investment Coordinating Board (BKPM). The government must ensure that any freeze on permits complies with existing investment treaties and does not expose the state to international arbitration claims from foreign investors.
Global market implications
The ripple effects of Indonesia's supply management strategy are already being felt in global commodity markets. Analysts note that a sustained reduction in Indonesian NPI exports could force stainless steel producers in China and India to seek alternative sources or accelerate the adoption of scrap-based production methods. This shift could inadvertently benefit nickel producers in jurisdictions like the Philippines and Australia, provided they can scale their operations to meet the displaced demand.
Securing the downstreaming legacy
For the Indonesian administration, the downstreaming policy remains a cornerstone of its economic agenda, credited with significantly boosting export revenues and transforming the nation's trade balance. However, the transition from volume-driven growth to value-driven industrialization requires precise policy calibration. The proposed moratorium on semi-finished nickel smelters represents a necessary correction to ensure that Indonesia's finite mineral wealth is leveraged for maximum long-term economic benefit rather than short-term market saturation.
As the government finalizes the regulatory framework for the moratorium, global markets will be watching closely. The decision will not only dictate the future of Indonesia's mining sector but also influence the global pricing and supply dynamics of the critical minerals required for the worldwide transition to electric mobility.

articles.title: The link between FDI enterprises and Vietnamese enterprises goes beyond just buyer-seller relationships. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The link between FDI enterprises and Vietnamese enterprises goes beyond just buyer-seller relationships.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On October 8, 2026, in Hanoi, the Finance and Investment Newspaper organized a seminar titled "Connecting Vietnamese Businesses in the Global Supply Chain," aiming to widely disseminate the implementation of Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW of the Politburo , as well as Resolution No. 280/NQ-CP of the Government.
Strengthening linkages between the domestic economic sector and the FDI sector.
According to Deputy Minister of Finance Tran Quoc Phuong, the Vietnamese economy is in the final stretch to achieve its 2026 targets. In the third quarter and the first nine months of the year, Vietnam's GDP growth is estimated at 9.95% and 9.01% respectively, the highest in many years.
Against the backdrop of a generally positive economic picture, attracting foreign investment is a bright spot. In the first nine months of 2026, total registered foreign investment in Vietnam reached US$50.36 billion, a 76.4% increase compared to the same period last year, while implemented foreign investment reached US$21.07 billion, a 12.1% increase compared to the same period last year, the highest in the past five years. This figure brings the total FDI attracted to Vietnam over the past nearly 40 years to over US$570 billion, a remarkable achievement reflecting the confidence of foreign investors in the investment and business environment and the growth potential of the Vietnamese economy.
Foreign investment in Vietnam has not only increased rapidly in quantity but has also significantly improved in quality recently. Vietnam has attracted many large-scale FDI projects in the fields of electronics, semiconductors, digital transformation , artificial intelligence, etc. This has affirmed Vietnam's increasingly important role in the global semiconductor supply chain and high-tech manufacturing.
However, the reality of nearly 40 years of attracting FDI shows that although the foreign-invested economic sector has continuously developed, not only supplementing important investment resources but also contributing to promoting economic restructuring, innovating growth models, forming several key industries, expanding export markets, and gradually integrating Vietnam deeper into global production networks and value chains, the quality and effectiveness of attracting, managing, and utilizing FDI capital have not been commensurate with the potential and advantages, and have not met the development requirements of the country in its new phase. In particular, the linkages between the domestic and FDI sectors remain limited, and technology transfer, research, and development have not met expectations. The percentage of Vietnamese enterprises participating in global supply chains is still not high…
Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026, on the development of the foreign-invested economy, marks a strategic turning point, comprehensively changing the methods and thinking of attracting foreign investment in Vietnam in the new phase. Instead of focusing solely on the number of projects and investment capital, Vietnam will prioritize creating a high-quality FDI ecosystem, valuing quality, efficiency, added value for the economy, and the ability to integrate with the domestic sector. The strategic combination of Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW and Resolution 68-NQ/TW on the development of the private economy and Resolution 79-NQ/TW on the development of the state-owned economy can be said to create a solid "three-legged stool" for the Vietnamese economy to break through.
Deputy Minister Tran Quoc Phuong affirmed that the opportunities for Vietnam are immense. With a stable macroeconomic foundation, a safe political and social environment, and a wide network of free trade agreements, Vietnam has always been one of the safest and most attractive destinations for foreign investors.
The next chapter of FDI in Vietnam will move beyond cost advantages.
Mr. Kamijo Hiroki, Deputy General Director and Head of Transaction Banking and Foreign Investment at Vietnam Prosperity Commercial Bank ( VPBank ), affirmed that the next chapter of FDI growth in Vietnam needs to go beyond cost advantages and be built upon ecosystem advantages.
Mr. Kamijo Hiroki stated that, in the past, many investors chose Vietnam due to its competitive labor costs and favorable production environment. These strengths remain important, but they are not sufficient in isolation.
Currently, investors are asking broader questions. Can Vietnam support complex and resilient supply chains? Can treasury operations be managed with high speed and full transparency? Is there sufficient human resources for advanced industries? Can commitments to sustainable development be implemented within the domestic market? And can the ecosystem support long-term expansion?
These expectations highlight five interdependent capabilities: supply chains and infrastructure; technology and digital capabilities; talent and innovation; sustainable development and green growth; and integration through global partnerships.
Therefore, the model is shifting from cost-based growth to a connected ecosystem model. Success will depend not only on the ability to attract investment, but also on the ability to support investors in operating efficiently, expanding with confidence, and building deeper connections with Vietnamese businesses.
Mr. Kamijo Hiroki argues that sustainable growth requires the participation of six stakeholders: the government , Vietnamese businesses, foreign investors, industry associations, universities, and financial institutions. However, the value of the ecosystem is not simply created by bringing these entities together at the same table. The true value comes from the way in which these parties cooperate with each other.
This roadmap comprises four practical steps. It's a roadmap from connection to implementation: agreeing on common priorities, connecting complementary capabilities, mobilizing capital and expertise, and scaling up solutions to build stronger value chains and drive long-term growth.
A representative from VPBank affirmed that the next chapter of FDI growth in Vietnam will not only be built on cost advantages, but also on the strength of the ecosystem. This is an ecosystem where capital, capabilities, talent, sustainable development, and partnerships mutually reinforce and strengthen each other.
According to Mr. Cha Ji Ho, Deputy General Director in charge of the Purchasing Center at Samsung Vietnam, to enhance the participation of Vietnamese businesses in the supply chain, Samsung is shifting its focus from supporting improved production capacity to developing deeper expertise and building a supplier ecosystem in Vietnam.
Mr. Cha Ji Ho stated that in the coming period, Samsung aims to expand its support scope regionally, increase the number of participating businesses, and enhance the depth of its capabilities.
The program will be expanded from areas such as Bac Ninh and Ho Chi Minh City to Phu Tho, Hai Phong, and Thai Nguyen, while strengthening cooperation with local suppliers. Samsung also focuses on developing a workforce with practical skills within the company, capable of independently solving problems, utilizing data, and maintaining innovation.
Notably, Samsung proposed promoting systematic cooperation between the Government, Samsung, and Vietnamese businesses, based on a supplier database, clear policies, and support framework.
The goal is to increase the localization rate, expand access to the supply chain, and enhance the competitiveness of domestic manufacturing businesses. Samsung also proposed publishing an annual "Supplier Development White Paper," thereby creating a mechanism for cooperation and monitoring the long-term progress of the supply chain.
Following this direction, the linkage between FDI enterprises and Vietnamese enterprises will not only stop at the buyer-seller relationship, but will aim for joint development, building sustainable partnerships, and enhancing the competitiveness of the entire production ecosystem in Vietnam.

articles.title: Malaysia hosts Myanmar junta leader as repatriations top 10,000 amid rights outcry - streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.summary: Malaysia hosts Myanmar junta leader as repatriations top 10,000 amid rights outcry  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
Malaysia and Myanmar have pledged to deepen bilateral cooperation across trade, energy, and education sectors, as Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim prepares to host Myanmar's military leader Min Aung Hlaing in Kuala Lumpur. The high-stakes diplomatic engagement comes amidst intense scrutiny from human rights organizations over Malaysia's deportation of thousands of Myanmar nationals.
The bilateral talks mark a significant shift in regional diplomacy, signaling Kuala Lumpur's willingness to engage directly with the State Administration Council despite widespread international condemnation of the junta that seized power in a 2021 coup. The discussions are expected to focus on people-centric cooperation, including expanding cross-border investment and addressing energy security, reflecting Malaysia's pragmatic approach to managing its relationship with a volatile neighbor.
A Controversial Diplomatic Engagement
The impending visit of Min Aung Hlaing represents a delicate balancing act for the Malaysian government. While ASEAN officially maintains a consensus barring the Myanmar junta's political leadership from high-level summits, bilateral state visits operate outside the bloc's formal multilateral restrictions. For Anwar, hosting the Myanmar commander-in-chief is framed as a necessary diplomatic channel to address pressing bilateral issues, particularly the status of migrant workers and regional security.
Malaysia relies heavily on foreign labor to sustain its manufacturing, plantation, and construction sectors, with Myanmar nationals forming a substantial portion of this workforce. However, the political instability and escalating civil war in Myanmar have triggered a massive exodus, complicating immigration enforcement and labor management in Malaysia. By bringing the junta leadership to the negotiating table, Kuala Lumpur aims to formalize labor agreements and streamline the management of undocumented migrants.
The Repatriation Controversy
Shadowing the diplomatic summit is a deeply contentious repatriation program. According to official figures, Malaysia has repatriated over 10,000 Myanmar nationals in 2026. The government maintains that these individuals were undocumented migrants or immigration offenders who voluntarily opted to return home, explicitly stating that no Rohingya refugees have been included in the deportation lists.
Human rights monitors, however, have fiercely condemned the practice. Organizations such as Fortify Rights have urged the Malaysian government to immediately suspend all returns and cancel Min Aung Hlaing's visit. Advocates argue that the volatile security situation in Myanmar, characterized by widespread forced conscription, arbitrary detention, and active armed conflict, makes any repatriation inherently unsafe. Rights groups contend that the distinction between "undocumented migrants" and asylum seekers is frequently blurred in immigration detention centers, raising severe non-refoulement concerns.
In response to mounting criticism, Malaysian officials have reiterated that the deportations are conducted in strict accordance with domestic immigration laws and bilateral agreements with the Myanmar embassy. The government argues that managing the overflow of undocumented migrants is a sovereign necessity, especially as post-pandemic economic recovery demands a regulated labor market.
ASEAN's Fractured Stance
The bilateral engagement also highlights the deepening fractures within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations regarding the Myanmar crisis. Since the 2021 military takeover, ASEAN has struggled to enforce its Five-Point Consensus, which demanded an immediate cessation of violence and inclusive dialogue. The bloc's decision to exclude junta leaders from top-tier summits was intended to pressure the military into compliance, but the lack of tangible progress has led to diplomatic fatigue among member states.
Malaysia's decision to host Min Aung Hlaing bilaterally suggests a growing belief within parts of the ASEAN leadership that isolation has failed to alter the junta's behavior. Proponents of engagement argue that maintaining direct communication channels is more effective than diplomatic boycotts, particularly when dealing with urgent transnational issues such as cross-border crime, narcotics trafficking, and migrant labor flows.
Economic and Strategic Calculus
Beyond the immediate labor disputes, the pledge to enhance cooperation in energy and trade points to broader strategic interests. Myanmar possesses significant untapped natural gas reserves and critical geographic positioning along the Bay of Bengal, making it a relevant player in regional energy grids and maritime logistics. For Malaysia, a major energy hub, securing stable regional energy partnerships is a long-term economic imperative.
As the summit approaches, the international community and regional civil society groups continue to monitor the situation closely. The outcome of the Anwar-Min Aung Hlaing talks will likely set a precedent for how ASEAN nations navigate the complex intersection of domestic labor needs, human rights obligations, and the grim realities of engaging with an entrenched military regime.

articles.title: Vietnam's banks tap investors for US$7 bil as economy runs red hot - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: Vietnam's banks tap investors for US$7 bil as economy runs red hot  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
HANOI (Oct 7): Vietnamese banks are planning nearly US$7 billion in share sales as the country's fast-growing economy fuels demand for capital, opening a window for foreign investors to expand in the tightly controlled sector.
Communist-run Vietnam, which reported growth of nearly 10% in the last quarter, has one of Asia's fastest-growing banking industries but access has been restricted, with cumulative foreign ownership capped at 30%, individual stakes limited to 20% and offshore borrowing subject to strict limits.
But in recent months, top leader To Lam's drive to turbocharge economic growth with major infrastructure spending has ushered in a more open approach, as policymakers view larger foreign participation as necessary to meet growing credit demand amid a domestic funding squeeze.
As a result, bank share sales could raise nearly US$7 billion by the end of next year, according to Reuters calculations based on public disclosures and a Fitch Ratings report, which noted that this was likely Vietnam's largest-ever wave of capital raisings by lenders.
The ceiling on offshore borrowing was also raised this year by 11% to US$6.1 billion and it could rise further. Three local lenders have been allowed to increase their foreign ownership limits to 49%, while stock-market reforms secured Vietnam's upgrade to emerging status by index provider FTSE Russell last month. Separate plans to set up international financial centres also promise more foreign capital inflows.
A couple of foreign lenders involved in equity talks with Vietnamese partners cited gains on their financial investments and greater access to the country's growing consumer market for products like insurance as reasons to expand there, according to two people familiar with the discussions who requested anonymity because the matter was private.
Vietnam is allowing more foreign capital into its banks as "it is beginning to rethink how its next phase of growth will be financed," said Quynh Nguyen, a finance lecturer at Hoa Sen University in Ho Chi Minh City. She cautioned, however, that the move was selective and did not amount to a wholesale liberalisation.
The share offers have increased foreign interest, "particularly from strategic investors who are already familiar with Vietnam and are now considering deeper exposure," Quynh said.
Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp (SMBC) is in talks with Vietnamese partner VPBank to raise its stake to 20% from 15% as VPBank seeks a private placement worth US$560 million at current market prices, Reuters reported in September. VPBank is allowed to raise its foreign ownership cap to 49%.
Vietcombank, the country's largest lender, has also unveiled plans to sell 6.5% of its shares by the end of this year in a transaction worth around US$1.2 billion at current prices. Japan's Mizuho Bank, its current largest foreign investor with a 15% stake, "may potentially increase its holding," according to minutes from a Vietcombank shareholder meeting in April. Mizuho declined to comment.
BIDV, Vietnam's second-largest lender, sold roughly 3% of its shares to dozens of investors in March and intends to sell almost another 11% by the end of next year for a total value of approximately US$1.4 billion, according to public disclosures.
Its top foreign shareholder, South Korea's KEB Hana, did not participate in the first placement but is considering whether to participate in the new plan, a spokesperson said.
"We see some opportunities among the smaller banks to score some tie-ups down the line, provided Vietnam can maintain its growth story," Fitch's Willie Tanoto said.
HDBank HDB.HM has said it plans to sell a 10.7% stake by the end of next year. The private bank — linked to Vietnam's largest private airline Vietjet — does not have a large foreign investor and is allowed to raise its foreign ownership to 49%.
Separately, Techcombank, one of the country's largest private lenders, has discussed a stake sale with foreign lenders, Reuters reported in August.
Meanwhile, Vietnamese banks and corporations disclosed offshore borrowing plans for an aggregate value of US$5.3 billion this year, according to FiinRatings, an S&P Global partner.
The finance ministry is also considering an offshore sovereign bond sale that would be the country's first since 2014. Banks are also weighing offshore bonds while large municipalities may be able to tap international capital markets with debt offerings under new rules.
The equity sales have been driven by the need to bolster capital as Vietnam transitions to stricter global Basel III requirements by 2030. The need has become pressing because of rapid loan growth, which Moody's-backed VIS Rating said could further deteriorate loss-absorption buffers.
The government's push for annual economic growth of at least 10% through 2030 is also fuelling the inflation of asset prices, particularly in the real estate sector, which accounts for roughly a quarter of all loans and where bad debts are rising quickly, according to an August internal report from the central bank.
Fitch said the capital-raising drive "is unlikely to materially improve most banks' capitalisation" because the fresh funds will be rapidly deployed into new lending.
Yet those risks may also create new opportunities as "further large capital injections are likely to be needed in the coming years," Fitch said.
