articles.title: Malaysia PM says he will do whatever possible to ensure Myanmar’s acceptance in regional community - 104.1 WIKY
articles.summary: Malaysia PM says he will do whatever possible to ensure Myanmar’s acceptance in regional community  104.1 WIKY
articles.full_text:
By Rozanna Latiff and Hasnoor Hussain
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 8 (Reuters) – Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Thursday his government would do “whatever possible” to ensure Myanmar was re-integrated into the Southeast Asian bloc ASEAN, even as pro-democracy activists warned against legitimising the rule of its military-backed leader Min Aung Hlaing.
Anwar also pledged to continue working with Myanmar, including on the repatriation of thousands of Myanmar nationals from Malaysia – a move that has been widely criticised by the United Nations and rights groups concerned about the risks from an ongoing civil war.
Former Myanmar junta chief Min Aung Hlaing is on a two-day visit to Malaysia as he seeks greater international legitimacy after becoming president in April following an election that Western nations and rights groups widely criticised as a sham.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since 2021 when Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup against a democratically elected government, triggering armed conflict across much of the country.
Min Aung Hlaing and other senior Myanmar officials have been barred from attending summits of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) after failing to adhere to an ASEAN-brokered peace plan following the coup, but some member countries, including Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, have sought to re-establish ties.
Malaysia’s Anwar acknowledged ongoing concerns about democratic processes in Myanmar but said differences must be respected, adding that Min Aung Hlaing had shown a willingness to be collaborative.
“I would say that we and our part in Malaysia, will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration and ultimately, take Myanmar as part of our community of nations, without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN,” Anwar told a media briefing, following a meeting with Min Aung Hlaing.
MYANMAR TO SEND MORE NAVY SHIPS TO REPATRIATE ITS CITIZENS
Anwar also expressed appreciation to Min Aung Hlaing for accepting the repatriation of 10,493 Myanmar nationals from Malaysia so far.
Malaysia has said it can no longer take in refugees from Myanmar, saying they had become a financial burden and a security risk. Malaysia is not a party to the UN refugee convention and treats asylum-seekers as illegal migrants.
The country last month sent back around 1,500 people on Myanmar naval ships, part of a wider repatriation programme that could see as many as 5,000 people deported.
Min Aung Hlaing said at Thursday’s briefing Myanmar citizens currently held at Malaysian immigration detention centres would be brought back as soon as possible.
“Because the current weather is favourable, I will dispatch navy ships to repatriate them,” he said, adding that he would invite Anwar to visit Myanmar “when the time is right”.
Anwar and Min Aung Hlaing did not mention if their discussions included plans to repatriate Rohingya Muslim refugees, many of whom fled Myanmar after a brutal 2017 military crackdown in the country’s Rakhine state that is now the subject of a genocide case at the International Court of Justice.
Muslim-majority Malaysia widely criticised the crackdown at the time. But public sentiment has turned in recent years, with the Rohingya in Malaysia facing increasing harassment and scrutiny, amid a surge of online hate speech and misinformation.
Anwar has said he would push for Myanmar to accept Rohingya refugees.
As of February, Malaysia was hosting around 193,000 refugees and asylum seekers from Myanmar in Malaysia, about 65% of them Rohingya, according to UN data.
Buddhist-majority Myanmar does not recognise the Rohingya as one of its official ethnic groups and denies citizenship to most.
RESISTANCE GROUPS URGE ASEAN NOT TO LEGITIMISE MYANMAR LEADER
Min Aung Hlaing’s visit was met with protests by Myanmar’s pro-democracy activists and resistance groups, who urged ASEAN not to confer political legitimacy on his presidency.
“His legitimacy is a nightmare for the whole nation, for the people who have lost their lives, who have sacrificed their homes,” said Swam Saung, a member of the Myanmar Affairs Alliance, at a gathering in Kuala Lumpur.
He also expressed fear for Myanmar nationals being repatriated, saying they could face forced conscription given that the military remained in conflict with various ethnic armed groups.
“They are forcing their own people to fight against their own people. So this is horrifying,” he said.
The Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), an umbrella organisation that includes several major Myanmar armed ethnic groups and democratic bodies, said Malaysia had traditionally upheld principles of humanitarian values, democracy, and human rights during engagements on Myanmar within ASEAN.
“Receptive diplomatic hosting of Min Aung Hlaing at the head-of-state level stands in direct contradiction to these established principles,” it said in a statement.
(Reporting by Rozanna Latiff and Reuters staff; Additional reporting by Hasnoor Hussain and Ahmad Luqman Ismail; Editing by David Stanway, Kate Mayberry and Raju Gopalakrishnan)

articles.title: Myanmar's military-backed leader seeks closer ties on visit to Malaysia as he pivots to diplomacy - Newsday
articles.summary: Myanmar's military-backed leader seeks closer ties on visit to Malaysia as he pivots to diplomacy  Newsday
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia — Myanmar’s military-backed leader pressed on with his pivot to diplomacy on a visit to Malaysia, his first since becoming president earlier this year, holding talks Thursday with the country's prime minister and other officials in an effort to boost ties.
But the visit by Min Aung Hlaing, a former military chief inaugurated as president in April after a general election judged by rights groups as designed to cement the military’s hold on power, has not been free of criticism.
The Myanmar leader has also faced pressure from other members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the regional bloc known as ASEAN, to end the civil war in his country.
The visit comes just days after nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals were returned to Myanmar from Malaysia. The United Nations refugee agency and rights groups have slammed the repatriations, saying that the security and humanitarian situation in parts of Myanmar remains volatile, and returnees could face persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone.
Myanmar’s government is also seeking to restore international ties. Last month, the Trump administration sent a high-level delegation to Myanmar to help secure the release of American businessman Adam Castillo, who was subsequently freed and returned to the United States.
Myanmar’s state-run Global New Light of Myanmar suggested the decision was made to curry favor and maintain friendly relations with Washington.
After landing in Kuala Lumpur on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing sought to reassure Malaysian investors that Myanmar was on a path toward democracy and that his government was working to restore stability, state-run MRTV television reported in its evening news program.
Myanmar seeks to normalize ties with other ASEAN members
The visit was also Min Aung Hlaing’s fifth to a fellow ASEAN member. Critics and analysts say expanding bilateral engagement could gradually normalize his government’s regional standing — even as ASEAN blocks Myanmar from top-level meetings since the country's 2021 military takeover that triggered an armed resistance.
On Thursday, after an official welcome and honor guard, he met with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, who assured him that Kuala Lumpur wanted to strengthen cooperation with Myanmar while continuing to raise concerns over the lack of democratic reforms and ongoing violence.
“We will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration and ultimately take Myanmar as part of our community of nations without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN,” Anwar said.
Anwar said bilateral trade had increased by more than 140% year-on-year, while Min Aung Hlaing said Malaysia was Myanmar’s fourth-largest trading partner and ninth-largest investor.
“I firmly believe that enhancing our bilateral economic cooperation will bring highly practical economic benefits and joint opportunities for the people of both countries,” the Myanmar leader said.
Min Aung Hlaing earlier visited Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and Cambodia in attempts to rebuild regional ties that deteriorated after he ousted Aung San Suu Kyi’s government in February 2021 while serving as army chief.
Malaysia has stressed that inviting Min Aung Hlaing, who became president in April following a much-criticized election, does not amount to diplomatic recognition of Myanmar’s government.
Malaysia's red-carpet welcome is seen as a step forward for Myanmar
The high-profile reception awarded Min Aung Hlaing could help reposition him internationally, said Khoo Ying Hooi, an associate professor in international relations at University Malaya. But she warned that such engagements could weaken ASEAN's leverage to push Myanmar to end its conflict.
“There's a serious contradiction here,” she said. "ASEAN continues to demand progress to end the violence but their collective pressure is already weakened” with bilateral engagement focusing on economic cooperation.
Inside a Kuala Lumpur building on Thursday, a few dozen people gathered as rights groups held a protest against the visit.
“We do not want to see ASEAN nations help him gain his legitimacy,” said Swam Saung, of the Myanmar Affairs Alliance.
Repatriations to Myanmar are a thorny issue
Malaysia's prime minister has defended the repatriation policy, saying his country cannot host the undocumented foreign nationals indefinitely and that Myanmar must take responsibility for its citizens.
Anwar said 10,493 Myanmar citizens have so far been returned from Malaysia to Myanmar on flights and naval ships this year, including nearly 1,500 who were returned last week — the first of some 5,000 people who have agreed to be repatriated in stages.
Min Aung Hlaing promised to expedite the process and send a naval vessel to Malaysia to assist with further repatriations. Malaysia says 11,804 Myanmar nationals are still held at detention facilities across Malaysia.
It's unclear if any of the returnees included minority Muslim Rohingya, who are facing persecution in Myanmar and have been denied citizenship.
Malaysia is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum-seekers registered with UNHCR, including about 126,000 Rohingya who make up one of Southeast Asia’s largest refugee communities. Despite hosting them, Malaysia isn’t a party to the U.N. Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants.
Rohingya have faced growing public hostility in Malaysia because of their increasing numbers, fueled by concerns over jobs, public services and security.

articles.title: Godrej Consumer Products Indonesia builds new Rp 500 billion factory in Kendal - The Jakarta Post
articles.summary: Godrej Consumer Products Indonesia builds new Rp 500 billion factory in Kendal  The Jakarta Post
articles.full_text:
The first phase of the facility occupies 2.5 hectares of GCPI’s total 5.5-ha site in Kendal, serving as a manufacturing hub for household insecticides for both Indonesian and export markets.
T Godrej Consumer Products Indonesia (GCPI) has constructed a new manufacturing facility in the Kendal Industrial Park, Kendal regency, Central Java, with an investment value of Rp 500 billion. The new plant represents the next phase of the company's production capacity expansion in Indonesia; Godrej previously operated a manufacturing facility in Bogor.
This investment marks the continuation of GCPI’s journey in Indonesia. Since its acquisition in 2010, GCPI’s business has grown approximately 4.5-fold. Brands such as HIT, Stella, Mitu and NYU are present in one out of every four Indonesian households.
The first phase of the facility occupies 2.5 hectares of GCPI’s total 5.5-ha site in Kendal and is dedicated to household insecticide products. The facility will serve as a manufacturing hub for household insecticides, meeting Indonesian market demand while also supporting export markets.
The inauguration ceremony was attended by the Indian Ambassador to Indonesia Sandeep Chakravorty, representatives of the Governor of Central Java and the Regent of Kendal, and representatives from the Investment and Downstreaming Ministry/BKPM, alongside stakeholders, partners and senior leadership from global and Indonesian divisions of Godrej Consumer Products.
Aasif Malbari, managing director & CEO of Godrej Consumer Products Limited, explained, "This new facility in Kendal marks a major step for Godrej in meeting the evolving needs of Indonesian consumers and we do not shy away from investing in Indonesia."
The additional production capacity is expected to support Godrej’s long-term growth ambitions in Indonesia. The company targets long-term sales volume growth that outpaces the growth of the gross domestic product (GDP).
Meanwhile, Rajesh Sethuraman, business head for Indonesia and global head for business transformation and digital at Godrej Consumer Products Limited, stated that the construction of this new factory aims not only to meet domestic market demand but also to capture opportunities for expansion into international markets.
"We chose the Kendal location due to its strategic position on Java—one of Indonesia's largest centers of demand—and its proximity to the port. Godrej sells its products in around 85 countries, so export destinations depend on where the demand arises," he said.
Regarding the workforce, the Kendal facility will begin operations with approximately 120 employees, with a target to gradually increase this number to around 500 as production scales up.
"We remain optimistic about the prospects for the consumer goods business in Indonesia, amidst the prevailing domestic and global economic climate. This is because the demand for daily necessities tends to be relatively resilient to changing economic conditions," he stated.
Beyond strengthening manufacturing capacity, the Kendal facility reflects GCPI’s investment in people and responsible operations. Its focus encompasses developing local capabilities, creating more inclusive employment opportunities, and ensuring resource efficiency in operational activities.
“The way we grow is just as important as the growth itself. In Kendal, inclusion has been part of the work environment from the very beginning. We are targeting a workforce that is 50 percent female, while also opening up meaningful employment opportunities for people with disabilities,” said Vaibhav Ram, global head of human resources at Godrej Consumer Products Limited.
These same principles are applied to the facility's operations, ranging from resource efficiency and energy monitoring to biodiversity and waste management.
"We want to ensure that inclusion and responsibility are integral to the way we conduct business every day," he stated.
Meanwhile, Ambassador Chakravorty highlighted how "India and Indonesia share deep-rooted historical and cultural ties, alongside immense potential to build an equally strong economic partnership. Godrej, one of India’s leading companies, has been present in Indonesia since 2010."
He noted that Godrej products have become a part of the daily lives of Indonesian consumers thanks to their quality and affordability.
"The Kendal plant stands as a tangible manifestation of this partnership. It will serve both the Indonesian market and export destinations, while strengthening the links between investment, manufacturing, and trade. We hope to see more Indian and Indonesian companies investing, growing, and creating shared value," said Sandeep. (*)

articles.title: Việt Nam, Laos strengthen “strategic cohesion” in economic sector - vietnamnews.vn
articles.summary: Việt Nam, Laos strengthen “strategic cohesion” in economic sector  vietnamnews.vn
articles.full_text:
| Vietnamese Prime Minister Lê Minh Hưng and Lao Prime Minister Saleumxay Kommasith witness the exchange of investment cooperation agreements between businesses of the two countries. — VNA/VNS Photo | 
VIENTIANE — Prime Minister Lê Minh Hưng and his Lao counterpart Saleumxay Kommasith attended and delivered remarks at the Việt Nam-Laos Investment Promotion Conference in Vientiane on the afternoon of October 8 as part of the Vietnamese leader’s official visit to Laos.
The conference was attended by leaders of ministries, sectors and localities, as well as a large number of representatives from businesses and investors of both countries.
At the event, delegates introduced Laos's investment environment and policies; reviewed Việt Nam-Laos investment cooperation and orientations for the coming period; assessed the investment and business cooperation potential of enterprises from both countries; and put forward proposals and recommendations to address difficulties and obstacles facing businesses.
They also discussed measures to promote specific cooperation projects, particularly in such fields as minerals, rubber, energy, railways, roads, seaports and other areas.
According to reports presented at the event, two-way trade between Việt Nam and Laos reached nearly US$3 billion in 2025, up 32.7 per cent year-on-year and the highest level ever recorded.
Laos continued to be Việt Nam's largest destination for outward investment, with more than 300 projects and total registered capital of over $7 billion. In the first nine months of 2026 alone, 24 new projects were licensed with total investment capital of $670 million, 1.7 times higher than the figure recorded in the same period of 2025.
The two sides are promoting strategic infrastructure connectivity projects, including the Hà Nội-Vientiane expressway, the Vientiane-Vũng Áng Railway, Vũng Áng Port, energy infrastructure and electricity cooperation.
Việt Nam is accelerating construction and shortening the implementation time to complete the Vinh-Thanh Thủy Expressway ahead of schedule. Projects invested in by Vietnamese enterprises have created jobs and increased incomes for hundreds of thousands of Lao workers, while contributing an average of around $300 million annually to the Lao state budget.
Speaking at the conference, the two PMs highly appreciated the successful organisation of the event as the two countries are actively preparing to celebrate the 65th anniversary of diplomatic relations (1962-2027) and the 50th anniversary of the signing of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation (1977-2027).
They emphasised that this is an important occasion to concretise agreements reached by the high-ranking leaders of the two countries, particularly the goal of raising two-way trade to $10 billion by 2030, while discussing solutions to deepen investment cooperation during the 2026-2030 period in a substantive and effective manner.
While acknowledging and highly appreciating the achievements made, the leaders frankly noted that economic cooperation between the two countries still faces limitations. Some projects remain behind schedule, while investment procedures, land issues, payments and infrastructure connectivity continue to face obstacles, as reflected by businesses. Two-way trade in the first eight months of 2026 reached only around $1.65 billion.
Sharing information on Việt Nam's socio-economic situation, PM Hưng said that as Việt Nam enters a new era of development, the country is determined to strongly renew its growth model, with science and technology, innovation and digital transformation, human-resource quality, productivity and competitiveness serving as the key drivers. Việt Nam aims to achieve double-digit growth during the 2026-2030 period and become a developed, high-income country by 2045.
Việt Nam has issued and is resolutely implementing a number of breakthrough resolutions on science and technology and digital transformation; international integration; law-making and law enforcement; development of the private economic sector, the state economic sector and the foreign-invested sector; energy security; education and training; culture; and people's healthcare.
Despite continued global volatility, Việt Nam's macroeconomy has remained basically stable, inflation has been controlled, high economic growth has been maintained, and major economic balances have been ensured. In particular, GDP growth in the first nine months of 2026 reached more than 9.01 per cent, the highest level in many years.
Total import-export turnover reached $888 billion, up 30.4 per cent year-on-year; registered foreign direct investment (FDI) capital reached $50.36 billion, up 76.4 per cent, while disbursed FDI hit $21.07 billion, up 12.1 per cent. articles.title: Thailand struggles economically even with revised World Bank GDP growth for 2026 coming in at 2% for 2026 - Thai Examiner
articles.summary: Thailand struggles economically even with revised World Bank GDP growth for 2026 coming in at 2% for 2026  Thai Examiner
articles.full_text:
The kingdom’s fiscal 2025 accounts expose a ฿898.8 billion deficit as spending surges and tax collections disappoint. The World Bank lifts 2026 growth to just 2%, against Vietnam’s 7.4%. Meanwhile, the IMF warns of debt, energy shocks and AI risks.
Thailand’s final fiscal 2025 accounts expose a staggering ฿898.8 billion deficit, up 20.6%, as the World Bank lifts its 2026 growth forecast to a meagre 2%. Government spending raced ahead of revenue, all three major tax departments missed targets, and public debt reached 65.08% of GDP, nearing the 70% ceiling. Meanwhile, the AI export boom offers limited relief as Vietnam races ahead with projected growth of 7.4%. Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanpraphas faces mounting fiscal pressure amid proposals for higher taxes, including VAT. Now, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva warns of soaring global debt, energy shocks and risks surrounding the AI boom. Thailand’s growth outlook has improved, but its public finances tell a far grimmer story.
The World Bank has upgraded Thailand’s economic growth forecast to a meagre 2% for 2026. However, the improvement comes amid weakening public finances, disappointing tax collections and rapidly rising government expenditure.
Final figures for fiscal 2025 show a budget deficit approaching ฿900 billion, up more than 20%. Excise receipts missed their target by almost 12%, while government spending increased more than six times faster than revenue. Meanwhile, public debt reached 65.08% of GDP, moving closer to the statutory 70% ceiling. The kingdom faces growing fiscal pressures despite stronger exports linked to the global artificial intelligence boom.
The World Bank announced its revised forecast on Tuesday, October 6. It raised Thailand’s projected GDP growth from 1.3% to 2%, an increase of 0.7 percentage points.
Thailand’s upgraded 2% growth forecast still leaves the kingdom far behind its regional neighbours
The improvement reflects stronger demand for electronics and high-technology products used in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Nevertheless, the kingdom remains among the region’s slowest-growing major economies. The bank also upgraded its East Asia and Pacific growth forecast from 4.2% to 4.5%.
In contrast, Vietnam received a larger upward revision of 1.1 percentage points, lifting projected growth to 7.4%. Malaysia’s forecast increased to 5.1%, while China is expected to expand by 4.4%.
Consequently, Thailand’s revised projection remains less than half the regional average. Vietnam is expected to grow more than three times as quickly. The figures highlight the widening differences in economic performance across Southeast Asia.
The World Bank attributed much of the regional improvement to rising international demand for AI-related products. These include electronics, semiconductors and computer components required for data centres and advanced computing infrastructure.
Notably, AI-related goods accounted for more than 70% of export growth across Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam and the Philippines. However, the bank found that trade growth outside the technology sector remained weak or negative across several economies.
World Bank warns AI export boom has yet to deliver wider economic gains and stronger domestic demand
World Bank Vice President for East Asia and Pacific Carlos Felipe Jaramillo highlighted the challenge of extending these gains. “The challenge now is to turn the region’s strength in producing AI-related goods into widespread AI adoption that boosts productivity and creates more and better jobs for millions of people.”
Despite stronger technology exports, Thailand continues to face weak domestic demand, sluggish productivity and limited investment. Household purchasing power remains constrained by high indebtedness, while the ageing population presents additional long-term economic difficulties.
Furthermore, the World Bank identified energy costs and climate-related disruptions as continuing risks. Its latest assessment therefore raises Thailand’s headline growth projection without indicating a comparable recovery across the wider domestic economy.
The upgraded forecast coincides with the release of final government accounts for fiscal 2025. These figures reveal a substantial deterioration in the kingdom’s budgetary position. Government revenue reached ฿2.824 trillion during the financial year ending September 30, 2025. This represented an annual increase of approximately 1%. However, expenditure climbed 5.1% to ฿3.723 trillion, substantially outpacing the growth in government income.
Thailand’s fiscal deficit surges 20.6% to ฿898.8 billion as spending outstrips government revenue
As a result, Thailand recorded a budgetary deficit of ฿898.8 billion, compared with ฿745.5 billion in fiscal 2024. The shortfall increased by approximately ฿153.3 billion, equivalent to 20.6%. Moreover, government spending rose by ฿180.7 billion, while revenue increased by only ฿27.4 billion.
Expenditure growth therefore exceeded revenue growth more than sixfold. The imbalance left a substantially larger gap between the money collected by the government and its spending commitments.
The borrowing figures reveal the scale of the shortfall. During fiscal 2025, the government borrowed ฿922.7 billion to finance its operations. Meanwhile, the cash deficit before borrowing, after non-budgetary transactions, reached ฿856.5 billion. These figures accompanied weak tax collection performance across the kingdom’s three principal revenue departments. Although overall receipts increased year-on-year, all three departments failed to meet their annual targets.
Together, the Revenue, Excise and Customs departments collected ฿2.992 trillion during fiscal 2025. This represented growth of 2.8% over the previous financial year. Nevertheless, collections missed official targets by ฿112.2 billion, equivalent to 3.6%. The shortfall was concentrated particularly heavily in excise taxation, where revenue proved substantially weaker than expected.
The Excise Department collected ฿537.5 billion, missing its annual target by ฿72.2 billion, or 11.8%. Remarkably, this accounted for almost two-thirds of the combined shortfall across the three departments.
Weak automobile sales and electric vehicle incentives drive major shortfalls in Thailand’s tax receipts
The Finance Ministry identified disappointing automobile tax receipts as a major contributing factor. Thailand’s vehicle industry has faced subdued domestic demand and changing consumer purchasing patterns. In addition, government incentives supporting electric vehicles have reduced certain excise collections.
The decline against target is significant because automobile taxation forms an important component of excise revenue. Government measures encouraging electric vehicle adoption have also changed the composition of tax receipts from the industry.
Meanwhile, weakness in conventional vehicle demand has affected collections from internal-combustion models. The resulting revenue shortfall contributed heavily to the government’s overall failure to meet its fiscal targets.
Separately, the Revenue Department collected ฿2.335 trillion, approximately 3% more than during fiscal 2024. However, its receipts remained ฿37 billion, or 1.6%, below target. Corporate income tax and VAT collected on imports were among the weaker categories. These figures emerged against a background of subdued domestic consumption and difficult conditions for many businesses.
The Customs Department also reported disappointing collections. Its revenue reached ฿119.1 billion, falling ฿3.1 billion, or 2.5%, below expectations. The Finance Ministry identified the stronger baht, trade liberalisation and declining imports of conventional vehicles as contributing factors.
Overall, net government revenue missed its budget target by ฿64.3 billion, equivalent to 2.2%. Additional income from other government agencies partly offset the shortfalls recorded by the principal tax departments.
Government revenue grows but fails to keep pace with spending as debt and ageing costs increase
Importantly, the figures do not show an outright collapse in total tax revenue. Government income increased during fiscal 2025, but its growth remained substantially below expenditure growth. The distinction is important. Tax collections failed to meet government expectations while spending commitments continued to expand. Consequently, the budget deficit widened sharply despite positive annual revenue growth.
The World Bank’s February 2026 assessment identified increased capital expenditure as one reason for the deterioration. Government investment spending had returned towards normal levels following delays during the previous budget cycle.
Therefore, part of the expenditure increase reflected the timing of public investment rather than entirely new spending commitments. Nevertheless, the kingdom faces additional financial pressures from healthcare, pensions, elderly support and infrastructure requirements.
Thailand’s demographic position adds another dimension to its fiscal difficulties. An ageing population is increasing demand for healthcare and social protection. At the same time, a shrinking working-age population presents challenges for future income-tax collection.
The government must also continue servicing existing public debt while financing current expenditure and investment commitments. These pressures coincide with relatively weak economic growth and a narrow personal income-tax base.
By September 30, 2025, Thailand’s public debt had reached ฿12.226 trillion. This represented 65.08% of GDP, compared with the statutory debt ceiling of 70%. Furthermore, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development has identified significant limitations in Thailand’s taxation system. Its 2025 economic survey estimated that approximately 90% of the labour force did not pay personal income tax.

articles.title: US opens direct talks with Myanmar's generals, reversing years of isolation - CNA
articles.summary: US opens direct talks with Myanmar's generals, reversing years of isolation  CNAUS shifts policy to engage Myanmar military government directly in September talks  Nation ThailandThe Trump Administration’s Shift on Myanmar Is a Disastrous Decision  Council on Foreign Relations (CFR)Washington Ends Post-Coup Freeze, Opens Direct Talks with Myanmar  The Diplomatic InsightMyanmar Junta Rare Earth Talks US Strategy Risks  Rare Earth Exchanges
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON: The Trump administration has begun direct talks with Myanmar’s military-installed government, according to US officials and others familiar with the outreach, in a sharp reversal of Washington’s efforts to isolate the country’s generals after the 2021 coup.
The US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research, Michael Vance, played a leading role in the outreach, which has focused on shutting down scam centres that target Americans but could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, according to seven current and former officials and others familiar with the policy shift.
Vance joined talks with Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing in the capital Naypyidaw on Sep 15 and Sep 16. The meeting was aimed at securing the release of American businessman Adam Castillo but also provided an opening for further engagement, four of the people said.
Last month’s meeting - the highest‑level contact since the coup - underscores a broader Trump‑administration foreign policy tilt away from democracy promotion toward transactional engagement.
The presence of Vance, who was confirmed as the State Department’s top intelligence official in August, and his ongoing role in US policy toward Myanmar have not been previously reported.
MILITARY LEADER REMAINS UNDER US SANCTIONS
Min Aung Hlaing, the former military chief, remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of hundreds of thousands of Rohingya Muslims that Washington declared a genocide.
Less than two weeks after Vance’s visit, Myanmar’s military conducted an airstrike on a crowded marketplace in Rakhine state, killing over 50 people and injuring scores more, according to United Nations human rights officials.
The State Department said it engages with all groups in Myanmar on issues affecting US interests and raises the need to cease violence and release political prisoners.
“You don't solve problems by ignoring them. You solve problems by addressing them,” spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement.
A spokesperson for the military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment. Min Aung Hlaing, who has cited electoral fraud to justify the coup and labelled his opponents as terrorists, is seeking international legitimacy for his nominally civilian government.
Current and former officials say Vance has met players from all sides of Myanmar’s complex conflict and helped shape the Trump administration’s policy toward the country.
Intelligence chiefs - such as Vance - do not typically steer policy because of concerns about compromising analytic independence.
“If you let policy dictate to intelligence, you can't be sure you're getting a real honest assessment of the facts,” said Richard Betts, an adjunct senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations who has consulted for US intelligence agencies.
Pigott declined to address Vance’s role but said the administration “operates as a team with the president as the lead”.
A DETAINED AMERICAN, AND AN OPENING
Castillo, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, was detained at Yangon airport on Jun 11 by Myanmar authorities on what his supporters have described as trumped-up charges. The US government has not commented on whether Castillo was wrongfully detained.
People familiar with the matter said White House, National Security Council and State Department officials held back-channel negotiations with Myanmar officials to secure his release. One person said Myanmar asked only "to have an official engagement at the right level with the US government" in return.
Castillo declined to comment beyond crediting President Donald Trump for his release.
The meeting builds on a June meeting between US and Myanmar officials in Tokyo also involving Vance, four people said. One of the people said officials from the Treasury Department, which oversees sanctions, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Pentagon took part.
It was unclear who represented Myanmar at the talks.
Vance, who became involved in Myanmar policy while advising Vice President JD Vance on Asian affairs, has also met in person and virtually with the democratic opposition and ethnic armed groups fighting the military, five of the people said.
A major focus of the US push is getting Myanmar's help in shuttering scam hubs operating on its territory that run romance and other frauds, which have scammed Americans out of billions of dollars. Two people familiar with the matter said the FBI has had direct contact with Myanmar’s authorities on cyber scams.
Researchers say many scams are run from areas under militia control, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether Myanmar’s leaders are serious about enforcement.
US officials also discussed access to Myanmar’s massive deposits of heavy rare earths that are used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. US officials acknowledge obstacles: the deposits mainly lie in territory held by ethnic armies fighting Myanmar’s military government, and China, currently the main importer, could see any US role as a challenge.
Still, with Washington seeking to diversify supply chains away from China, Myanmar's deposits remain a recurring topic in conversations, the people said.
ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus
Following a 2021 military coup, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has excluded Myanmar from high-level meetings as it has yet to make meaningful progress on the bloc's Five-Point Consensus to end hostilities.
During a meeting in April 2021, all ASEAN leaders reached a consensus about the situation in Myanmar.
The five points are:
First, there shall be immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar and all parties shall exercise utmost restraint.
Second, constructive dialogue among all parties concerned shall commence to seek a peaceful solution in the interests of the people.
Third, a special envoy of the ASEAN chair shall facilitate mediation of the dialogue process, with the assistance of the secretary-general of ASEAN.
Fourth, ASEAN shall provide humanitarian assistance through the AHA Centre.
Fifth, the special envoy and delegation shall visit Myanmar to meet with all parties concerned.
FROM SANCTIONS TO ENGAGEMENT
After the 2021 coup, President Joe Biden's administration froze Myanmar's assets at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and imposed sanctions on senior officers and military‑linked businesses.
In 2022, Congress authorised non-lethal support for the opposition, funding early-warning systems for airstrikes and incentives for officers to defect.
Most of those programs were cut during Trump’s foreign-aid overhaul last year, according to four current and former officials and State Department correspondence with Congress reviewed by Reuters.
The State Department said its engagement with the military government does not diminish its relationships with other groups. The US continues to provide assistance to areas outside military control, it said, without detailing that aid.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said the shift was “contrary to both our values and our interests”.
“By engaging Min Aung Hlaing while failing to implement congressionally mandated sanctions and deploy appropriated democracy funding, Secretary (Marco) Rubio is ceding US leadership and providing this murderous regime greater international legitimacy,” Meeks said in a statement to Reuters.
Myanmar's government, installed after elections criticised by rights groups as a sham, has hired lobbyists to press its case in Washington.
In April, Roger Stone, a longtime Trump adviser, began consulting for DCI Group on behalf of Myanmar's Ministry of Information, according to Foreign Agents Registration Act filings. Stone was convicted in 2019 of obstructing a congressional investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. Trump later pardoned him.
A newsletter distributed by DCI warned in June that Washington risked being shut out of access to critical minerals if it did not engage with Myanmar.
Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing is on a two-day visit to Malaysia as he looks for greater international legitimacy after being installed in April as civilian president.

articles.title: Commerce Minister says that a November signing of a US Thai trade deal is in sight as exporters stand by - Thai Examiner
articles.summary: Commerce Minister says that a November signing of a US Thai trade deal is in sight as exporters stand by  Thai Examiner
articles.full_text:
Trump wants a November trade deal with Thailand, but the final agreement remains unfinished. Anutin says talks are nearing completion as Suphajee targets the ASEAN summit. Meanwhile, American tariff threats persist and Vietnam moves ahead with talks.
A US–Thailand trade deal is heading for a November signing after President Donald Trump wrote directly to Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul. However, critical terms remain unresolved despite agreement in principle. Commerce Minister Suphajee Suthumpun is targeting the ASEAN summit in the Philippines. Meanwhile, Thai exporters face existing US tariffs and further Section 301 threats. Vietnam is advancing its own deal, while Thailand seeks parity with regional competitors. Even a November signing may leave exporters waiting for implementation.
Thailand and the United States are approaching a major reciprocal trade agreement, with formal signing now targeted for November. However, the final deal remains unfinished despite both governments reaching an agreement in principle.
US President Donald Trump has written directly to Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, proposing a signing during his forthcoming Asian visit. Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister and Commerce Minister Suphajee Suthumpun confirmed Thursday that technical and legal negotiations were continuing.
The ASEAN summit in the Philippines has emerged as a possible venue. Nevertheless, Thai exporters still face uncertainty over American tariffs and the prospect of additional duties.
The latest developments follow three days of diplomatic exchanges between Bangkok and Washington. On Thursday, October 8, Suphajee met Anutin at Government House to review progress. Afterwards, she confirmed that both countries had settled the principal elements of the proposed agreement.
Thailand and US target November trade signing as Trump writes to Anutin but legal details remain
However, technical provisions, legal wording and other outstanding details still required attention. The Commerce Minister identified November as the anticipated signing period, particularly during the ASEAN summit in the Philippines. She stopped short of announcing a fixed date or confirming that the final document was ready.
The November timetable follows direct communication between Trump and Anutin. On Tuesday, October 6, government spokesman Ekkapop Pianpises confirmed that the American president had written to the Thai prime minister.
In his letter, Trump expressed interest in concluding negotiations and signing the agreement during his forthcoming Asian visit. Subsequently, Anutin instructed Suphajee to advance the remaining discussions and prepare the necessary arrangements.
The communication established a proposed political timetable for concluding the agreement. However, the final legal text remained unfinished, leaving further work for both negotiating teams.
Anutin says US trade deal is nearing completion as Suphajee confirms agreement on main principles
On Wednesday, October 7, Anutin addressed the negotiations during the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore. Speaking before international business leaders, the prime minister described the agreement as approaching completion.
Indeed, he said both countries were effectively writing the final paragraph of their Agreement on Reciprocal Trade. He also disclosed Trump’s letter and its connection to the proposed signing. Nevertheless, Anutin did not announce that the agreement had been completed. His remarks indicated that the principal negotiating framework was settled, while the final legal provisions remained outstanding.
The following day, Suphajee provided a more detailed account of the remaining work. Following her meeting with Anutin, she confirmed that both countries had reached an agreement in principle.
However, technical and legal discussions were still underway. Importantly, she identified November as a possible signing window rather than a binding deadline. Her comments clarified the distinction between agreement on the main principles and completion of the final document. Consequently, the proposed November signing does not establish that negotiations have broken down or that Washington has rejected Thailand’s proposals.
ASEAN and APEC summits offer November signing opportunities while US tariff questions remain
Instead, both governments are continuing work on the outstanding provisions while preparing for a possible meeting between their leaders. The timing coincides with two major diplomatic gatherings in Asia.
The ASEAN summit is scheduled for November 16–18 in the Philippines. Subsequently, the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting takes place in China on November 18–19. Both events have been mentioned as possible opportunities for Trump and Anutin to meet.
Nevertheless, no venue or signing date has been formally confirmed. Suphajee has specifically identified the ASEAN summit as a possible occasion for concluding the agreement.
Behind the diplomatic timetable, substantial commercial questions remain unresolved. In particular, the final American tariff treatment Thailand will secure remains a central question. The United States is Thailand’s largest export market, making the final terms important for manufacturers and exporters.
In September, Thai officials identified an existing 12.5% US tariff as a continuing concern. Moreover, they warned that a separate American investigation into industrial overcapacity could result in additional duties. That investigation remains distinct from the reciprocal trade discussions. Therefore, signing the bilateral agreement would not necessarily eliminate every potential American tariff measure.
Section 301 tariff threat remains as Thailand seeks US trade parity with Malaysia and Indonesia amid talks
The possibility of additional action under Section 301 of American trade law presents another unresolved issue. Such measures could impose further duties independently of the reciprocal agreement.
Meanwhile, Thailand is seeking trade conditions comparable to those available to regional competitors, particularly Malaysia and Indonesia. Both countries compete with Thailand in important manufacturing and export markets.
Accordingly, Bangkok has sought conditions that would prevent Thai exporters from facing less favourable American tariff treatment. However, the final tariff provisions have not been publicly confirmed, and negotiations over the remaining details are continuing.
Washington has also pressed Thailand on several issues beyond tariffs. These include market access, non-tariff barriers and investment conditions. Separately, purchases involving American agricultural commodities and aircraft have featured in the discussions.
The proposed agreement therefore covers a broader commercial relationship than the tariff rate alone. Nevertheless, the final provisions governing these matters remain outstanding. The two governments must settle the technical arrangements and legal wording before the document can be completed. Until then, the agreement in principle does not establish the precise commercial obligations that will apply.
November signing may precede Thai Cabinet, public hearings and parliamentary approval requirements
Furthermore, formal signing will not necessarily make the agreement immediately effective. Thai officials have previously identified domestic procedures that may be required before implementation.
These include Cabinet approval, public hearings and parliamentary consideration. Consequently, a November signing could be followed by additional legal and political steps in Thailand.
The timetable for implementation will depend on the completed text and the applicable approval requirements. Therefore, exporters face uncertainty over both the final tariff provisions and the date when any new arrangements would take effect.
For Thai businesses, the immediate position remains unchanged until the outstanding negotiations are concluded. The United States continues to represent Thailand’s largest export market. However, manufacturers still lack confirmation of the final reciprocal trade conditions.
Equally, the separate American investigation into industrial overcapacity remains a potential source of additional duties. Any further Section 301 action would create another trade issue outside the bilateral agreement. As a result, the proposed November signing cannot presently be treated as confirmation that all American tariff risks have been settled.
Vietnam advances US trade negotiations as Thailand seeks comparable terms with regional competitors
Meanwhile, developments elsewhere in Southeast Asia are adding urgency to the regional trade calendar. On Thursday, October 8, Vietnam announced that its reciprocal trade negotiations with Washington were largely completed.
The announcement followed seven rounds of discussions between the two countries. Vietnam’s progress came as Thailand confirmed its own agreement in principle. Nevertheless, neither announcement established that a completed agreement had entered into force.
Both countries maintain substantial manufacturing sectors and significant export relationships with the United States. Consequently, the final American trade conditions will be important for companies operating across regional supply chains.
Thailand’s negotiations also involve comparisons with Malaysia and Indonesia. Bangkok has sought tariff conditions comparable to those secured by these regional competitors. However, the precise treatment Thailand will receive remains subject to the final agreement.
The comparison is particularly relevant because manufacturers across Southeast Asia compete for orders in the American market. At the same time, Washington is negotiating trade arrangements with several regional economies. Therefore, the final terms agreed with Thailand will form part of a wider pattern of American trade conditions across Southeast Asia.

VIETNAM’S first investment-grade sovereign rating from a Japanese credit assessor could open a new avenue for financing the country’s ambitious double-digit economic expansion plans.

Rating and Investment Information (R&I) on Thursday (Oct 8) raised Vietnam’s foreign-currency issuer rating to BBB- from BB+, with a stable outlook, making it the first agency to assign the country an investment-grade rating.
The decision reflects optimism about Vietnam’s economic trajectory. The agency expects strong growth to continue following a roughly 9 per cent expansion in the first nine months of 2026, supported by public investment, foreign capital and structural reforms, including the government’s second-generation reform programme known as “Doi Moi 2.0”.
Nguyen Quang Thuan, chairman at Hanoi-based FiinRatings and FiinGroup, said the decision was particularly significant for Japanese institutional investors because R&I is recognised by Japan’s Financial Services Agency as a designated rating agency.
“Institutions whose investment rules require ‘BBB- or higher from at least one designated agency’ can now include Vietnam in their portfolios,” Thuan said in written comments.
“By contrast, institutions applying a ‘lowest rating’ or ‘second-best rating’ rule remain constrained by the Big Three’s BB+ ratings.”
R&I currently assigns more favourable sovereign ratings than global peers to some South-east Asian economies. Vietnam remains below investment grade under the methodologies of S&P, Moody’s and Fitch, or the “Big Three” global rating agencies, which are more widely used by international institutional investors.
The distinction means the upgrade could open some previously restricted funding channels without necessarily triggering a broad reclassification of Vietnamese debt across global investment portfolios.
Under the Basel III standardised approach, the regulatory risk weight on Vietnam’s foreign-currency government bonds could also fall from 100 per cent to 50 per cent for banks permitted to use R&I’s rating, Thuan added.
Such a reduction would lower the capital required to hold the exposure, potentially making Vietnamese sovereign debt more attractive to qualifying financial institutions.
Tyler Manh Dung Nguyen, chief market strategist at Ho Chi Minh City Securities Corporation, wrote in a note on Thursday that the upgrade could benefit the government and major state-linked companies, including VietinBank, Agribank and Vietnam Electricity, by improving their access to Japanese institutional investors and yen-denominated Samurai bonds.
The upgrade follows a renewed push by Japan, Vietnam’s largest bilateral aid provider, to finance the country’s development. A day earlier, the Japan International Cooperation Agency announced plans to provide Vietnam more than 100 billion yen (US$630 million) in annual official development assistance loans.
A US$1.45 trillion financing challenge
The credit upgrade comes as Vietnam faces an increasingly difficult task of mobilising sufficient capital to meet its economic ambitions.
Maybank Investment Bank Vietnam (MSVN) estimates that the country will require about US$1.45 trillion in total social investment between 2026 and 2030, equivalent to roughly 40 per cent of gross domestic product over the period.
Based on the government’s investment structure, about 53 per cent would come from the private sector, 32 per cent from the state and the remaining 15 per cent from foreign direct investment.
Quan Trong Thanh, head of research at MSVN, said that the government should take the lead in raising offshore capital for major infrastructure projects, while banks should remain the primary financiers of private-sector investment.
“In our view, one sure thing is that Vietnam must mobilise more offshore funds, especially from 2028,” Thanh said in comments shared with The Business Times.
He believes Vietnam must deepen its capital markets, including corporate bond and equity markets, but cautions that market development alone cannot meet the country’s financing requirements within the planned timeframe.
“I don’t think it can develop fast enough to achieve the target to support the national growth plan,” Thanh said.
Some local authorities are already exploring new fundraising mechanisms.
Ho Chi Minh City is seeking feedback on a proposal to issue municipal and project bonds, including foreign-currency debt, through Vietnam’s international financial centre, or VIFC, to fund major infrastructure projects and develop capital-market services.
Thanh welcomed the prospect of local governments becoming more active in raising project financing, but said pricing would ultimately determine whether such instruments could attract investors.
Road to broader investment grade
MSVN has noted that achieving broader investment-grade sovereign status could eventually lower Vietnam’s borrowing costs by 150 to 300 basis points, while helping attract institutional capital from pension funds, insurers and sovereign wealth funds.
It would also signal macro stability, reducing currency volatility and hedging costs, as well as improve individual corporate ratings.
“The most critical is forging a right framework for developmental finance and getting the sovereign-rating upgrade to investment grade sooner that its original plan (2030) in order to structurally bring down its funding costs,” Thanh noted.
Vietnam’s banks remain the primary financing channel for businesses, even as policymakers seek to develop deeper capital markets.
In its assessment, R&I highlighted the country’s high ratio of outstanding bank loans to GDP, which exceeded 140 per cent at the end of 2025, alongside tight banking-sector liquidity, substantial real estate-related lending and relatively limited capital buffers.
Those weaknesses could make banking reforms important to securing further sovereign upgrades.
The State Bank of Vietnam issued Circular 50 in September, introducing a phased transition towards Basel III-aligned liquidity standards, including the liquidity coverage ratio and net stable funding ratio. Mandatory implementation begins in October 2028.
Thanh described the regulation as “a positive development for Vietnam banking sector’s operation in the long run”, saying it would strengthen liquidity management and “contribute to the attempts in sovereign-rating upgrade.”
He also argued that banks would need to play a more selective role in directing capital into productive investments.
“The role of the banking system in the coming period must extend beyond merely expanding credit,” he added.
“It needs to shift towards enhancing the quality of capital allocation to support the development of strategic industries, and formation of national champions.” THE BUSINESS TIMES

articles.title: Increased credit growth, diversification of credit limits, and the need for risk-based management. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Increased credit growth, diversification of credit limits, and the need for risk-based management.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
System-wide credit continues to grow, with differentiated credit limits and strict risk management requirements, promoting sustainable development of banks and the economy.
System-wide credit continues to increase, but the ability to supply capital varies among banks. Adjusting credit limits needs to be linked to financial capacity and loan quality, while accelerating the transition to risk-based credit management.
Adjust the spending limit according to actual needs.
At the State Bank of Vietnam's press conference on October 7, 2026, Deputy Governor Pham Thanh Ha stated that as of September 30, the total outstanding loans of the credit institution system reached approximately VND 20.75 million billion, an increase of 11.59% compared to the end of 2025 and 16.69% compared to the same period last year. According to Mr. Ha, this increase is consistent with the credit management target for the whole year.
According to the Deputy Governor, during the course of its administration, solutions were implemented to create room for credit institutions to provide credit for certain important needs serving economic growth and to facilitate credit provision for certain types of real estate in line with the Party and State's policies and guidelines.
Accordingly, it was directed that the additional credit outstanding compared to the end of 2025 for social housing, industrial parks, export processing zones; restaurants, hotels, tourist areas, ecological and resort areas should not be included in the credit outstanding for the real estate sector when controlling the growth rate of real estate credit.
In addition, excluding outstanding credit/loan balances arising annually, supplementary credit growth limits will be granted to commercial banks to provide credit to businesses for the implementation and investment of large-scale, key projects with spillover and linkage effects, promoting regional and local economic development as directed by the Government leadership to achieve the "double-digit" growth target.
It's important to understand that this mechanism addresses real estate credit limits and does not mean that all loans are exempt from growth restrictions. These preferential mechanisms also need clear guidance on eligible borrowers, how to determine outstanding debt, and reporting responsibilities, to ensure that funds reach their intended purpose and are properly managed during use.
However, the overall growth rate of the system does not fully reflect the capital capacity of each individual bank. When credit growth limits are allocated separately to each institution, a situation may arise where a bank has eligible borrowers but its lending capacity has narrowed, while another bank has not yet used up its quota.
According to TCBS Research's updated banking sector report, by the end of Q2 2026, NCB recorded a 30.7% increase; VPBank a 23.2% increase; HDBank a 21.8% increase; Techcombank a 15.2% increase; and MB a 13.2% increase. Techcombank and MSB, with growth rates of 15.2% and 11.4% respectively, were assessed by TCBS as having nearly used up their credit limits after six months.
According to TCBS Research, credit developments in the second half of the year therefore depend on two major variables: the possibility of being granted additional credit limits and the ability to raise capital. For banks that are close to reaching their credit limit, being granted additional limits is only one condition; to actually disburse funds, banks must also find corresponding sources of capital.

This shows that adjusting credit limits should be linked to the actual capital supply capacity of each bank. For organizations needing to expand credit, adjustments should be based on their loan portfolio, debt collection progress, capital sources, and risk control capabilities. The remaining capacity should be prioritized for production and business needs with feasible plans and clear debt repayment cash flows.
Lending capacity doesn't solely depend on the available credit limit. Capital sources, equity, safety ratios, and asset quality all determine the actual disbursement capacity. Therefore, increasing credit limits must be accompanied by strengthening financial capacity, addressing bad debts, and managing maturity mismatches.
Experts believe that adjusting the ratio of short-term capital to medium- and long-term loans and the method of calculating State Treasury deposits in the LDR will be significant in the second half of the year, gradually removing bottlenecks in capital sources and safety ratios so that they can be converted into actual capital for the economy.
With the remaining allocation of available funds, the regulatory body needs to continue reviewing the situation based on asset quality, mobilization capacity, equity capital, compliance levels, and loan structure. Banks with a solid foundation and a good ability to meet the capital needs for production should be considered promptly, thereby limiting localized bottlenecks.
Gradually shift towards risk monitoring.
Expanding credit availability does not mean lowering lending standards. As credit volume increases rapidly and banks continue to shoulder the majority of the economy's capital needs, requirements for loan quality, liquidity management, and bad debt control become even more crucial.
Directive 01/CT of 2026 from the State Bank of Vietnam requires credit institutions to promote safe and efficient credit growth; direct capital towards production, business, priority sectors and growth drivers, while strictly controlling credit to sectors with potential risks. Facilitating customer access to capital must go hand in hand with compliance with the law , and credit granting conditions should not be relaxed in order to limit bad debts.
Deputy Governor Pham Thanh Ha emphasized that the economy has a huge demand for capital, but "credit expansion must be linked to improving credit quality, controlling risks, handling bad debts, and ensuring the safety of the system."
You may also like
For banks that have almost used up their lending limit, TCBS Research experts believe that the disbursement rate depends on whether additional limits are granted. The remaining constraint lies in the source of capital – new deposits have increased by 5.5% since the beginning of the year, equivalent to six-tenths of the credit growth rate, so only banks that can secure new capital will be able to use up their lending limit.
However, recent policy adjustments are expected to support credit growth in the second half of 2026, including easing the roadmap for the ratio of short-term capital to medium- and long-term loans and including Treasury time deposits in the calculation of LDR. These adjustments could remove bottlenecks in safety ratios, creating more room for banks to boost lending.
In particular, state-owned banks – which hold the majority of Treasury deposits and are subject to the strictest LDR (Loan-to-Deposit Ratio) constraints – are expected to benefit more significantly, thereby increasing the pace of disbursements in the final months of the year.
In the long term, the requirement is to gradually shift from performance-based management to management based on the financial capacity, asset quality, and risk level of each bank. Therefore, short-term adjustments to the operating limit should be selective, and the roadmap for changing the operating method must be accompanied by corresponding supervisory capacity.
The ultimate measure is not just how much credit increases, but whether the capital flows to the right businesses, for the right purposes, and generates results. Credit limits are only truly effective when accompanied by capital sources, credit quality, and governance discipline, thereby supporting growth while ensuring the safety of the system.

articles.title: From Constraints to Cooperation: Singapore and Southeast Asia’s Energy Transition - Singapore EDB
articles.summary: From Constraints to Cooperation: Singapore and Southeast Asia’s Energy Transition  Singapore EDB
articles.full_text:
Across Southeast Asia, most countries have articulated net-zero or carbon-neutrality targets, signalling a clear collective commitment to the energy transition.1 However, translating these ambitions into implementation remains a structural challenge: how do we mobilise capital at scale, reduce risk, strengthen regional cooperation, and ensure the transition delivers both climate and development outcomes?
Using the United Nations Development Programme’s (UNDP) framework on innovative governance for private sector engagement, this article – through examining how Singapore supports the region’s energy transition by developing governance and financial frameworks to mobilise investment and strengthen collaboration – showcases how partnership-oriented governance and financial mechanisms can help align private incentives with public and regional development objectives2.
Energy Transition in Southeast Asia: A Structural and Development Challenge
Electricity demand in Southeast Asia has tripled over the past two decades, driven by economic growth, industrialisation, and expanded access to electricity.3 Yet this growth has largely been met through fossil fuels, particularly coal, which continues to account for around 45% of the region’s power generation.4 Although renewable deployment is accelerating, the pace of change remains insufficient to meet climate targets while supporting inclusive and resilient development.
These gaps do not stem from a lack of renewable resources or national ambition. Many ASEAN countries possess abundant access to renewable energy, such as solar, wind, and hydropower and have committed to net-zero pathways. The challenge lies instead in the fragmented grid systems, limited cross-border interconnections, and high financing costs.5 Together, these structural challenges raise project risk, undermine bankability, and lead to slow progress. These impacts are most acute in lower-income and emerging markets with limited fiscal headroom.
In contrast, Singapore has limited land and natural resources, but has strong regulatory institutions, deep financial markets, and policy credibility, which position Singapore well in the climate transition.6 This creates opportunities to move beyond isolated national approaches and towards cooperation built on complementary roles.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) has estimated that countries in Southeast Asia will need to double annual investment to nearly US$30 billion (S$38.4 billion) by 2035 to integrate renewable energy at scale.7 Meeting this need requires more than capital availability; it depends on mechanisms that reduce risk, improve coordination, and align private investment with public and regional priorities. Singapore’s contribution sits primarily at this enabling layer, consistent with UNDP’s emphasis on partnership-oriented governance.
Sustainable Finance as an Enabling Mechanism
Over the past decade, Singapore has developed sustainable and transition financing frameworks that correspond to the realities of Southeast Asia’s development pathways. The Finance for Net Zero (FinZ) Action Plan by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) marked a shift from a narrow focus on green assets, towards recognising the importance of financing credible transition activities, particularly in carbon-intensive sectors that remain central to many Southeast Asian economies.8
This approach is especially relevant for developing countries, where decarbonisation often involves gradual system transformation rather than immediate replacement. Financing frameworks that recognise transition pathways, while maintaining safeguards against greenwashing, can help unlock capital aligned with national climate transition priorities.
The Singapore-Asia Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance, the world’s first multi-sector transition taxonomy, provides a practical reference for classifying economic activities into green, transition, and ineligible categories.9 Its adoption at the regional level, including alignment with the ASEAN Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance,10 highlights how shared standards can reduce uncertainty for investors while respecting diverse national contexts.
These tools represent examples of direct policy actions that enable decarbonisation pathways in the region.

articles.title: Q4/2026: Growth driven by corporate loan demand; credit continues to outpace deposits. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Q4/2026: Growth driven by corporate loan demand; credit continues to outpace deposits.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Credit growth for the whole year was approximately 16.4%, and liquidity improved.
 The Forecasting and Statistics Department (State Bank of Vietnam - SBV) has just announced the results of a survey on business trends of credit institutions conducted in the fourth quarter of 2026.
 In this survey, credit institutions assessed that customer demand for banking services (including deposit services, payment services, and loans) in the third quarter of 2026 will continue to "improve".   In particular, demand for deposits and payments was assessed to have improved significantly compared to the previous quarter. While demand for loans was still assessed to have improved the most, the improvement was less than in the previous quarter.
 The demand for loans from corporate clients continues to be higher than that of individual clients, with a clear increase observed in the demand for loans from small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Small-scale commercial banks are the group that expects the strongest increase in customer demand for banking services in Q3 2026.
 In the fourth quarter of 2026 and throughout 2026, credit institutions expect customer demand for banking services to continue to improve more strongly than anticipated in the previous survey.
 The liquidity of the banking system in the third quarter of 2026 continued to maintain a "good" state and is expected to continue improving in the fourth quarter of 2026 and throughout 2026 and 2027. This development shows that credit institutions generally have a positive assessment of liquidity and a tendency to improve in the coming period, although the pressure to balance capital sources still needs to be monitored in the context of continued high credit demand.
 In this survey, credit institutions expect capital mobilization to grow at an average rate of 4.1%, while credit growth will be 5.3%. For the whole year, credit institutions expect capital mobilization to increase by 14.3% and credit to increase by 16.4%.
 Encouragingly, asset quality is assessed favorably by banks. According to the survey results, the non-performing loan ratio/credit outstanding ratio of the entire system showed clear signs of improvement in the third quarter of 2026 and is expected to continue improving in the remaining months of the year in most groups of credit institutions.
 Over 86% of credit institutions expect positive profit growth.
 The improving business performance continued to strengthen in Q3 2026 and is expected to be even more positive in Q4 2026, thereby creating a springboard for the prospect of pre-tax profit for the whole year 2026.
 The survey results show that 86.1% of credit institutions expect pre-tax profits to grow positively compared to 2025, while 10.4% are concerned about negative growth and 3.5% expect no change.
 Internal factors are perceived by credit institutions as continuing to play a positive supporting role in their business operations, with 73.9 - 76.3% of credit institutions assessing and expecting these factors to contribute to improving business performance in the third quarter and the whole year of 2026.
 The improvement in the third quarter was more positive than the previous quarter, while optimism regarding the outlook for the whole year 2026 was slightly revised downward compared to the previous survey. At the same time, credit institutions also assessed that objective factors continued to have a positive impact on business performance.
 For the banking sector's labor market, the situation is gradually shifting from a labor shortage to a more balanced state, with recruitment demand remaining stable, the labor shortage rate decreasing continuously in the first three quarters of the year, but without any surplus of manpower.

articles.title: Indonesia vows to protect investment at launch of battery, solar, aluminium plants - Mining.com
articles.summary: Indonesia vows to protect investment at launch of battery, solar, aluminium plants  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Indonesia is committed to respecting and safeguarding all investments, President Prabowo Subianto said on Thursday, as he launched nickel- and aluminium-based projects worth billions.
Prabowo was speaking at a launch ceremony for commercial operations of industrial facilities and construction of other projects in an industrial park at Weda Bay partly controlled by Chinese steelmaker Tsingshan Holding Group.
He also launched the first exports of EV batteries, produced by REPT Battero, at the ceremony.
“I emphasise here an Indonesian government commitment to respect and safeguard all investments, from wherever,” he said. “We are committed to safeguarding our partnership as well as possible. It is a matter of honour for the Indonesian people to support our partners.”
Indonesia has attracted massive investment into its metal industry and smelting, mainly from China, with firms drawn to its rich nickel reserves, but recent policies have raised concerns from some business players.
Chinese companies operating in Indonesia have called for more business-friendly policies, warning the president in a letter that tighter mining quotas, higher taxes and a new pricing formula were driving up costs and threatening investment.
Country is world’s top exporter of nickel products
Indonesia, which holds the world’s largest nickel ore reserves, banned exports of raw nickel in 2020 to promote domestic processing industries.
The policy has helped Indonesia become the world’s top exporter of nickel products, making up around 60% of global supply, with export value growing from $3.3 billion in 2017 to over $33 billion by 2024.
Among companies investing in the new projects at Weda Bay are PT Guang Ching Nickel Cobalt, PT Weda Bay Aluminium and PT Flatsolar Energy Indonesia, the Investment Ministry said.
The four projects were worth $3.4 billion, while investment in six other projects is expected to reach $6.8 billion, investment minister Rosan Roeslani said at the same event on Thursday.
The new constructions include facilities to produce nickel-based battery material, battery components, and photovoltaic glass for solar panels, Rosan said. Development of two aluminium plants was also launched on Thursday, he added.
