articles.title: Vietnam has been upgraded by R&I to BBB-, entering the Investment Grade category. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam has been upgraded by R&I to BBB-, entering the Investment Grade category.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On October 8, 2026, Rating and Investment Information, Inc. (R&I) upgraded Vietnam's foreign currency issuer rating from BB+, Positive outlook, to BBB-, Stable outlook. This marks the first time Vietnam has been included in the Investment Grade rating group.
Vietnam has been upgraded by R&I to BBB-, entering the Investment Grade category.
This is the first time Vietnam has been placed in the Investment Grade category by an international credit rating organization, R&I, marking a significant step in strengthening its creditworthiness in the international market.
The upgrade to Investment Rating reflects R&I's positive assessment of Vietnam's economic growth fundamentals, structural reform prospects, fiscal space, and resilience to external shocks. R&I believes high growth will continue to be sustained by the transition to a productivity- and innovation-based growth model, expanded public investment, and foreign direct investment inflows.
During the national credit rating review in April and May 2026, based on the macroeconomic results achieved in recent years and on the basis of experience working with international credit rating agencies such as Moody's, Fitch, and S&P, the Ministry of Finance proactively coordinated with ministries and agencies and directly worked with R&I, providing updated information on Vietnam's macroeconomic, fiscal, public debt, and reform results.
R&I assesses Vietnam as maintaining strong growth momentum, higher than other Southeast Asian countries. According to R&I, the reforms being implemented by the Government , focusing on streamlining the state apparatus, promoting the private sector, improving the institutional framework, and developing the capital market, will contribute to consolidating growth potential and enhancing the resilience of the economy. R&I positively evaluates this comprehensive reform program and expects that the consistent implementation of reform measures will help Vietnam maintain high growth more stably.
Regarding fiscal policy, R&I notes that the public debt-to-GDP ratio remains relatively low, creating room for increased development investment spending. Although budget deficits and public debt ratios are projected to increase in the near future, R&I believes there are no concerns about debt sustainability, as expanded public investment is expected to support future growth while the government prioritizes controlling recurrent expenditures.
Regarding external economic relations, R&I noted that the current account balance continued to be in surplus, foreign direct investment inflows were maintained, and the foreign debt burden remained relatively low, supporting resilience to external shocks. At the same time, R&I pointed out issues requiring continued attention related to credit growth, bank liquidity, real estate lending, the financial system's capital adequacy, and foreign exchange reserves.
In the context of a volatile and challenging global economy, Vietnam's first-ever upgrade to Investment-level credit rating by an international credit rating agency is a significant milestone in the country's credit reform and improvement process. This result affirms the solid macroeconomic foundation, the continuous efforts to achieve high and sustainable growth, maintain public debt safety, and implement comprehensive reforms. Consequently, Vietnam's credit standing in the international market continues to be strengthened, contributing to increased investor confidence and creating more favorable conditions for mobilizing long-term resources for socio-economic development.
The Ministry of Finance and other government agencies will continue to work closely with R&I and other credit rating agencies, providing full and timely information on the socio-economic, fiscal, and public debt situation, to ensure that the assessment of Vietnam's national credit profile is carried out on the basis of accurate and up-to-date information.

articles.title: Thanh Hoa Logistics: From Infrastructure Advantages to Competitive Capabilities - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Thanh Hoa Logistics: From Infrastructure Advantages to Competitive Capabilities  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
With its diverse transportation system, deep-water seaport, and ever-increasing volume of industrial goods and import/export activities, Thanh Hoa is poised to become a crucial logistics hub in the North Central region. However, for this advantage to truly become a competitive advantage, logistics needs to be viewed not only as a transportation support service, but as a vital link in the production, trade, and import/export chain.
Thanh Hoa has many favorable conditions for developing large-scale logistics. Its location between Northern and North Central Vietnam, its connection to the Northwest region, Laos, and international shipping routes, along with its road, rail, sea, and air transport systems, provides the province with a foundation that not every province possesses.
In this context, the Nghi Son Economic Zone and the seaport system are identified as the core of the logistics network. According to data from the Thanh Hoa Department of Industry and Trade, by 2025, the volume of goods passing through Thanh Hoa's seaport system will reach approximately 57 million tons. According to the orientation until 2030, the province's seaport system will continue to be invested in and upgraded to improve its operational capacity, serving industry, energy, trade, and logistics.
Along with that, Thanh Hoa's industrial and import-export goods sources are expanding. The province currently has 333 enterprises exporting goods to 68 countries and territories, with many key product groups such as textiles, paving stones, cement, car tires, and petrochemical products. This is an important source of goods for the formation and development of logistics services with higher scale and added value.
However, the reality of business operations reveals a paradox: Thanh Hoa has sources of goods, seaports, and transportation infrastructure, yet a significant portion of the value of logistics services is still being provided outside the province.
According to feedback from businesses at the Conference connecting import-export businesses with logistics businesses organized by the Thanh Hoa Department of Industry and Trade in September 2026, the majority of the province's export goods are still traded under FOB terms. Therefore, logistics businesses in Thanh Hoa province mainly handle domestic transportation by road, while a significant amount of import-export goods still utilize logistics ecosystems outside the province, especially in Hai Phong . This is a point that needs consideration.
If goods are produced in Thanh Hoa but many value-added logistics stages are carried out elsewhere, the advantages in terms of supply sources and infrastructure cannot be fully translated into economic benefits for the locality. In other words, Thanh Hoa does not lack logistics potential; the problem is how to retain more of the flow of goods, services, and added value within the province.
Connecting to form a logistics ecosystem.
Therefore, logistics development cannot simply stop at building more warehouses, opening more transport routes, or increasing port capacity. More importantly, it must form a logistics ecosystem capable of fully serving the needs of manufacturing, import-export, and trading businesses.
The Thanh Hoa Logistics Service Development Plan until 2030, with a vision to 2050, has set fairly clear goals: an average logistics growth rate of 16-20% per year; increasing the proportion of businesses outsourcing logistics services; promoting the application of digital technology ; forming modern regional or national-level logistics centers, provincial-level centers linked to inland ports, and inter-communal logistics centers. Notably, the Plan identifies infrastructure development and the creation of goods sources as two key stages.
This is the right approach, because logistics can only develop sustainably when it is linked to the supply of goods. Investing in seaports without a stable supply of goods will make it difficult to achieve the expected operational efficiency. Building logistics centers but lacking regular business use will make it difficult to create a distribution hub. Logistics businesses wanting to invest in vehicles, warehouses, and technology will struggle to expand if they lack long-term orders. Therefore, there needs to be a strong shift from a mindset of developing individual links to a mindset of developing the entire chain.
You may also like
First and foremost, it is necessary to strengthen the links between manufacturing businesses, import-export businesses, and logistics businesses. The networking conferences recently organized by the Thanh Hoa Department of Industry and Trade need to be promoted in a more substantive way, not just for exchanging information, but towards forming specific contracts, transportation plans, and supply chains.
Large enterprises, FDI companies, and industries with stable supply chains should be considered "core customers" for logistics businesses in the province to develop suitable services. Once orders are secured, logistics businesses will have the basis to invest in warehouses, vehicles, technology, and human resources.
Furthermore, it is necessary to improve the capacity of logistics businesses within the province. The current reality shows that most logistics businesses are small and medium-sized, with limited value-added services; the warehousing system is not yet synchronized, and the level of automation and management of storage conditions is low. Thanh Hoa has also not yet developed a regional logistics center and an inland container depot (ICD) system as expected.
These are bottlenecks that need to be addressed through appropriate policies, while also creating conditions for capable businesses, including large domestic and foreign logistics companies, to participate in investment.
Another indispensable requirement is the development of multimodal logistics. If goods remain primarily dependent on road transport, logistics costs will be difficult to reduce significantly. Connecting seaports with roads, railways, inland waterways, air transport, and logistics centers needs to be considered within a single system.
In this context, Nghi Son Port needs to continue to play a central role, but its development should not be isolated. The value of the port will only be enhanced when it is supported by a system of warehouses, distribution centers, multimodal transport, customs services, storage, packaging, sorting, and other value-added logistics services.
Simultaneously, digital transformation and green transformation need to become an essential part of the development process. Order management, vehicle tracking, warehouse management, and data connectivity between shippers, logistics companies, seaports, and regulatory agencies will help reduce time, lower costs, and improve supply chain control.
A modern logistics system should not only move goods faster, but also help businesses forecast better, manage better, and compete better.
Speaking with a reporter from the Industry and Trade Newspaper, Mr. Nguyen Tien Hieu, Director of the Thanh Hoa Department of Industry and Trade, said: Logistics development needs to be placed within the overall development of the province's industry, trade, and import-export. The focus is on strengthening connections between manufacturing businesses, import-export businesses, and logistics businesses; effectively utilizing the seaport system, especially Nghi Son Port; and promoting the application of technology and the development of multimodal logistics services. Through this, the quality of services will be gradually improved, logistics costs will be reduced, and conditions will be created for Thanh Hoa businesses to be more proactive in the supply chain and enhance their competitiveness.
From advantage to real value
It is clear that Thanh Hoa is at a favorable time to build a new logistics hub. Planning, infrastructure, supply sources, and policy orientations are all opening up significant potential. Recent articles by Thanh Hoa Newspaper also show that the province has shifted strongly from identifying advantages to seeking out the "bottlenecks" that need to be addressed to transform logistics into a genuine competitive advantage. But to reach the goal, the most important thing remains the ultimate effectiveness.
An export container, if transported through a provincial port and utilizing warehousing, transportation, customs clearance, and other logistics services provided by local businesses, will generate significantly greater value than simply using Thanh Hoa as a production location and then transporting the goods to another locality to handle most of the logistics chain.
Similarly, a manufacturing business that can access integrated logistics services locally will reduce costs, shorten delivery times, and increase its ability to proactively respond to market fluctuations.
Therefore, the measure of logistics development should not be just the number of projects, the number of kilometers of roads invested, or port capacity. More importantly, it should be how much cargo is retained, how many businesses use logistics services within the province, how much logistics costs are reduced, and how much added value is created in the area.

articles.title: Vietnam requires public EV charging stations to support compatible vehicles - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam requires public EV charging stations to support compatible vehicles  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Public electric-vehicle charging stations in Vietnam must be technically designed to serve compatible EVs from different brands, starting July 1, 2027, under new regulations issued by the Ministry of Industry and Trade.
The ministry's Circular 61/2026/TT-BCT on technical standards for EV charging poles and stations requires charging infrastructure to provide compatible connectors, charging modes, and technical specifications so that compatible vehicles can use the same facilities.
Charging station control systems must not restrict charging for vehicle configurations publicly declared as compatible, provided technical, authentication and safety conditions remain unchanged.
The obligations cover stations in public areas, parking facilities, and rest stops, as well as outdoor sites and those under standalone shelters. Chargers in basements, indoor garages, and enclosed parking areas are exempt.
The regulations do not apply to private charging stations, wireless charging equipment, vehicle-supplied chargers, or testing and research equipment.
The requirement is focused on technical compatibility. The circular does not explicitly require charging operators to open their services to vehicles from every brand or prohibit operators from limiting access based on their business models.
Vietnam's EV charging infrastructure is currently operated by automakers, distribution networks, and independent charging service providers. Some networks already allow vehicles from other brands to use their chargers, while others primarily serve their own customers.
Under the new rules, commercial charging stations must disclose prices or charging methods and electricity consumption to users before and during each transaction.
The rules introduce additional safety requirements. Charging stations must have automatic warning and power-cut systems capable of responding to fires, flooding, and overheating.
Charging poles manufactured or assembled domestically, as well as imported equipment, must carry required labels, meet conformity requirements, and undergo testing and acceptance before being put into operation.
Existing charging stations given time to comply
Charging stations installed before July 2027 will be allowed to remain in operation, as long as they are properly maintained and meet safety requirements.
Existing stations must undergo a safety review within six months. Operators will have up to 24 months from July 1, 2027, to rectify identified problems. Any repair, renovation, or expansion carried out after that date must comply with the new technical standards.
The rules come as Vietnam's electric-vehicle market expands and charging infrastructure faces growing demand.
Vietnam currently has about 6.7 million cars, around 3% of which are electric, and about 70 million motorcycles, with EVs accounting for roughly 4.3%. Most electric vehicles are concentrated in major cities, increasing demand for both parking facilities and charging infrastructure.
Under Vietnam's roadmap to net-zero emissions by 2050, the country aims for electric vehicles to account for 50% of urban vehicles and for all buses and taxis to run on electricity by 2030.
The World Bank estimates that Vietnam may need about $2.2 billion in investment in charging infrastructure by 2030 and $32.6 billion by 2050 to develop a nationwide charging network.

articles.title: Thailand Must Build AI Operating System Within Two Years to Escape Low-Growth Trap, Leaders Warn - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Thailand Must Build AI Operating System Within Two Years to Escape Low-Growth Trap, Leaders Warn  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Industry leaders at Thailand Economic Outlook 2027 urge immediate action on AI, data centres, and regulatory reforms to secure 5% annual GDP growth.
Thailand stands at a pivotal junction where it must rapidly modernize its infrastructure, expand artificial intelligence adoption, and bridge a widening digital skills gap to avoid being left behind in the new global economy.
Speaking at the Thailand Economic Outlook 2027: New Horizon Beyond the Trap conference, organised by Krungthep Turakij, top leaders from industrial real estate, telecommunications, and global technology offered a unified blueprint: Thailand must overhaul its economic foundation within a tight two-year window or risk missing out on high-value foreign investments.
The call to action comes as the Southeast Asian nation aims to escape the middle-income trap by accelerating annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth from its current subdued pace to 5%.
Achieving this ambitious target requires transitioning away from traditional, labour-intensive manufacturing toward a digital economy anchored by artificial intelligence, green energy, and advanced infrastructure.
Jareeporn Jarukornsakul, chairman and Group CEO of WHA Corporation PCL, warned that Thailand’s manufacturing sector—traditionally the engine of national output—has seen its share of GDP fall from 27% to 24.3%. The decline comes amid heightened geopolitical friction, the US-China technology trade war, and an ageing domestic population.
Despite these headwinds, Thailand remains a foreign direct investment (FDI) magnet. Total Board of Investment (BOI) applications recently hit a record 1.8 trillion baht ($52.9 billion), driven by 1.36 trillion baht ($40 billion) in FDI.
In the first half of the year alone, foreign investment expanded by more than 80%. Notably, 1.1 trillion baht ($32.4 billion) of these inflows were concentrated in digital infrastructure and data centres, attracting tech giants such as Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS).
"Thailand is currently in a transition period," Jareeporn said. "If we fail to seize this opportunity within the next two years, everyone will be left to fend for themselves. This is Thailand's new horizon. Whether our horizon is bright or dark depends entirely on the work we do right now."
To capture this momentum, Jareeporn outlined ten strategic future industries—spanning AI processing, circular economy models, food tech, and small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs).
She urged the Thai government to implement a "regulatory guillotine" to slash bureaucratic red tape, offer targeted investment incentives, and replace populist cash handouts with targeted skills training, SME loan access, and debt restructuring.
While big-tech investments and data centre capacity are surging, the practical rollout of AI among domestic businesses faces significant operational barriers.
Sigve Brekke, chief executive officer of True Group, highlighted that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) form the backbone of the Thai economy, accounting for 70% of total employment and generating 35% of GDP. However, 85% of these enterprises operate on annual revenues under 1.8 million baht ($52,900).
Although a True Group survey revealed that 70% of Thai SMEs have experimented with basic AI tools like web searches, only 9% have integrated AI directly into their core business processes or revenue models.
"The primary obstacle to digital transformation is not the technology itself, but a legacy mindset," Brekke explained. "The real threat is not that AI will take people's jobs, but that individuals who do not know how to use AI will be replaced by those who do."
Brekke advocated for a three-point strategy to support small enterprises: simplifying AI tools for micro-merchants, accelerating workforce upskilling, and establishing a flexible "Responsible AI" regulatory framework that allows startups to safely test innovations.
The demand for underlying computing power is expanding at an exponential rate. David Li, CEO of Huawei Technologies (Thailand), noted that global AI foundation models have expanded from 175 billion parameters in 2020 toward an estimated 100 trillion parameters by 2030.
This computational boom is mirrored locally. On Huawei Cloud Thailand, monthly token processing volume expanded 185-fold between April and September 2026, while nationwide token consumption grew 30-fold.
However, only 12.4% of Thailand's working-age population currently utilises AI tools—lagging regional peers such as Singapore and Vietnam.
Li stressed that Thailand possesses the foundational assets to elevate itself from a regional digital hub into a regional AI hub, supported by a 2.87-gigawatt data centre pipeline, 5G-Advanced connectivity, and a 2,000-megawatt direct power purchase agreement (PPA) pilot for green energy.
To secure long-term competitiveness, Huawei proposed building a sovereign Thai AI ecosystem anchored on three key pillars: open infrastructure utilising neutral hardware and open-source models to prevent vendor lock-in; robust data governance that protects local data while unlocking its value; and a youth talent engine focused on practical experience.
"Data is the economic infrastructure that will serve as the core foundation of a nation's competitiveness," Li emphasised. "Protect, govern, and then create value."
Li also pointed out that AI innovation is increasingly driven by younger creators, with the average age of global AI unicorn founders dropping from 40 in 2020 to 29 today. Cultivating Thailand's domestic AI workforce, he noted, requires providing hands-on environments where young developers can build, deploy, and scale real-world systems.

articles.title: Austria's VAMED plans €1.2 bln Vietnam investment, explores hospital ship in Phu Quoc island - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Austria's VAMED plans €1.2 bln Vietnam investment, explores hospital ship in Phu Quoc island  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Austria's VAMED Engineering GmbH plans to invest EUR1.2 billion in Vietnam over the next five years and is exploring a hospital ship project in Phu Quoc island to expand healthcare capacity and support international events.
The plans were discussed during a meeting on Wednesday between Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Pham Thi Thanh Tra and César Louis-Philip Marseille, managing director of VAMED Engineering GmbH and a member of the board of VAMED+WWH Group of Germany.
Stressing that Vietnam is one of VAMED's important partners in Southeast Asia, Marseille said the planned investment of €1.2 billion over the next five years is expected to create thousands of jobs and promote knowledge and technology transfer, he added.
VAMED also wants to expand cooperation through concessional financing projects, public-private partnerships, and partnerships with private-sector investors. The group plans to supply medical products from Austria and Germany to Vietnamese partners.
Notably, VAMED proposed studying a hospital ship in Phu Quoc off Vietnam's southern province of An Giang, subject to the necessary conditions.
The company said the model would be a new approach for Vietnam's healthcare system and could provide medical services to large numbers of patients while strengthening the country's healthcare capacity.
Deputy PM Tra, in reply, welcomed the proposal, noting that Vietnam's long coastline and diverse healthcare needs create conditions for developing mobile healthcare models at sea. Such facilities could also help Vietnam respond to natural disasters and other emergencies, she said.
The proposed medical ship in Phu Quoc is also consistent with Vietnam's efforts to combine healthcare and tourism, particularly as the island prepares to host the APEC Economic Leaders' Week in 2027.
Tra said the project should be designed as a long-term healthcare asset rather than being developed solely to serve the APEC event. It should help strengthen local medical capacity, support the organization of international events, and improve healthcare services for the wider population.
She asked VAMED to quickly complete a detailed proposal covering technology, operations, and implementation mechanisms for the project.
Tra required the Ministry of Health to work with other ministries, agencies, and An Giang authorities to assess the hospital-ship concept, including its feasibility, technical requirements, standards, regulations, and other conditions needed for implementation.
The An Giang People's Committee was tasked with coordinating with relevant agencies to review the project's documents, investment conditions, and procedures.
In addition to the hospital ship proposal, Tra suggested VAMED invest in elderly healthcare and care facilities in Vietnam as the country faces growing demand for healthcare services.
VAMED has operated in Vietnam since 1997. Over nearly three decades, the group has deployed about €158 million in official development assistance (ODA) funding and implemented 10 major projects, helping upgrade medical equipment at 15 military hospitals, as well as Bach Mai Hospital, Cho Ray Hospital, and Hue Central Hospital. VAMED has also supported the development of medical-waste incineration facilities serving 25 local hospital clusters.

articles.title: Vietnam enters investment-grade ratings category for first time - DTiNews
articles.summary: Vietnam enters investment-grade ratings category for first time  DTiNews
articles.full_text:
Vietnam has received its first investment-grade credit rating from Japanese agency Rating and Investment Information (R&I), which upgraded the country's foreign-currency issuer rating from BB+, with a positive outlook, to BBB-, with a stable outlook, on October 8, according to the Ministry of Finance.
The ministry said the upgrade reflected R&I's positive assessment of Vietnam's economic growth fundamentals, prospects for structural reform, fiscal headroom and resilience to external shocks.
R&I expects strong growth to continue as Vietnam shifts towards a model driven by productivity and innovation, expands public investment and attracts foreign direct investment.
During its sovereign credit assessment in April and May, the Ministry of Finance worked with other government agencies and engaged directly with R&I, providing updated information on Vietnam's macroeconomic and fiscal conditions, public debt and reform progress. The ministry drew on its experience working with international rating agencies Moody's, Fitch and S&P.
R&I said Vietnam had maintained strong growth, outperforming other Southeast Asian economies. Government reforms aimed at streamlining the state apparatus, promoting the private sector, strengthening institutions and developing capital markets were expected to bolster the country's growth potential and economic resilience.
The agency welcomed the broad reform programme and said consistent implementation would help Vietnam sustain high growth more reliably over the longer term.
On public finances, R&I noted that Vietnam's public debt-to-GDP ratio remained relatively low, leaving room to increase development investment. Although the budget deficit and public debt ratio are expected to rise, the agency said debt sustainability was not a major concern, as higher public investment was expected to support future growth while the government sought to control recurrent spending.
On the external front, the agency highlighted Vietnam's continued current-account surplus, sustained foreign direct investment inflows and relatively low external debt burden as factors supporting resilience to global shocks.
However, R&I also flagged risks that warrant attention, including credit growth, banking-sector liquidity, property lending, the financial system's capacity to provide sufficient capital and the level of foreign exchange reserves.
The upgrade comes amid continued volatility and uncertainty in the global economy. The Ministry of Finance described Vietnam's first investment-grade rating from an international credit rating agency as an important milestone in the country's efforts to strengthen its sovereign creditworthiness and advance economic reforms.
The ministry said the rating reflected Vietnam's solid macroeconomic foundations, sustained efforts to achieve high and sustainable growth, prudent public debt management and far-reaching reforms. It added that the upgrade would strengthen investor confidence and improve access to long-term financing for socio-economic development.
The ministry and other government agencies will continue working closely with R&I and other credit rating agencies, providing timely and comprehensive information on Vietnam's socio-economic conditions, public finances and debt to ensure future assessments are based on accurate, up-to-date data.

articles.title: US expert: APEC 2027 is an opportunity for Vietnam to elevate its position. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: US expert: APEC 2027 is an opportunity for Vietnam to elevate its position.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Amidst escalating US-China competition, continued shifts in global supply chains, and the reshaping of the regional economy by artificial intelligence (AI), Vietnam is preparing to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Forum for the third time in 2027. Compared to its previous hosting in 2006 and 2017, Vietnam enters APEC 2027 with significantly changed economic standing and international role.
In an interview with The National Bureau of Asian Research (NBR) , a US-based policy research organization focusing on Asian affairs and international relations, Marc Mealy, Executive Vice President for Research and Head of Policy at the US-ASEAN Business Council, stated that APEC 2027 will provide Vietnam with an important platform to advance its strategic, economic, and diplomatic goals; while strengthening the role of the private sector, attracting investment, and enhancing Vietnam's competitiveness in global value chains.
Vietnam enters APEC 2027 in a different position.
According to Marc Mealy, compared to its two previous hosting stints in 2006 and 2017, Vietnam enters APEC 2027 in a very different position.
After recently being officially reclassified as an upper-middle-income economy , over the past two decades, Vietnam has transformed from a low-income developing economy into one of the most dynamic manufacturing and trading hubs in the region. GDP has increased from approximately US$66 billion in 2006 to over US$500 billion today, while total trade has risen from US$85 billion to nearly US$1 trillion.
Marc Mealy noted that the domestic political landscape has also changed significantly, while economic development is placed at the center of policy planning. Vietnam is pursuing an ambitious economic agenda, focused on maintaining an annual growth rate of over 10% through domestic reforms. New strategies and policy initiatives focus on enhancing national competitiveness, moving Vietnam up the global value chain, attracting higher-quality investment, and deepening international integration.
In this context, according to Marc Mealy, Vietnam will leverage its role as APEC host as a platform to pursue important strategic, economic, and diplomatic goals. APEC creates space for Vietnam to build its agenda in areas such as food security, the digital economy, and the “silver economy” to serve national interests. As it implements its economic transformation program, Vietnam can use APEC to promote national and regional initiatives focused on economic resilience, productivity-driven growth, and trade dynamism.
Furthermore, APEC will allow Vietnam to host dialogues between leaders of global economies and business leaders during a period that is both witnessing numerous global challenges and the increasingly prominent role of Asia in the world economy.
Marc Mealy believes that successfully promoting the APEC 2027 theme of “Connectivity: Building Inclusive and Resilient Economies” will demonstrate the country’s ability to bridge the gap between major powers, particularly the US and China , while maintaining a focus on substantive economic cooperation.
Strengthening its position as a manufacturing and logistics hub.
You may also like
According to Marc Mealy, fundamental changes in US trade policy and shocks to the global economy are prompting governments around the world to pursue a range of policies and strategies to ensure energy security, diversify trade, and enhance economic resilience.
As one of the world's leading countries in utilizing preferential free trade agreements (FTAs) as a competitive advantage to attract FDI, Vietnam can leverage APEC to strengthen its image as a "reliable" preferential trading partner by enhancing strategic trade management capabilities and strengthening regional cooperation in digitizing customs and trade processes and procedures.
According to Marc Mealy, Vietnam has actually expanded its FTA network from just two agreements in 2006 to 18 agreements currently, including a newly signed FTA with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which includes Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Switzerland.
AI and digital transformation: A new space for collaboration.
Assessing Vietnam's agenda at APEC 2027, Marc Mealy noted that the program currently revolves around themes such as science, technology, and innovation; digital transformation; economic and trade connectivity, including supply chain resilience. Human resource development and the role of AI are also likely to be emphasized topics.
According to him, as Vietnam aims to rapidly expand the role of the digital economy in promoting innovation-based economic growth, it can leverage several APEC work programs, such as the principles of trade digitalization discussed at the Ministerial Meeting on Trade, as well as private sector-led initiatives like the APEC RISE (Resilient, Inclusive and Sustainable Economies) project of the US Government, to promote regional cooperation and public-private partnerships on AI and digital trade governance.
APEC will also provide an opportunity for Vietnam to showcase its domestic initiatives, such as promoting Ho Chi Minh City as a national hub for "finance and digital technology".
According to Marc Mealy, this is also an opportunity for Vietnam to promote greater synchronization between digital governance initiatives in the Asia-Pacific region and regional efforts such as the ASEAN Framework Agreement on the Digital Economy, thereby strengthening its role as a bridge between ASEAN and the broader Asia-Pacific region, while promoting more compatible digital trade regulations and technology standards.
Attracting investment for green transformation
Marc Mealy stated that hosting APEC 2027 provides Vietnam with a strategic platform to attract international capital for the green transition process, while ensuring economic growth and energy security.
According to him, Vietnam is one of the important case studies in the world among emerging markets, demonstrating how a rapidly growing economy can address the need for large-scale investment and reforms to support projects that enhance energy security in the short term, while also facilitating projects that support the energy transition in the medium term.
APEC 2027 provides an opportunity for the country to shape regional discussions on green trade, financing for transformation, sustainable infrastructure, and climate resilience; thereby helping to attract the necessary capital and expertise to address major gaps in infrastructure financing, particularly for energy projects.
You may also like
In particular, according to Marc Mealy, the CEO Summit will be a place where Vietnam's public and private sectors can showcase investment opportunities in these projects.
Measures of success for APEC Year 2027
Looking ahead to 2027 and beyond, Marc Mealy believes Vietnam is benefiting from strong growth in trade and FDI. APEC 2027 will provide a crucial opportunity for Vietnam to demonstrate its ability to implement ambitious reform plans and build international support for its long-term development vision.
According to him, a successful APEC Year can be judged by its contribution to the country's economic transformation program, its support for strategic trade management and trade diversification efforts, and its ability to attract investment into key sectors of society.
Against the backdrop of a rapidly evolving regional economy and geopolitics, APEC 2027 will be an opportunity for Vietnam to both advance its domestic development priorities and contribute to common regional issues. Vietnam is currently among the world's top 20 exporters of goods and services. “As APEC continues to enhance Vietnam’s global competitiveness to attract FDI and elevate the country’s position in global value chains for technology manufacturing and higher value-added sectors, this can contribute to sustaining Vietnam’s impressive development record in the long term,” concluded Marc Mealy.

articles.title: 46% of APAC Consumers Likely to Use Stablecoins by 2031: Visa Survey - Fintech Singapore
articles.summary: 46% of APAC Consumers Likely to Use Stablecoins by 2031: Visa Survey  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
Visa has released survey findings on stablecoin awareness and consumer sentiment across Asia Pacific.
Nearly half of consumers (46%) say they are likely to use stablecoins, digital tokens pegged to an asset such as the US dollar, within five years, yet only 16% have used them in the past 12 months.
The Visa Consumer 360 study surveyed 14,250 consumers aged 18 to 65 across 14 markets, including Singapore, with fieldwork carried out in June and July 2026.
According to Visa, consumers are beginning to see stablecoins as a tool for everyday spending rather than a crypto-trading instrument. Interest extends to online purchases, travel spending and overseas shopping.
Visa survey points to cross-border potential
Cross-border money movement is another area of interest, with 49% of respondents believing stablecoins could become a common way to send money abroad within five years.
Visa said this points to possible relevance for remittances and international transfers.
Hong Kong (84%), India (80%) and Thailand (77%) recorded the highest awareness of stablecoins. Vietnam and India, both at 67%, showed the strongest intent to use them within five years. Visa did not publish a market-level figure for Singapore.
“We’re seeing a meaningful shift in how consumers across Asia Pacific think about stablecoins,”
said Nischint Sanghavi, Head of Digital Currencies, Asia Pacific, Visa.
“Consumers are beginning to see how stablecoins could support the ways they already spend and move money, particularly through online purchases, travel and cross-border transfers.”
Awareness runs ahead of understanding
Two-thirds of consumers in the region (66%) are aware of stablecoins, but only 6% demonstrate an accurate understanding of how they work.
Among those who are aware, 49% believe stablecoins can only be used to buy and sell other cryptocurrencies, while 41% believe stablecoins always increase in value.
Fraud concerns weigh on adoption. Among consumers who know about stablecoins but have never used them, 38% cited worries about fraud or scams and 36% pointed to a lack of understanding.
Respondents placed the most trust in regulated providers, ranking government or central bank-linked entities (27%) and banks or regulated financial institutions (26%) highest.
Visa said adoption will depend on whether stablecoins can be made understandable, secure and useful in everyday payments.
The company is working with banks, regulated financial institutions and payment partners to connect stablecoin capabilities with familiar ways to pay.
That work includes the Visa Stablecoin Platform, which Visa unveiled in July for a select group of beta clients to issue, move and manage stablecoins.
“Consumers want stablecoins to feel like a natural part of the payments they already trust, not a separate system,”
said Sanghavi.
“Our role is to connect emerging stablecoin technology with the secure, familiar payment experiences consumers rely on every day.”
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is consulting on amendments to the Payment Services Act that would give its stablecoin framework legal force.

articles.title: Vietnamese steel stocks poised for new growth cycle - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnamese steel stocks poised for new growth cycle  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnamese steel demand is recovering strongly on the back of public investment and residential construction, while some companies have completed or are nearing the commissioning of major capacity expansion projects.
However, growth across the sector remains uneven, with hot-rolled coil (HRC) and construction steel benefiting more clearly, while coated steel producers continue to face pressure from exports and excess capacity.
Growth driven by domestic demand
According to the Vietnam Steel Association (VSA), the steel industry is showing positive growth. In the first seven months of the year, production of finished steel products reached 21.4 million tons, up 15.4% from the same period in 2025, while sales rose 15.6% to 21.2 million tons.
HRC has been one of the key growth drivers, while construction steel has continued to play a leading role. By contrast, cold-rolled steel output fell 1.6% and coated steel declined 9%. Notably, growth has been supported mainly by domestic demand, while steel exports fell slightly by 1.4%.
For the third quarter, MBS Securities forecasts that steel consumption will continue to rise. With infrastructure and residential construction driving domestic demand, domestic steel output is expected to reach 7.68 million tons, up 20% year-on-year. Construction steel and HRC are expected to be the main drivers, with output projected to rise 26% and 35%, respectively.
In addition to favorable demand, the imposition of anti-dumping duties on wide-width HRC has helped lift the domestic HRC market share to above 70%, from around 60% in 2025, as steel imports from China fell more than 10% year-on-year.
Stronger demand and easing pressure from Chinese steel have also supported selling prices. According to MBS, construction steel prices rose about 7% year-on-year to $560 per ton, while HRC prices increased 6% to $550 per ton in the third quarter.
On the cost side, raw material prices have moved in different directions. Iron ore prices have remained around $96 per ton, while coal prices rose about 15% to $265 per ton. Although higher coal prices are putting pressure on input costs, improving steel prices and stable iron ore prices are expected to help steelmakers further improve their margins.
First-half results showed that gross margins at most steel companies increased from a year earlier. Hoa Phat Group (HPG) posted a gross margin of 17.4%, up from 16.3% a year earlier, while Nam Kim Steel (NKG) saw its margin rise from 6.7% to 7%. Vietnam Steel Corporation (TVN) increased its gross margin from 4.2% to 5.3%.
The VSA said Vietnam's steel industry continues to face challenges from global overcapacity, which is fuelling greater protectionism in steel export markets. However, with the government targeting double-digit GDP growth and a number of public and private projects overcoming obstacles and accelerating construction, domestic steel demand has further room to grow.
Which steelmakers stand to benefit?
The industry outlook shows that growth in steel output is clearly uneven. While HRC and construction steel are expanding strongly, coated steel, cold-rolled steel and exports are declining. This suggests that the benefits will vary across steel companies.
According to Techcombank Securities (TCBS), listed steel companies can be divided into three groups.
The first group comprises producers of crude steel, long steel products and steel pipes, including HPG, TVN, TIS, VGS and POM. These companies either produce billets themselves or purchase billets for rolling, so their revenue is relatively directly linked to domestic construction demand.
The second group consists of coated steel and downstream flat steel producers, including HSG, GDA, NKG and DTL. These companies purchase hot-rolled coil and process it into coated steel and steel pipes. Exports have historically accounted for a large share of their sales, but the group is facing growing pressure from trade defence measures and protectionist policies in major markets.
The final group comprises steel traders and processors, including SMC, TLH and VCA. These companies mainly trade steel and provide basic processing services, with thin margins and earnings that are highly dependent on steel price movements while inventory is held.
According to data, first-half revenue at 12 listed steel companies reached VND185,654 billion ($7.18 billion), up 23.8%, while net profit attributable to shareholders of parent companies rose 98.3% year-on-year to VND16,533 billion ($639.53 million).
However, growth was uneven. While Hoa Phat and Vietnam Steel reported higher revenue, Hoa Sen, Ton Dong A and Nam Kim recorded declines. For coated steel producers, improved margins were mainly driven by higher selling prices rather than higher output.
On the stock market, steel shares have also been moving on expectations of benefits from accelerated public investment and a recovery in residential construction.
Against a weak broader market, HPG shares have fallen about 28% over the past year to VND20,000 ($0.77). TVN is trading around VND9,700, down 13% from its June 2026 level but still 17% higher than a year ago.
Meanwhile, NKG, HSG and SMC have suffered steeper declines, losing 40-80% of their value over the past year. NKG is currently trading at VND9,340, its lowest level since February 2023. HSG has also fallen back to around its April 2025 level, when tariff-related disruption hit markets, at VND9,990 ($0.39).
Major investment cycle nearing completion
One notable feature of the steel sector is that many companies are entering the final stages of major investment projects. This could become a new growth driver, but it also places greater demands on their ability to generate sales and operate efficiently.
Hoa Phat Group said its flagship Dung Quat 2 steel complex (Quang Ngai province), with total investment of VND85 trillion ($3.29 billion), reached full operation from the first quarter of 2026, with HRC as its main product. The expansion lifted the group's total HRC capacity to 8.6 million tons per year.
With the new capacity, Hoa Phat's HRC output reached 3.4 million tons in the first half, up 57% year-on-year and significantly faster than overall industry growth. Total sales volume rose 32% to 6.5 million tons.
At Nam Kim, the Nam Kim Phu My roofing steel project, with total investment of VND6.2 trillion (VND239.87 million) and annual coated steel capacity of 800,000 tons, is also nearing commercial operation.
Company executives said at the 2026 annual general meeting that the project produced its first steel coil on April 10, 2026, targeting official operation by the end of the second quarter and commercial output from the third quarter.
However, Nam Kim's first-half financial statements showed that construction in progress for the steel plant stood at VND5,149 billion ($199.2 million) at the end of June and had largely not yet been transferred to fixed assets.
Ton Dong A is also developing its fourth plant at the Phu My Specialized Industrial Park, with total capacity of 1.2 million tons per year and total investment of VND7 trillion ($270.82 million).
The company began preparing the project and obtained its investment licence in the fourth quarter of 2024. However, construction did not begin until June 2026, with the first phase, featuring annual capacity of 600,000 tons, expected to come online in 2027.
Like Nam Kim's Phu My plant, Ton Dong A's fourth plant is targeting specialized steel products for industries with high technical requirements, including home appliances, furniture, automobiles and manufacturing. Company executives said these products have strong growth potential and are aligned with Vietnam's move to upgrade its industrial production value chain.
The new wave of steel investment is therefore not only aimed at expanding capacity but also at developing higher-value-added products to support industrialization and the upgrading of domestic supply chains.
As the major investment cycle enters its final stages, steelmakers have an opportunity to accelerate growth as new capacity begins contributing to output and revenue. However, this is also a period when companies will face pressure from sales, operating costs and interest expenses.
The new steel cycle is therefore unlikely to generate uniform growth across the sector. The advantage will favor companies that combine new capacity with a product mix suited to domestic demand, while maintaining tight control over costs and sales. For companies still heavily reliant on exports or trading activities, higher overall industry output may not necessarily translate into a comparable increase in profit.

articles.summary: Co-pilot accused of trying to hijack Flydubai plane probably acted alone, Israeli sources say  Yahoo News SingaporeFlydubai co-pilot in murder-suicide mission trained to fly in Britain, Telegraph says  The Straits TimesFlydubai cockpit attack: Israel to honour Indian pilot Smit Machchhar with top civilian bravery award  The Times of IndiaFlydubai co-pilot completed portion of his flight training in New Zealand, police say  CNAWhat are the five questions be...
articles.full_text:
The co-pilot accused of attacking his colleague on board the Flydubai flight to Israel and trying to seize the controls probably acted alone, Israeli sources told CNN.
International investigators are still working to determine a motive but an Israeli official said information from the inquiry suggested the suspect acted alone.
Another Israeli source said that, at the moment, Israel does not know of any link to a group or government. Both stressed this was their understanding so far.
The United Arab Emirates and Israel are both investigating the incident. The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing, is also conducting investigations.
The attorney general of the UAE, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said the co-pilot on board the flight had attempted to seize control of the plane by attacking his colleague with a crash ax – a piece of equipment required on most aircraft. The attorney general called the attempted hijacking a "terrorist act."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday that Israel understands the suspect "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" collected during the suspect's ongoing questioning. Netanyahu did not give any further details.
In the immediate aftermath of the attack, US President Donald Trump said that the suspect could be linked to Iran "based on what I'm hearing." But he gave no other details.
Flydubai flight FZ1073 narrowly avoided disaster on its journey from Dubai, plummeting thousands of feet in a matter of minutes amid the attack on the plane's captain.
Despite being wounded, pilot Captain Smit Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door and signal his distress to passengers and crew, who bravely rushed into the cockpit to regain control of the aircraft.
Sources told CNN the suspect, named as Hamam al-Hammami, is an Omani national who had been removed from a previous job at Oman's national airline last year following concerns about his extremist views.
A LinkedIn profile bearing the name Hamam al-Hammami said he worked at Oman Air for seven years, leaving in February 2025, before joining the Moroccan airline Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and departing in January 2026. One source told CNN that the profile belongs to the Flydubai pilot in Wednesday's incident. The profile has since been deleted and CNN has reached out to LinkedIn for comment.
A post made to the LinkedIn profile on Wednesday, about nine hours after the incident, included a photo of the former leader of al Qaeda. It is unclear who published the posts or whether they were scheduled in advance.
An Israeli official told CNN that al-Hammami had worked for Flydubai for only eight months.
Another source said the alleged assailant had previously worked for Royal Air Maroc. In a statement to the Associated Press, Air Maroc said the suspect trained with the airline for three months in 2025 as part of the pre-employment process but he was not selected.
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) also told CNN that it is investigating al-Hammami's links to the country, and said an update will be provided when appropriate.
New Zealand Police confirmed to CNN on Monday that the co-pilot spent time in the country, and that authorities there are also now investigating.
Questions remain over how a citizen of Oman, a country which does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel, was authorized to co-pilot a plane bound for Tel Aviv, despite Israel's strict security regulations.
The names of all passengers and crew were provided to Israeli authorities before the flight had taken off, Israel's Tax Authority confirmed, adding that it is the Transportation Ministry's responsibility to give answers on the matter of vetting. But a Transportation Ministry spokesperson told reporters on Saturday that its protocols do not include checking the names of flight crew members.
The incident has triggered criticism of the Israeli government, particularly Transport Minister Miri Regev, and some opposition figures have called for her removal from office.
CNN's Abbas Al Lawati, Kylie Atwood, Isaac Yee, Avery Schmitz, Thomas Bordeaux, Teele Rebane and Todd Symons contributed to this report.

articles.title: Singapore stands out among wealthiest nations because of its ‘lower-income neighbourhood’, says Ho Ching - The Independent Singapore
articles.summary: Singapore stands out among wealthiest nations because of its ‘lower-income neighbourhood’, says Ho Ching  The Independent Singapore
articles.full_text:
SINGAPORE: On Tuesday (Oct 6), former Temasek Holdings executive director and CEO Ho Ching shared a post on social media that featured Singapore in the top 10 richest countries for 2026.
Ranked sixth on the list, Singapore has an estimated value of US$107,758 (approximately S$138,000) per capita.
The post Madam Ho, the wife of Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong, had shared was from The Financial Coconut, which used data from the International Monetary Fund’s World Economic Outlook 2026. Liechtenstein ranks first with an estimated value of US$226,809 (approximately S$290,000) nominal GDP per capita.
“Singapore’s position among the world’s highest-GDP-per-capita economies is not simply a story of high salaries. It reflects an economic model built around trade, finance, technology and the ability to generate significant output from a relatively small domestic base,” reads the post from The Financial Coconut, though it acknowledged that due to its heavy reliance on international trade, imported energy and external technology demand, the Singapore model comes with exposure.
It also pointed out that the IMF noted that the city-state “has a relatively lower labour share of income,” which means the greater part of economic resources goes to businesses instead of directly to households.
“This is one reason why exceptionally high GDP per capita should not automatically be interpreted as equivalent household income,” it added.
But back to Mdm Ho. She pointed out that on the top 10 list, aside from the United States, every single country is a small economy, “most of whom are also resource poor.”
Indeed, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg (ranked 2nd), Ireland (3rd), Switzerland (4th), Iceland (5th), Singapore, Norway (7th), Denmark (9th), and the Netherlands (10th) are all small-to-medium economies in that they are physically and demographically small, especially in comparison to the superpowers, China and the US.
She added, however, “Of these, SG stands out as a centre in lower-income neighbourhood(s) while the rest of the small wealthiest per capita economies have got wealthy neighbourhoods,” and called it food for thought.

articles.title: Edging upwards in real estate transparency - Vietnam Economic Times
articles.summary: Edging upwards in real estate transparency  Vietnam Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The Global Real Estate Transparency Index (GRETI) 2026 report, released recently by JLL, showed that Vietnam currently ranks 50th out of the 88 countries and territories surveyed, with a transparency score of 3.15 that sees it remain in the “Semi-Transparent” category. Notably, Vietnam is one of ten markets with the strongest score improvement globally during the 2024-2026 survey period, alongside Poland, Thailand, Australia, Qatar, South Korea, India, Saudi Arabia, Dubai, and Abu Dhabi. “Vietnam’s inclusion in the Top 10 most-improved transparency markets globally in the 2026 GRETI reflects years of consistent effort,” said Ms. Le Thi Huyen Trang, Country Head and Head of Research and Advisory for Vietnam at JLL.
Positive signs
Globally, two-thirds of the 88 markets surveyed recorded increases in their transparency score over the past two years. However, the gap between leading and other markets continues to widen: the “Highly Transparent” and “Transparent” groups now attract over 98 per cent of total global commercial real estate investment, with the “Highly Transparent” group accounting for some 81 per cent.
In contrast, the “Semi-Transparent” group, where Vietnam currently sits, accounts for about 1.3 per cent of global capital flows, indicating significant potential to attract more investment as the market continues to enhance its transparency.
Vietnam was in the “Low Transparency” group prior to 2020, with typical challenges including limited market data and a complex legal framework, particularly for foreign investors on property ownership matters, according to JLL and LaSalle data.
From 2020 to present, the country moved into the “Semi-Transparent” group, with 2024 serving as a critical year for the development of the legal framework: the amended Land Law, Law on Housing, and Law on Real Estate Business all took effect; the new Law on Prices requires appraisers to hold professional certificates and maintain verifiable valuation records; and real estate transactions must be conducted through the banking system.
Decree No. 357 regulating the establishment, management, and operation of information systems and databases on housing and the real estate market officially came into effect in 2026, with the goal of completing the national land database by the end of the year. Vietnam has also seen increasing adoption of sustainable development practices in the real estate sector.
Mr. Vo Van Huu Phuoc, Head of Valuation & Risk Advisory for Vietnam at JLL, said the country is gradually digitizing land records and establishing a unified real estate registration system, moving toward the adoption of international valuation standards such as International Property Measurement Standards (IPMS). “These are key factors that help bridge the gap, enhance the reliability of valuation results, and strengthen foreign investors’ confidence in the market,” he added.
Ms. Trang said that from 2012 to now, the market has evolved from its early stages to establish a much stronger foundation due to ongoing legal reforms. “In particular, the comprehensive changes from 2025 - from improving the legal framework and streamlining administrative procedures to economic policy reforms - have delivered initial positive results, as evidenced by continually increasing total registered FDI figures,” she continued. “Notably, seven-month 2026 figures came in at $38.1 billion; nearly equal to total registered FDI for the entire previous year and a record high over the past decade. This clearly demonstrates that Vietnam remains one of the most attractive destinations in the Asia-Pacific region.”
However, she added that the rapid pace of regulatory change reflects both positive developments and certain challenges. While legal regulations previously remained unchanged for extended periods, the recent acceleration in the pace of change requires stakeholders to take time to adapt. For foreign investors, this situation fosters a degree of caution, as they must weigh whether the regulations currently in effect will remain applicable and suitable in the future.
Cost no longer an advantage
Amid rising global economic and geopolitical instability, JLL views real estate market transparency as increasingly critical for investors. However, cost is no longer Vietnam’s primary advantage; a trend clearly reflected in the industrial real estate sector.
According to JLL research, while Vietnam was previously known as a low-cost destination, the post-Covid-19 era has seen a shift in focus away from cost and toward the efficiency and production capabilities of the Vietnamese workforce. A key issue has arisen - though labor costs in Vietnam remain lower than in many other countries, they are rising faster than labor productivity is improving. This matter is particularly significant as Vietnam seeks to attract high-value FDI, which demands higher levels of labor efficiency and workforce capability.
Ms. Trang pointed out that Vietnam’s property market is currently prioritized due to various competitive advantages. Vietnam boasts a highly-strategic geographical location. Research into the industrial real estate sector reveals that its location and extensive coastline play a pivotal role in linking international maritime networks with the manufacturing bases of the entire region, not just Vietnam itself. This is an advantage that is difficult to replicate and remains a key factor keeping Vietnam firmly on the map in FDI attraction.
While it possesses a young workforce that continues to grow in size, the growth rate is decelerating while labor costs are rising. Though labor productivity has improved, it has not yet reached the necessary levels. While these issues warrant attention, the positive aspect is that there is still room for improvement.
A high degree of economic openness, as evidenced by the presence of numerous FDI enterprises and an extensive network of signed trade agreements, represents another advantage for Vietnam. A business establishing production facilities in the country gains access to a global market of over 5 billion people across nations with which Vietnam has signed trade agreements. This offers a distinct advantage over other countries in the region.
Connectivity infrastructure is another crucial factor. When compared to other Southeast Asian nations and taking into account geographical characteristics and recent investments, Vietnam retains certain advantages. However, this edge could be lost if the country fails to maintain its focus on investment and infrastructure development. “Overall, when all these factors are considered, Vietnam remains among the leaders in the region,” said Ms. Trang. “However, Vietnam also needs to make further efforts to leverage its existing advantages while improving factors that can make a difference in the near future.”
Route to a transparent market
Among the nearly 260 criteria used to assess the GRETI 2026, the first four indicators play a decisive role and account for approximately 80 per cent of the total weight: performance measurement (25 per cent), regulatory & legal (23.5 per cent), market fundamentals (16.5 per cent), and transaction processes (15 per cent). According to Mr. Phuoc, Vietnam is currently making solid progress on the middle three indicators, including regulatory & legal, market fundamentals, and transaction processes.
However, the combined weight of these three factors is only around 55 per cent, while the first indicator - performance measurement - accounts for 25 per cent of the total and is an area where Vietnam has seen little improvement. “This suggests that to enhance transparency, the primary focus should be on these initial factors, as they carry significant weight and are crucial for improving the country’s ranking,” Mr. Phuoc said.
Based on the experience of more advanced markets, JLL believes the roadmap to bring Vietnam closer to Transparent Market status will continue to focus on six key areas: completing land record digitization; establishing a unified nationwide real estate registration system; adopting IPMS; publishing data on the commercial real estate credit market; promoting green building certification linked to master planning and clear databases; and strengthening disclosure requirements for listed companies.
JLL noted that amid increasing global economic and geopolitical uncertainty, real estate market transparency has become more important than ever for investors, especially as factors such as AI applications, capital reallocation into structural growth segments, energy security, and credit market transparency are reshaping investment decision-making globally.

By Philip J. Heijmans
(Bloomberg) – Singapore's top diplomat touted what he called "a moment of great potential" for Southeast Asia, as economies expand rapidly on surging technology demand even as much of the world faces growing uncertainties.
Speaking during a conference on Wednesday, Minister for Foreign Affairs Vivian Balakrishnan said semiconductors and AI were major drivers helping the region's economies outperform expectations. He noted that the city-state expanded 6.1% in the first half of the year, with Taiwan overtaking China to become its biggest trading partner.
"In the midst of a crazy world, in the midst of the breakdown in world order, the breakdown in trade, the disruption to supply chains, we're having significant growth," he said. "In fact, to the point where you start having to worry – why is it so high?"
Asia's powerhouse economies have seized the lion's share of trade growth in the global AI boom, because they make the chips and other equipment needed for data centers springing up around the globe. The World Bank cites several Asian economies that have outpaced expectations on high-tech exports, with Vietnam expected to grow 7.4% in 2026, Indonesia 5.2% and Malaysia 5.1%.
Singapore's electronics exports surged 132% in August from a year earlier, and the island nation has upgraded its 2026 economic growth forecast to between 4.5%-5.5%. Vietnam and Malaysia have likewise strengthened their roles in electronics supply chains as firms spread production across more locations.
But the World Bank has also warned that the region's dependence on AI-related industry could become a weakness if global investment in the technology slows.
Balakrishnan acknowledged the risks posed by the technology itself, saying "loss of control is a real threat." He also said rogue states and non-state actors could use AI to develop new forms of disruption, including in chemistry, biology and weapons of mass destruction.
Still, with Singapore set to chair the regional bloc known as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations next year, the diplomat said the region should use the momentum to deepen economic integration.
"This is a moment of great potential and peril," Balakrishnan said – later adding: "There's also a lot of money to be made."

articles.title: MAS rolls out AI risk management guidelines for Singapore’s financial sector - The Business Times
articles.summary: MAS rolls out AI risk management guidelines for Singapore’s financial sector  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
Expectations include accountability for managing risks from third-party artificial intelligence use
[SINGAPORE] The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has issued new guidelines spelling out supervisory expectations for financial institutions to manage risks arising from artificial intelligence use.
The Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management will take effect on Oct 7, 2027, and apply to all financial institutions and all forms of AI technologies.
The central bank noted in a media statement on Wednesday (Oct 7) that financial regulators and international bodies are “highlighting the need to manage AI risks effectively while enabling firms to realise the benefits of adoption”.
The guidelines follow a public consultation, where respondents expressed “strong support” for a principles-based and risk-proportionate approach, said MAS.
Meanwhile, financial institutions should assess how to best meet these expectations based on the nature and scale of their AI use, it added.
They may implement the guidelines in phases, and should meet the expectations set out in Sections 3 to 4 from Oct 7, 2027, and Sections 5 and 6 by Oct 7, 2028.
The release of the guidelines follows the formation of the AI-Driven Cyber and Technology Risk Taskforce in July by MAS and the Association of Banks in Singapore to strengthen collective cyber and technology resilience in response to the emerging risks posed by frontier AI models.
Key expectations
The guidelines laid out four key expectations for financial institutions to manage risks arising from AI use.
First, the board and senior management of financial institutions should provide effective oversight of AI risks with clear accountabilities. This includes setting clear risk appetite, management frameworks, policies and procedures.
MAS noted that existing governance structures may be used where they provide adequate oversight and cross-functional coordination, and financial institutions need not establish a dedicated AI committee solely to meet this expectation.
Second, financial institutions should identify, assess and manage AI risks across the AI life cycle and apply proportionate controls.
These controls, which should be reviewed regularly, include data governance, testing, human oversight, cybersecurity, monitoring and change management.
MAS said it intends to further consult the financial sector in 2027 on what additional guidance on agentic AI would be useful.
Third, financial institutions should manage the risks from third-party AI use. This includes remaining accountable for AI used in the services they deliver, including AI developed, operated or provided by third parties.
If the risks cannot be brought within the institution’s risk appetite, it should consider limiting, suspending or replacing the use of the third-party AI service, noted MAS.
Lastly, financial institutions should apply the guidelines in a risk-proportionate manner, meaning that the extent and sophistication of controls should depend on its risk exposure.
Ho Hern Shin, deputy managing director at MAS, said that AI has “significant potential” to improve financial services.
“Realising these benefits sustainably requires financial institutions to understand and manage the risks that come with increasingly capable AI systems,” she pointed out.
“With greater regulatory clarity on financial institutions’ AI usage, financial institutions can innovate with confidence, while maintaining the trust of customers and the resilience of Singapore’s financial system,” she added.

articles.title: Malaysia’s innovation shortfall stems from a structural phenomenon - Newswav
articles.summary: Malaysia’s innovation shortfall stems from a structural phenomenon  Newswav
articles.full_text:
Murray Hunter
THE core causes of the lack of innovation, such as rent-seeking dominance, policy distortions, institutional weaknesses, cultural barriers, and brain drain, track closely with observable economic patterns.
Other nations that achieved a high innovation economy, like Japan in the 1980s, South Korea in the 1990s–2000s, and more recently China, were able to shift from commodity/OEM dependence toward proprietary technology, branding, process excellence, and dense private-sector ecosystems.
It is clear that Malaysia has not been able to make that transition yet.
Malaysia’s Core Economic Structure
Malaysia’s GDP is still heavily weighted toward government and household consumption, commodities (palm oil, petroleum, rubber), and OEM/electronics assembly exports.
Government-linked companies (GLCs) control large swathes of banking, utilities, plantations, and infrastructure, where many operate with soft budget constraints and political mandates rather than pure commercial pressure.
This crowds out private risk-taking. The informal sector is substantial and under-measured, while the roughly one million MSMEs are mostly low-productivity, family-run operations focused on local trade or basic services rather than scalable product or process innovation.
Industry 4.0, AI, and “new frontier” rhetoric appear in official five-year plans, yet the country consistently underperforms peers on actual technology adoption, venture scaling, and high-value IP commercialisation.
Brain drain is well-documented, with skilled talent and startup founders relocating to Singapore, Australia, the US, or Europe, citing opportunity, rule of law, and less bureaucratic friction.
Patents and academic publication counts are imperfect proxies. They reflect research funding volume more than commercial impact.
More telling indicators are total factor productivity growth, share of high-tech exports that are Malaysian-owned brands or IP, venture-capital exits of domestic origin, and the density of firms that iteratively improve products and capture global margins.
Policy and Institutional Barriers
Equity rules, which include the controversial 30% Bumiputera equity requirement in certain sectors and licensing preferences, raise the cost of capital and reduce founders’ control over ownership and governance.
For capital-intensive or talent-driven startups, the ability to choose investors and align incentives is a very important consideration for technopreneurs.
Any government mandate that constrains that choice acts as a disincentive to any experimentation.
Similar protectionist licensing, quota, and oligopoly arrangements in logistics, distribution, professional services, and other sectors raise barriers to entry relative to more open markets.
Direct-selling and multi-level marketing regulations, for example, are tighter than in many comparator economies.
Corruption and weak intellectual-property enforcement compound the problem.
When ideas can be appropriated with limited recourse, or when contracts and permits depend on political connections, the expected return on genuine innovation falls.
Tall-poppy dynamics and high power-distance cultural norms further suppress the open challenge of hierarchy that is common in high-innovation environments.
Education, Culture, and Human Capital
The current education system emphasises rote learning and exams over sustained critical inquiry and creative problem-solving. Combined with hierarchical workplace norms that discourage subordinates from proposing ideas the boss did not originate.
This produces fewer people willing or able to drive incremental technical and commercial improvement. Psychological safety, i.e., the willingness to take interpersonal risk, is lower when status competition and envy are strong.
Racism, Diversity, and Innovation Evidence
Cross-disciplinary research does show that systemic exclusion of talent reduces the size of the invention pipeline (“lost Einsteins”), that reduced psychological safety wastes cognitive resources, and that homogeneous teams underperform cognitively diverse ones on complex problem-solving.
Historical US data on the effects of racial violence and segregation on patenting rates (Lisa Cook and related work) is clear. At the same time, the causal pathway is primarily through blocked access to education, capital, networks, and safety rather than some abstract “racism score.” Cultural creativity under adversity is real, yet commercial scaling and IP capture still require open institutions.
Malaysia’s post-independence ethnic preferential policies were designed as a response to colonial-era imbalances and 1969 communal violence.
They have produced measurable gains in Malay participation in the formal economy and higher education, but they also create ongoing distortions in capital allocation, firm ownership, and talent selection.
The net effect on aggregate innovation capacity is negative when the policies raise the cost of starting and scaling high-potential firms or push talent abroad. Treating the entire society as a single “racist” unit is less precise than examining the concrete mechanisms like equity quotas, licensing preferences, public-sector hiring patterns, and informal networks. These mechanisms effectively allocate economic opportunity.
What Successful Transitions to Innovation Economies Look Like
Japan, South Korea, and later China combined have showed the most important chrematistics of an innovation economy are:
An export discipline that forced continuous quality and cost improvement.
A heavy private investment in applied R&D and process engineering, not just academic papers.
Relatively open capital markets for high-growth firms and willingness to let unsuccessful firms fail.
Education systems that, over time, raised technical competence and, in the Korean and Chinese cases, increasingly rewarded performance over pedigree, and Institutions that, imperfectly, protected IP and contracts enough for firms to capture returns.
Malaysia still possesses advantages that can be leveraged upon.
These include strategic location, English proficiency among elites, existing electronics clusters, and fiscal resources.
Converting those into sustained innovation requires reducing rent-seeking opportunities, lowering ownership and licensing barriers for startups, strengthening IP enforcement, reforming education toward problem-solving and technical depth, and making the country a place where high-ability people of any background prefer to build rather than leave.
Without changes in those structural incentives, the economy risks remaining in the commodity-OEM-consumption equilibrium while others pull further ahead on proprietary technology and branding. – October 9, 2026
