articles.title: Generative AI becomes shopping adviser for 58% of urban Vietnamese consumers - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Generative AI becomes shopping adviser for 58% of urban Vietnamese consumers  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming part of the shopping journey in Vietnam, with 58% of urban users turning to tools such as ChatGPT and Gemini to research products and services before buying, according to a survey by market research firm Q&Me.
The survey of 200 generative AI users aged 20 to 49 in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi found that 96% had used generative AI within the previous month. The findings suggest conversational AI is moving beyond general information retrieval to become an increasingly important part of the consumer purchase journey.
ChatGPT and Gemini dominate AI use
OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini account for a combined 90% of primary generative AI tool usage among respondents.
ChatGPT had the broadest reach, with 80% of respondents reporting use of the platform and 53% identifying it as their most-used tool. Gemini followed with a 68% usage rate, while 37% named it their primary platform.
Usage patterns varied by age and gender. Gemini was particularly popular among consumers in their 30s, with adoption reaching 83%. ChatGPT was more popular among women, with 63% of female respondents choosing it as their primary tool, compared with 44% of men.
Other platforms had significantly smaller user bases. Meta AI was used by 25% of respondents, while Claude and Microsoft Copilot each recorded 17%. DeepSeek had a 14% usage rate, followed by Grok at 11% and Perplexity at 3%.
AI enters the shopping journey
General knowledge retrieval remained the most common use of generative AI, cited by 78% of respondents, followed by personal advice at 62%.
Meanwhile, commercial research has quickly become a major use case. About 58% of respondents said they regularly used generative AI to research products or services before making a purchase.
That put pre-purchase research ahead of workplace tasks at 57% and education and translation at 53%. Creative content generation accounted for 37%, while travel and spending planning stood at 36% and entertainment at 33%.
Consumers in their 30s were the most active users for shopping research, with 67% using AI to investigate products before buying. Respondents in their 20s were more likely to use AI for education and language-related tasks, at 63%.
Generative AI is also emerging as a significant product-discovery channel. Traditional search engines remained the leading source, with 86% of respondents using them for product searches, followed by Shopee and Lazada at 77%.
Facebook accounted for 59% of product inquiries. Generative AI, at 58%, ranked ahead of TikTok at 57%, YouTube at 52%, official brand websites at 50%, and recommendations from family and friends at 37%.
However, only 4% of respondents said generative AI was their single most-used shopping information source, suggesting that AI currently complements rather than replaces established channels.
Consumers use AI most for high-involvement purchases
Using AI to research products has become a regular habit for many urban consumers. About 62% said they always or often use AI before purchasing, including 9% who do so always and 53% who do so often. Another 30% use AI sometimes, while only 3% said they never use it for purchase research.
Usage was highest among consumers in their 30s, at 68%. Consumers in their 40s were more likely to use AI occasionally, with 44% selecting "sometimes".
Food and beverages were the most researched category, at 55%, followed closely by electronics and appliances at 54%. Fashion and accessories accounted for 47%, cosmetics and skincare 43%, hotels and travel 40%, restaurants and cafes 39%, and health and fitness 29%.
Gender differences were particularly pronounced in some categories. Men were more likely to use AI to research electronics and food, while women showed stronger demand for beauty-related information. Some 53% of female respondents used AI to research cosmetics, compared with 33% of men.
Saving time is the main appeal
The biggest attraction of generative AI is its ability to reduce the effort required to research products. About 70% of respondents said they valued receiving a ready-made summary rather than having to read information across multiple websites. Personalized recommendations were important to 54% of users, while 52% valued the speed of retrieving information.
Consumers in their 40s placed particular emphasis on customized recommendations, with 65% citing tailored options as an important benefit.
The findings highlight one of the key differences between conversational AI and conventional search. Rather than presenting users with a list of links, generative AI can consolidate information against a set of specific criteria and produce a shortlist.
From search to analysis
Consumers are increasingly using AI to evaluate products rather than simply locate them. Summarizing pros and cons was the most common analytical task, cited by 67% of respondents, followed by comparing products or brands at 62%.
Some 55% used AI to identify products matching specific needs, while 44% used it to check features or technical specifications. General product recommendations accounted for 42%, followed by customer-review summaries at 41% and price or value-for-money assessments at 38%. Only 12% used AI primarily to find where a product could be purchased.
Consumers in their 40s were particularly likely to use AI as a filtering tool, with 70% asking it to identify options that met specific conditions.
AI creates shortlists, but consumers still verify
Despite the growing reliance on AI recommendations, most consumers do not immediately act on an AI-generated suggestion. Only 15% said they would purchase an AI-recommended product without further verification.
Instead, 60% checked Shopee or Lazada after researching with AI, while 55% read user reviews and 49% conducted additional searches on Google. Another 43% checked TikTok, Facebook, or YouTube, while 41% visited official brand websites.
Physical stores remained part of the verification process, with 32% inspecting products in person. The same proportion sought opinions from family or friends.
Younger consumers were the most likely to verify AI recommendations. Among respondents in their 20s, 69% checked e-commerce stores. Consumers in their 40s were more willing to act directly on AI recommendations, with 23% purchasing the recommended product without further verification.
AI is changing the consumer discovery funnel
The survey suggests that generative AI is producing a structural change in how urban Vietnamese consumers research products.
Only 5% of respondents said AI had not changed their research habits. Half said they were discovering more new products and brands through conversational AI, while 46% said the technology was helping them reach purchase decisions faster.
The shift is also reducing reliance on some traditional digital channels. About 35% of respondents said they searched Google less frequently, 33% said they read fewer traditional websites, and 28% spent less time browsing customer reviews and social media feeds.
The changes point to a new challenge for brands. Search-engine optimization and social-media advertising remain important, but consumers are increasingly relying on AI systems to synthesize information and recommend products.

articles.title: CBN Deepens Nigeria-Asia Financial Ties, Signs Innovation MoU In Singapore - New Telegraph
articles.summary: CBN Deepens Nigeria-Asia Financial Ties, Signs Innovation MoU In Singapore  New Telegraph
articles.full_text:
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has intensified efforts to deepen Nigeria’s financial integration with Asia, with Governor Olayemi Cardoso holding high-level engagements in Singapore on financial-market development, innovation and cross-border connectivity.
The engagements, held ahead of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, included discussions with the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN), and a Nigeria–Asia Financial Connectivity Dialogue.
The CBN said the engagements were aimed at translating Nigeria’s ongoing financial-sector reforms into stronger international partnerships, deeper and more liquid markets, and practical channels for investment, trade and financial innovation.
During talks with MAS, the Nigerian delegation exchanged views on financial-sector development, regulation, market connectivity and innovation, while exploring areas for continued institutional cooperation between both countries.
The CBN said the discussions also provided an opportunity for both financial systems to share experiences and examine how stronger institutional relationships could support financial-market development and the adoption of emerging technologies.
In a related development, the CBN and GFTN signed an MoU to establish a framework for cooperation in financial innovation.
The agreement is expected to facilitate collaboration between relevant institutions and innovation ecosystems in Nigeria and Singapore, while creating opportunities to explore common areas of interest and practical initiatives.
At the Nigeria–Asia Financial Connectivity Dialogue hosted at J.P. Morgan’s Singapore offices, Cardoso outlined Nigeria’s ambition to build deeper, more liquid and internationally connected financial markets.
The Governor said recent reforms, particularly in the foreign-exchange market, were designed to remove distortions, improve transparency and strengthen confidence in the rules governing market participation.
“The real test of reform is not whether you can attract capital once; it is whether you create the confidence for capital to stay, return and grow,” Cardoso said.
He stressed that credible monetary policy, stronger governance, improved market functioning and predictable rules were critical to attracting and retaining both domestic and international investment.
According to him, stabilising the financial system was not an end in itself but a foundation for broader participation by long-term institutional investors, stronger market infrastructure and closer links with international financial markets.
The dialogue brought together investors, financial institutions, businesses and Nigerians living and working across Asia.
A panel moderated by J.P. Morgan’s Chief Economist for Africa, Gbolahan Taiwo, examined Nigeria’s reform trajectory, including capital formation, foreign-exchange market confidence, market liquidity and the infrastructure required to sustain international participation.
Panelists included Temi Popoola, Group Managing Director/CEO of Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX); Zeal Akaraiwe, Group Managing Director/CEO of FMDQ Group; Aderinola Shonekan, Director of Trade and Exchange at the CBN; and Olumayokun Ajibade, Special Adviser to the Governor on Financial Markets and Economic Policy.
Cardoso said Nigeria’s engagement with Asia was intended to go beyond attracting investment flows to building durable relationships among financial institutions, markets, businesses and Nigerians across the region.
He identified opportunities for stronger linkages between Nigerian and Asian banks and market institutions, more efficient payment and settlement channels, and increased participation by Nigerians living and working in Asia.
The Governor also highlighted the growing role of financial technology and artificial intelligence in improving financial services, strengthening risk management, expanding financial inclusion and enhancing regulatory capacity.
The Singapore engagements form part of the CBN’s broader institutional and market outreach across Asia, with further engagements scheduled in Beijing.

articles.title: Standard Chartered Targets Singapore With New Crypto Custody Push - The Coin Republic
articles.summary: Standard Chartered Targets Singapore With New Crypto Custody Push  The Coin Republic
articles.full_text:
Key Insights
- Standard Chartered plans institutional crypto custody services in Singapore.
- The offering covers selected cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, and tokenized real-world assets.
- Expansion follows Zodia Custody acquisition plans and broader institutional partnerships.
Standard Chartered announced plans on Oct. 8 to introduce institutional crypto custody services in Singapore. The bank aims to serve institutional investors seeking regulated digital asset safekeeping and servicing. The proposed offering remains subject to applicable regulatory requirements.
The expansion would extend the bank’s existing digital asset operations across major financial centers. It would also connect traditional securities services with cryptocurrency custody and tokenized asset infrastructure.
Standard Chartered Expands Crypto Custody Services in Singapore
In its official announcement, the bank outlined plans to safeguard selected cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, and tokenized real-world assets. Eligible customers would comprise institutional clients and corporate clients qualifying as accredited investors. However, the bank did not identify the specific cryptocurrencies that its proposed service would support.
The offering would complement its existing Financing and Securities Services business in Singapore. That division provides traditional institutional asset servicing, which the bank intends to extend into digital assets. The proposed arrangement would connect asset safekeeping with tokenization and other institutional financial services.
Patrick Lee, the bank’s chief executive for Singapore, ASEAN, and South Asia, discussed the expansion. He identified Singapore’s institutional financial sector and demand for trusted digital asset services as important factors.
Lee also emphasized infrastructure supporting the secure movement and safekeeping of tokenized assets. His remarks positioned the proposed offering around institutional requirements rather than direct retail cryptocurrency exposure.
Meanwhile, Ole Matthiessen, global head of Transaction Services and Digital Assets, outlined the bank’s institutional strategy. He described regulated custody as a foundation for broader participation in digital asset markets.
However, the announcement did not disclose custody fees, specific supported assets, or a commercial launch date. Those details remain important for institutions assessing the proposed service.
Standard Chartered Builds on Zodia Custody Acquisition Plans
The Singapore expansion followed the bank’s earlier efforts to consolidate its institutional digital asset businesses.
On May 18, the bank announced that Zodia Custody’s shareholders and noteholders had accepted its non-binding acquisition offer. The proposed transaction remained subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.
Under the arrangement, Zodia Custody’s regulated operations would join the bank’s Financing and Securities Services business. That integration would consolidate institutional custody activities within its existing banking structure.
Meanwhile, Zodia Solutions would operate separately under SC Ventures as a digital asset infrastructure provider. The business would support financial institutions developing digital asset services through its technology infrastructure.
The bank’s May 2026 investor presentation outlined wider ambitions across digital asset trading, custody, and tokenization.
The presentation identified institutional Bitcoin and Ether trading alongside existing digital asset custody capabilities. It also described tokenized securities, exchange-traded fund access, and collateral management initiatives.
These activities indicate a strategy connecting cryptocurrency trading with traditional financial market infrastructure. Custody represents one component of that broader institutional service model.
Standard Chartered Extends Existing Digital Asset Operations
Standard Chartered already operates digital asset custody businesses across the United Arab Emirates, Luxembourg, and Hong Kong.
On May 27, it announced institutional custody support for SOLOWIN Holdings in Hong Kong. The arrangement involved crypto asset safekeeping through infrastructure provided by a globally systemically important bank.
Separately, Standard Chartered expanded its institutional custody partnership with LMAX Group in September. The arrangement connected its custody infrastructure with institutional trading services in Luxembourg and Dubai.
Those developments preceded its proposed Singapore launch and expanded its institutional presence across several jurisdictions. However, the bank has not disclosed expected Singapore custody volumes or revenue contributions.
The planned service could also help institutions manage tokenized assets alongside conventional investment holdings. Its commercial impact will depend on regulatory permissions, supported assets, and client adoption.
Crypto Custody Plans Face Singapore’s Regulatory Framework
Singapore’s Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) maintains regulatory requirements for digital payment token services under the Payment Services Act.
The regulator has also continued developing rules governing stablecoin issuance and related safeguards.
On Sept. 1, MAS published proposals to implement its single-currency stablecoin regulatory framework. The proposals addressed issuer licensing, asset safeguards, and financial stability requirements.
MAS also proposed conditions for recognizing certain foreign-issued stablecoins under comparable regulatory frameworks. These proposals concern stablecoin issuers and do not independently authorize the bank’s proposed custody operations.
The regulator’s consultation closes on Oct. 16, 2026. Separately, the bank’s next commercial milestone remains confirmation of its Singapore custody launch timetable and applicable regulatory approvals.

articles.title: Cambodia’s Balancing Act: Can It Maintain Strategic Autonomy? - Cambodianess
articles.summary: Cambodia’s Balancing Act: Can It Maintain Strategic Autonomy?  Cambodianess
articles.full_text:
- 
                                    By:
                                    
                                    
                                
- Tep Sethakadet
- October 8, 2026, 7:15 PM
For Cambodia, maintaining good relations with major powers matters not only for diplomacy but also for its national interests and state survival.
Cambodia’s balancing strategy is most evident in its economic and diplomatic relations with China and the US.
Although Cambodia has developed close relations with China, it continues to maintain economic and diplomatic ties with the US rather than depending entirely on one major power.
However, the rivalry between China and the United States has intensified, making it harder for states to balance between the two powers. This has raised concern for Cambodia’s ability to maintain its strategic balance.
China-Cambodia Relations
The Cambodia-China relationship in the economic sector has grown significantly over the years. According to a report from the Ministry of Commerce on September 22, trade between the countries reached $15.53 billion in the first eight months of 2026, showing China's growing influence on Cambodia's economy.
China has also become an important source of investment and development cooperation through infrastructure and other projects.
This strong economic relationship between Cambodia and China has strengthened ties and made Beijing an important economic partner in Cambodia’s development.
However, Cambodia’s relationship with China extends beyond economic cooperation. The countries have developed close political and diplomatic relations, while cooperation has expanded into areas such as defence and security. This means China plays an important role across several sectors in Cambodia.
US-Cambodia Ties
Despite the close relationship with China, the US also plays an important role in Cambodia’s economy. According to the Office of the US Trade Representative in 2025, US goods imports from Cambodia reached an estimated total of $16.1 billion, up 19.8 percent from 2024.
While China is an important source of imports, investment, and development cooperation, the US is particularly important, especially in Cambodia’s export market.
This leads Cambodia to maintain relations with both countries to serve its national interests.
Cambodia’s engagement with the US can also be seen beyond trade. The USS Cincinnati visited Ream Naval Base on January 24 for a temporary port visit, during which the US and Cambodian navies held exchanges and meetings aimed at strengthening maritime cooperation.
However, Ream has become one of the most sensitive topics in China and the US influence competition, as it is geopolitically and geostrategically important for China.
Therefore, Cambodia’s strategy was not simply to choose between China and the US. Instead, Cambodia wanted to maintain different forms of cooperation with either side, depending on its economic, diplomatic, and security interests.
Growing US-China Rivalry
Cambodia has been concerned about the growing competition between the two major powers. The rivalry between China and the US has expanded beyond traditional economic competition. Trade, technology, military power, regional security, and diplomatic influence are also part of their strategic competition.
For Southeast Asia, the tension threatened their future stability and survival, emphasising their connection with China while they tried to maintain security, trade, and diplomatic relationships with the United States.
This dilemma challenged smaller states to prepare for uncertain future scenarios and how to balance between the powers.
ForCambodia, the challenge is even more sensitive because of its deep dependence on China.
Chinese investment and trade have become important parts of the Cambodian economy. At the same time, China’s role in developing Ream Naval Base has drawn greater attention to Cambodia’s security relationship with Beijing.
Yet Cambodia continues to maintain its military engagement with Washington, as shown by the recent US naval visit to Ream in January 2026, despite the base’s Chinese-supported modernisation. This raises concerns about Cambodia’s position between the powers, which could threaten its prosperity.
Challenges and Pressures
Cambodia has been dependent on external factors for decades. One of the main challenges to address is economic dependence.
Cambodia has benefited from large Chinese investment and imports across the country. In 2025, Cambodia'simports from China reached $18 billion, accounting for more than half of Cambodia’s total import value.
At the same time, Cambodia exported only around $1.68 billion to China. Chinese imports are mostly raw materials, machinery, and other inputs used by Cambodian businesses and factories. This shows how deeply Cambodia’s economy is connected to Chinese supply chains.
Another issue is that Cambodia’s exports to the US are much higher than its exports to China. At the same time, in 2025, Cambodia exported approximately $15.7 billion worth of goods to the US, meaning Cambodia’s economic interest is in maintaining access to Chinese suppliers and American consumers.
This problem could threaten Cambodia’s economy if the two powers compete strategically in economic policy, including trade, investment or supply chains.
The Ream Naval Base has become a key issue in discussions of Cambodia's strategic position. China's involvement in modernising the base has raised questions about its future military engagement in Cambodia.
Meanwhile, the US Navy’s visit to Ream also added to the uncertainty around Cambodia’s position between the major powers, as the US Navy said the visit was part of the US-Cambodia maritime partnership.
In addition, despite the US Navy’s visit to the Ream Naval Base, Cambodia’s defence relationship with the US has also continued to develop.
The countries agreed to strengthen their defence cooperation to improve the capability of Cambodia’s military. This also raises concerns in China, as Cambodia is now growing closer to the US in defence cooperation. On the other hand, Cambodia may need to pay closer attention to managing both relationships.
This shows that Cambodia can still maintain its security engagement with Washington while maintaining its close defence relationship with Beijing.
However, it may also show how difficult the balancing process could be. In Cambodia's view, it considers both sides of the military relationship as part of its national interest, though the major powers may view this as another power competition.
Cambodia’s Future Strategic Balancing
To balance between the two powers, Cambodia should consider a new economic approach and keep attracting and diversifying investment from other countries, rather than depending too heavily on one or two powerful countries.
Japanese investment in Cambodia is an example. In March 2025, a delegation of 38 Japanese companies visited Cambodia to explore investment opportunities, while the Cambodian government highlighted economic diversification as part of its long-term development strategy.
Japan has also continued supporting Cambodia through infrastructure projects and is the second-largest investor in Cambodia. This could help Cambodia expand its choices. Instead of relying solely on Chinese investment, Cambodia should consider attracting more investment from Japan, Europe, and other countries.
Meanwhile, Cambodia also needs to maintain the ability to make foreign policy decisions in line with its national interests.
To achieve this, Cambodia should strengthen its diplomatic and policy-making capacity by developing more human resources, including diplomats, researchers, and capable government officials.
It should also seek bilateral relations with more countries and among the ASEAN partners and avoid depending heavily on one major country.
Lastly, alongside economic and strategic autonomy, Cambodia should also focus on security cooperation to ensure state security and survival.
Singapore is a strong example: it maintains close security cooperation and a deep defence relationship with the US while expanding defence ties and military cooperation with China and other countries.
However, Cambodia does not need to choose a single security partner to depend on entirely. Instead, it could maintain cooperation with China while keeping military and maritime engagement with the US, Japan, Australia and other potential partners.
Tep Sethakadet is an undergraduate currently pursuing a bachelor’s degree in international relations from the Institute for International Studies and Public Policy. Her research interests lie in Cambodia’s public policy and ASEAN regional affairs.

The fourth meeting of Vietnam's 14th Party Central Committee concluded in Hanoi on Thursday after four days of work, completing all of its agenda.
Delivering his closing remarks, Party General Secretary and President To Lam stressed that building on the decisions made since the beginning of the 14th tenure, the meeting further concretized the Resolution of the 14th National Party Congress, linking the Party building with national governance and development.
The decisions issued at this meeting aim to strengthen leadership and implementation capacity and rally the strength of the entire nation, with the value of the plenum ultimately reflected in the issues addressed and improvements in people’s lives.

articles.title: Positioning a strategic approach to asset management and personal finance in the new context. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Positioning a strategic approach to asset management and personal finance in the new context.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| Ms. Luc Kim Thanh, Director of Digital Business at Kafi Securities Joint Stock Company, shared her insights on the program "The Wealth Box Talk" on VTV8. | 
 The asset management and finance industry in Vietnam is undergoing a significant transformation. The booming middle class and strong digitalization are driving the industry's growth, with the size of assets under management and advisory services projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 13.8% by 2031.
 However, according to experts, the asset and financial management industry in Vietnam is still in its "pivotal" stage, with limited management solutions and people's habits still primarily focused on traditional savings accounts. So how can this industry catch up with international standards and reposition personal asset and financial management strategies in the new context?
 Discussing this issue on the program "The Wealth Box Talk" on VTV8, Ms. Luc Kim Thanh, Director of Digital Business at Kafi Securities Joint Stock Company, stated that the asset management and financial market in Vietnam still has much room for development. This requires the continued improvement of market policies, as well as the need for financial institutions to enhance their capabilities and diversify asset and financial solutions to meet the increasingly high demands of the people in the new context.
 Asset management in Vietnam is at a "turning point".
 Madam, as an expert in asset management and finance, what stage of development would you consider this industry to be currently in Vietnam?
 Ms. Luc Kim Thanh: I believe Vietnam has been very good at creating assets, but is only just beginning to learn how to manage them. We are right at the crossroads between those two stages. The following two figures, placed side-by-side, will provide the answer.
 According to McKinsey's forecast, the total personal financial assets of Vietnamese people could reach approximately $600 billion by 2027, up from around $360 billion at the end of 2022. However, conversely, the total net asset value of all domestic investment funds is currently only about 93 trillion VND, equivalent to 0.7% of GDP. This means there is no shortage of money. What is lacking is a channel for that money to be managed professionally. The goal set for 2030 is to increase this ratio from 0.7% to 5% of GDP, meaning the fund industry must grow approximately sevenfold in four years. This figure illustrates both the ambition and the gap we must overcome.
 This is a classic sign of a market at a pivotal stage: assets are large enough to generate a need for management, but service providers are still in the process of formation. And the bottlenecks, in my observation, lie in three places: firstly, the limited diversity of products; secondly, the small number of specialized service providers; and most importantly, the habit of entrusting assets to a management organization is still not widespread among Vietnamese people. These three points are all changing, but it will take time. 
|  | 
| Ms. Luc Kim Thanh. | 
 As someone who needs financial asset management skills these days, Bach, do you find it easy to find information and manage your personal finances effectively?
 Mr. Pham Gia Bach, investor: In my opinion, finding information about finance and investment is much more convenient now than before, as there are many platforms and sources of information to consult. However, the problem is that there is so much information that sometimes it's hard to know which information is truly suitable for one's needs and financial capabilities. Especially when investing in stocks, it's not just about knowing how to buy or sell, but also understanding the risks, how to allocate capital, and investment goals. Therefore, for me personally, self-managing my finances still requires a lot of time to learn and isn't really that simple.
 So, according to Ms. Thanh, if we place Vietnam on the same development curve as more advanced markets like Singapore , Thailand, or Malaysia, where do we stand, and what makes Vietnam's current stage different from theirs at a similar point in time?
 Ms. Luc Kim Thanh, Director of Digital Business, Kafi Securities Joint Stock Company: If we were to draw a general growth curve, I see that most markets go through four fairly similar stages. Stage one is the accumulation of tangible assets, mainly through land purchases and savings deposits. Stage two is when standardized financial products such as open-ended funds, bonds, and investment-linked insurance products appear. Stage three is when asset-based advisory services are established, and stage four is estate planning, transferring assets across generations.
 In my opinion, Vietnam is currently in the latter half of the second stage and just beginning the third. It's worth noting that the leading markets, at a similar stage, also had portfolios primarily consisting of real estate and deposits. So I don't think we're moving slowly or incorrectly; we're following the right sequence. However, there are two things that make Vietnam's stage different from theirs.
 First , there's technology. Leading markets had to build physical infrastructure, open branches, recruit consulting teams, and it took decades to achieve widespread coverage. We can deploy directly on digital platforms from the start, so the entry threshold is lowered significantly and the time to widespread adoption is considerably shortened.
 Secondly , there's the speed. According to this year's BCG report, Vietnam's financial assets are growing at over 9% annually, among the highest rates in emerging markets. At the same time, Knight Frank notes that the number of individuals with net worth of $30 million or more in Vietnam has increased by approximately 29% over the past five years and forecasts a further increase of nearly 60% in the next five years, ranking fourth globally in terms of growth rate.
 Another factor has just emerged: the FTSE Russell upgrade of the Vietnamese stock market to a secondary emerging market, effective September 21st of this year. For me, the value of this upgrade isn't just about foreign capital inflows. More importantly, it will force an improvement in all domestic operational standards, transparency, and risk management. That's what will ensure long-term stability.
 Many believe that asset and financial management solutions in Vietnam are still quite traditional, primarily focusing on real estate, gold, or savings accounts, with the more dynamic option being stocks… How do you feel about investing in or developing your finances and assets today?
 Mr. Pham Gia Bach, investor: I see that the most popular investment channels currently are real estate, gold, savings accounts, and stocks. Personally, I am more interested in stocks because it is a flexible channel and I can be more proactive with my capital. However, I also hope to see more support solutions to make investing more systematic and effective. 
|  | 
| Mr. Pham Gia Bach, investor. | 
 And what is Ms. Thanh's assessment of the current portfolio structure of investors?
 Ms. Luc Kim Thanh: According to a 2026 survey of over 1,000 individual investors, savings deposits accounted for an average of 37% of their portfolios, real estate 36%, and gold 14%. Combined, these three traditional channels accounted for 87% of total assets. But there's a detail I find more interesting than that number: the survey also showed that 86% of respondents agreed that one shouldn't concentrate the majority of their assets in a single channel. However, 76% still preferred real estate or gold, reasoning that these are assets they understand better. This means the awareness is already there; the issue lies in the gap between knowing and doing.
 In my opinion, that gap isn't the investors' fault; it stems from three reasons. Firstly, tangible assets provide a sense of security because they are visible and tangible, while the domestic financial product portfolio remains limited. Secondly , Vietnamese people haven't yet developed the habit of entrusting their assets to an organization. Thirdly , there's the issue of trust, and trust must be built over time, not through words alone.
 This results in a portfolio that is unbalanced, illiquid, and tightly bound to a single cycle. When that cycle reverses, almost the entire asset class is affected simultaneously, and it often manifests precisely when people need money the most. The good news is that things are starting to change. The number of investors holding mutual funds is currently around 733,000, a 1.6-fold increase compared to the end of 2024. While still very small compared to the nearly 14 million securities accounts, this rate indicates a new habit is forming.
 From short-term trading to long-term asset management
 Furthermore, many believe that investor sentiment still heavily favors short-term buying, trading, and accumulation rather than a long-term, medium-term perspective. Do you agree with this, Bach?
 Mr. Pham Gia Bach, investor: My mindset used to lean towards short-term investments with easily visible results. But the more I learn, the more I realize that accumulating and investing for the medium and long term is more important if I want sustainable financial growth.
 And Ms. Thanh, could you share your observations on the prevailing investment views of the majority of individual investors today?
 Ms. Luc Kim Thanh: It must be acknowledged that the majority of Vietnamese investors are currently trading, not managing. The two differ fundamentally in one aspect: whether or not there is a plan. Decisions are made based on isolated opportunities; they invest wherever it seems promising, rather than as part of an overall plan. And success is measured by the profit or loss of each transaction, rather than by the progress toward achieving their financial goals.

articles.summary: Vietnam plans to split power transmission, distribution and retail from EVN generation  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam's Electricity and Renewable Energy Authority is steering a restructuring of state utility Vietnam Electricity (EVN) that would see power transmission, distribution and retail separated from the group which currently accounts for 40% of the country's power generation capacity.
The restructuring will be carried out in stages and linked to the development of a competitive electricity market, Bui Quoc Hung, deputy head of the Electricity and Renewable Energy Authority, said at a press briefing held by the Ministry of Industry and Trade (MoIT) on Wednesday.
The government has tasked the ministry with preparing two plans related to restructuring the power sector: a restructuring plan to support the development of a competitive electricity market and a restructuring plan for EVN.
The EVN restructuring plan has been assigned to the Ministry of Finance in coordination with the industry ministry, and was submitted to the government on September 15.
Vietnam's power sector includes many domestic and foreign companies, including foreign-invested firms. EVN currently owns only about 40% of the country's power generation capacity.
The restructuring plan aims to separate different stages of the electricity business and clearly distinguish activities that are natural monopolies from those that can be opened to competition.
"Transmission and power system dispatch have their own specific characteristics, while power generation, wholesale and retail are areas where competitive markets can be developed at different stages," Hung said.
Under the government's instructions, the industry ministry is reviewing the current structure of the power sector and developing a restructuring framework in line with the roadmap for a competitive electricity market, covering EVN and its subsidiaries.
State considers divestment from power generation companies
For power generation, the restructuring plan calls for the state to divest its stakes in EVN's generation companies. The government is also considering establishing a strategic national power generation corporation to manage strategic power sources and projects, such as multi-purpose hydropower plants and nuclear power projects.
The new entity could initially be part of EVN but would be considered for separation from the group in the longer term, according to Hung.
Power transmission to be separated from EVN
For transmission, the Vietnam National Power Transmission Corporation (EVNNPT) is expected to be separated from EVN under the restructuring plan to meet the requirements of a competitive electricity market.
For distribution and retail, the distribution and retail functions of EVN's five power corporations will initially be gradually separated.
In the longer term, the separation could extend to both organizational and ownership structures, in line with the development of a competitive retail electricity market, Hung said.
The separation of the different stages of the electricity business will need to be carried out gradually and in tandem with the development of successive levels of a competitive electricity market, he added.
Power supply projects face delays
On electricity supply, Hung said implementation of some power generation and grid projects remained behind schedule, creating difficulties for the implementation of Vietnam's Power Development Plan VIII.
Obstacles include the approval of investment policies and land allocation, while power generation projects require very large amounts of capital.
To address these issues, the industry ministry is urgently preparing amendments to the Electricity Law, which are expected to be submitted to the National Assembly at its second session.
The amendments are aimed at removing obstacles to project implementation and accelerating the rollout of the Power Development Plan VIII (PDP VIII).
The ministry has also made recommendations to the government to resolve difficulties facing projects included in the plan's implementation program and ensure adequate power supplies.

articles.title: Malaysia builds a new ‘Silicon Island’ to house its AI ambitions - The Straits Times
articles.summary: Malaysia builds a new ‘Silicon Island’ to house its AI ambitions  The Straits Times
articles.full_text:
1 of 2

PENANG – Just south of Penang, the historic trading island off Malaysia’s north-west coast, excavators are turning a stretch of blue-green sea into a new, man-made island. Dump trucks criss-cross freshly reclaimed sand as orange pipes snake across the emerging land mass, carrying fill pumped from dredgers offshore.
Once complete sometime next decade, this 930ha area, called Silicon Island, is expected to entrench Malaysia’s role in the global semiconductor industry, adding hundreds of billions of dollars to its economy and creating some 220,000 jobs by 2050.
Almost three times the size of New York’s Central Park, the island has also been envisaged as a home to office towers, hotels and waterfront apartments.
The project is an ambitious answer to a problem created in part by Penang’s own success.
After more than five decades building one of South-east Asia’s leading electronics and semiconductor hubs, one of Malaysia’s smallest states is running short of land.
Intel Corp, Advanced Micro Devices and ASE Technology Holding are among technology heavyweights that have expanded operations in recent years around Bayan Lepas, a sprawling cluster of factories near Penang’s airport that forms the heart of Malaysia’s semiconductor industry.
Silicon Island would give the sector room to grow while supporting Malaysia’s push beyond its traditional strengths of chip assembly and testing – the final stages of semiconductor production – into higher-value activities, such as design and advanced packaging.

It is also a bet that the artificial intelligence boom will supercharge the race to expand and diversify global chip production, sending more investment towards South-east Asia.
Space for further growth in Penang is “increasingly constrained”, the state’s Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow said in an interview with Bloomberg News.
“Silicon Island represents an important opportunity to build on Penang’s existing industrial strengths while positioning the state for the next phase of the global technology cycle.”
The potential payoff is substantial.
Silicon Island could contribute a cumulative RM1.1 trillion (S$344.6 billion) to Malaysia’s economic output through 2050 and attract about RM75 billion in investments, according to a Deloitte study cited by its developers, Silicon Island Development, a venture controlled by Malaysian infrastructure giant Gamuda and backed by the Penang state government.
Penang already accounts for about 5% of the world’s semiconductor exports, according to the state government. Its electronics industry meanwhile dates back to the early 1970s, when Penang, a centuries-old trading port that prospered on spices, tin and rubber, began courting foreign manufacturers to create jobs and diversify its economy.
Now, the rapid build-out of AI infrastructure is providing another source of demand.
Malaysia Semiconductor Industry Association president Wong Siew Hai recently raised his forecast for the nation’s electrical and electronics exports in 2026 by about 13% to more than RM900 billion.
Semiconductors account for almost three-quarters of those shipments, with Malaysia ranking as the world’s sixth-largest exporter.
The rush to build AI infrastructure is driving growth across the supply chain, leaving some manufacturers at capacity and searching for space to expand – demand that could draw companies to Silicon Island, said Wong, who previously spent 27 years at Intel.
Penang has also benefited as US-China tensions prompt companies to spread production across more countries.
Manufacturers seeking to reduce their reliance on Asia’s biggest economy have been adding capacity elsewhere, and Penang offers an established base of factories, engineers and suppliers.
Silicon Island has already drawn interest from local and international firms, with “particularly encouraging interest” from Taiwan and Japan, Chief Minister Chow said.
One prospective Japanese investor visited the site three times in just two months, with increasingly senior executives making the trip, from the company’s Malaysia chief executive to its Japan-based CEO and finally the chairman, said Tan Jun Jing, deputy project director at Silicon Island Development, a Gamuda executive who has helped deliver large-scale rail networks and townships across Malaysia.
When Tan asked them about the state of the sector, their answer underscored the urgency behind the search for more capacity. Demand from customers including Intel and Nvidia is so strong that cost has become less of a concern versus how quickly suppliers can ramp up production, Tan said.
“The current commitment these companies are asking for is ‘how much and how fast can you produce?’” she said. “That’s why a lot of them are really exploring expansion to meet customer demand.”
Still, turning land wrested from the sea into another Bayan Lepas will take time.
The island could take another three to four years just to fully reclaim and as long as 15 years to build out, Tan said, with the first industrial operations expected to start by early 2029.
Competition is also intensifying.
Singapore is pushing deeper into advanced manufacturing, while Vietnam is vying for a bigger share of projects. India is spending heavily to build a semiconductor industry, too.
Within Malaysia, states including Kedah and Selangor are also courting chipmakers.
Higher land prices could further narrow Silicon Island’s pool of potential tenants.
The cost of transforming sand into solid ground is likely to put the expense of being based there beyond the reach of some lower-margin manufacturers, making high-value technology companies its most likely occupants, Wong said.
For companies spending billions of dollars on a new facility, however, land represents a relatively small portion of the overall investment, he said.
Tan sees Silicon Island playing the same role for Penang in the next half of the century that the Bayan Lepas Free Industrial Zone has played over the past 50 years.
Intel, one of the early overseas manufacturers that helped establish Penang as a tech hub, is also part of the state’s effort to move beyond traditional assembly and testing.
Intel’s chief executive officer Lip-Bu Tan met Chow in December 2025 for an update on the US chipmaker’s RM12 billion advanced-packaging facility in the state.
At Silicon Island’s centre will be a roughly 283ha Green Tech Park targeting industries including semiconductor design, advanced packaging and automated testing.
The first phase is planned to run entirely on renewable energy, according to Silicon Island Development, and there will eventually be a 380m bridge connecting the development to the main island.
Its location helps define the companies Penang is targeting.
Businesses considering Silicon Island are likely to rely primarily on air freight to bring in materials and send out finished products, taking advantage of its proximity to Penang International Airport, Tan said.
Heavy manufacturers dependent on seaborne cargo would be better suited to the mainland, with easier access to the port, she said.
Gamuda, which has a 70% stake in Silicon Island Development, is financing the project’s RM14 billion in reclamation and infrastructure costs through a syndicated loan, Tan said.
The project expects to break even within eight years, with the first sale of industrial land planned for early 2027, she added.
As shareholder of the rest of the venture, Penang’s government is entitled to a 30% cut of the profits. According to Chow, the state will also fully own the reclaimed land and determine how it is ultimately allocated and developed.
One day, Silicon Island is also intended to be a place people call home.
The plans call for about 20,000 houses on 360 acres (145.7ha), including condominiums and affordable dwellings, alongside shops, amenities and restaurants. Almost one-fifth of the island will be green space, including parks, beaches and mangrove wetlands.
Silicon Island will also serve as a starting point for Penang’s first light-rail system. The 29½ km Mutiara Line will connect the development with Bayan Lepas, Penang’s airport and the state’s capital, George Town. A later extension will provide a link to the Malaysian mainland.
Operations are scheduled to begin by the end of 2031. A Gamuda-led consortium won a RM7.93 billion contract for the first civil-works package.
The sheer scale of the development invites comparisons with Forest City, the US$100 billion (S$128 billion) megaproject built on reclaimed land in southern Malaysia by Chinese property giant Country Garden Holdings and a local partner.
Conceived as a futuristic city for as many as 700,000 people, it relied heavily on overseas property buyers, particularly from China.
Demand faltered after Beijing imposed capital controls, while Malaysian political opposition, the Covid-19 pandemic and Country Garden’s subsequent financial troubles compounded its problems.
Today, only a fraction of the project, originally planned as four artificial islands, has been built and occupancy remains low.
But Silicon Island’s developers are betting on a different anchor: an industry that already exists on its doorstep. Here, the thinking is that factories and investment will come first, and the city will follow.
“A lot of people compare us to Forest City, but today when you look at it, it’s a pure residential and commercial play,” Tan said. “Our main catalyst will be industrial.” BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Vietnam cannot stand apart from global interest rate trend: central bank - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam cannot stand apart from global interest rate trend: central bank  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Federal Reserve is likely to continue raising interest rates, and Vietnam cannot stand apart from the global interest rate trend, the State Bank of Vietnam’s monetary policy chief Pham Chi Quang said.
Monetary policy prioritizes inflation control
As of September 30, outstanding credit across the banking system stood at about VND20,750 trillion ($798.68 billion), up 11.59% from the end of 2025 and 16.69% from a year earlier, the SBV said. This means bank credit had injected about VND2,200 trillion ($84.68 billion) into the economy in just nine months.
The figure highlights the continued role of bank funding in supporting growth. But rapid credit growth also puts greater pressure on monetary policy, particularly as Vietnam is pursuing double-digit economic growth in 2026.
2026 is the first year of implementing the 14th National Party Congress resolution and the 2026-2030 socio-economic development plan, with a target of double-digit growth while maintaining macroeconomic stability and controlling inflation.
This means credit cannot simply be viewed in terms of "injecting more capital", according to SBV Deputy Governor Pham Thanh Ha. The SBV said it had conducted monetary policy proactively and flexibly during the first nine months, in line with market developments and with a focus on keeping average inflation at around 4.5% in 2026.
The pressure on monetary policy is becoming more apparent in price developments. The National Statistics Office said the consumer price index rose 0.62% in September from the previous month and 5.08% from a year earlier. In the first nine months, CPI rose 4.52%, above the 4.5% target set in the government's Resolution 01/NQ-CP.
"These are the highest increases for September and the nine-month average in many years, showing that the pressure to manage prices and control inflation in the final months of 2026 is very high," Ha stressed.
Pham Chi Quang, director of the SBV's monetary policy department, also noted that the 4.52% increase in CPI in the first nine months showed there was limited room for monetary easing. If credit continues to grow rapidly while cost shocks from energy and global commodities persist, price pressures could intensify.
In other words, the need to control inflation is becoming one of the key constraints on the scope for deeper interest rate cuts.
Domestic rates cannot be separated from global trend
After analyzing the global backdrop, Quang said Vietnam's interest rates could not stand apart from the international monetary policy trend.
On September 16, the Fed raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points, bringing the federal funds target range to 3.75-4%. Several other major central banks also raised rates in September, increasing pressure on highly open economies such as Vietnam.
The monetary policy department chief said the Fed was likely to continue raising rates and Vietnam could not stand outside the global interest rate trend. Policymakers therefore need to find a balance between interest rates and the exchange rate rather than pursue a single objective, he said.
Domestic interest rate developments also show that the pressure has emerged. As of September 20, the average deposit rate for newly generated transactions stood at 6.38% a year, up 1.15 percentage points from the end of 2025, Deputy Governor Ha said. The SBV said interest rates remained under upward pressure, although the pace of increase had slowed and rates were settling around a new level.
Meanwhile, the SBV has kept its policy rates unchanged and asked credit institutions to stabilize market interest rates, disclose lending rates, and coordinate efforts to lower both deposit and lending rates.
Notably, interest rate pressure is not coming solely from domestic monetary policy. When global rates rise, the interest rate differential between the dong and U.S. dollar, capital flows and exchange rate expectations can all change. Cutting domestic rates too quickly could therefore put pressure on the exchange rate, while keeping rates too high for too long could increase companies' funding costs.
Quang said, however, that the exchange rate had been a positive variable, helping the SBV absorb some external shocks.
The Vietnamese dong has gained about 1.12% against the U.S. dollar, while many other Asian currencies have weakened by 2-7%. The move is notable as the Fed has just raised rates and the dollar has strengthened in global markets.
The resilience of the exchange rate has also been reflected in market developments. The SBV said it had managed the exchange rate flexibly while coordinating monetary policy tools to absorb external shocks, stabilize the foreign exchange market, and help control inflation. The legitimate foreign currency needs of the economy had been fully and promptly met, while the USD/VND exchange rate was managed flexibly in line with market conditions.
SBV to maintain flexible policy in fourth quarter
On monetary policy in the final quarter, Deputy Governor Ha said the global economy would continue to face numerous risks, with geopolitical factors, energy prices and fluctuations in the global economic and financial markets potentially weighing further on Vietnam's economy.
Recent data show that Vietnam continues to face significant pressures given its high degree of economic openness. The SBV will continue to conduct monetary policy proactively and flexibly while coordinating policies to help maintain macroeconomic stability, stabilize markets and support economic growth.
On interest rates, the SBV will closely monitor market developments and adjust policy in line with macroeconomic conditions, inflation developments and policy objectives. It will also take appropriate liquidity-management measures to ensure commercial banks' ability to make payments, while closely monitoring international markets and managing the exchange rate flexibly.
On credit, the SBV will continue to adjust policy in line with macroeconomic developments and the economy's capacity to absorb capital, supporting growth while ensuring the safety of credit institutions.
"Credit institutions are required to ensure safe and effective credit growth, while strictly controlling lending to potentially risky sectors; continue implementing credit programs and packages at the direction of the government and the SBV, ensuring effectiveness and making it easier for people and businesses to access capital," Ha said.
Banks must also continue improving the quality of their operations by strictly complying with regulations, ensuring safety and efficiency, controlling non-performing loans, and limiting the emergence of new risks.

The benchmark palm oil contract for December delivery on the Bursa Malaysia Derivatives Exchange slid 36 ringgit, or 0.79 percent, to 4,524 ringgit (USD1,107.20) a metric ton at close.

Palm oil tracks the price movements of rival edible oils, as it competes for a share of the global vegetable oils market. Crude oil prices were stable, with Brent futures holding above USD100 a barrel, as investors weighed higher Gulf exports against ongoing supply risks from the Middle East conflict and a storm heading for oil-producing regions in the United States. Stronger crude oil futures make palm a more attractive option for biodiesel feedstock.
The ringgit, palm’s currency of trade, weakened 0.1 percent against the dollar, making the commodity slightly cheaper for buyers holding foreign currencies.

Hanoi is finalizing its land database based on the criteria of "accurate - complete - clean - active". Once information on land use rights and assets attached to land is standardized and updated, this data source can provide a stronger basis for verifying assets in transactions, including credit activities.
Synchronizing land data adds a basis for appraisal.
For banks, the clearest link between land databases and lending activities lies in the verification of collateral. When a property is mortgaged, the credit institution needs to check the right of use, location, characteristics, legal status, and other relevant information about the property.

If this data is standardized and can be looked up and compared within the system, banks will have an additional source of information to verify the documents provided by customers. In particular, information about the mortgage registration status is directly significant, as it is the basis for determining which obligation the asset has been used to secure.
In lending operations, collateral assets need to be accurately identified in terms of ownership, location, current condition, and legal status before a bank decides to grant credit. In reality, numerous fraud cases in the lending sector have shown discrepancies between collateral asset records and the actual assets, potentially putting banks at significant risk.
On April 8, 2026, the Hanoi People's Court tried defendant Vu Van Tien for the crime of "Fraudulent appropriation of property." According to the indictment, in 2015, Tien and his wife borrowed 5 billion VND from a bank, mortgaging the right to use a plot of land valued at 6.7 billion VND. Taking advantage of loopholes in the property appraisal process, the defendant swapped the location of the mortgaged land plot, placing it on a main road instead of in an alley (valued at only 1.3 billion VND), and misappropriated 5 billion VND from the bank. The court sentenced Vu Van Tien to 16 years in prison.
You may also like
This case illustrates that asset verification cannot be limited to paper records alone. For banks, accurate information about the land plot is one of the conditions for properly assessing collateral before deciding to grant credit. Synchronizing land data is also consistent with the direction outlined in Resolution No. 21-NQ/TW dated July 28, 2026, on the views and directions for amending the Land Law and related laws.
The resolution aims for transparent land management, while also defining land as a strategic resource and calling for the improvement of the land database.
Dr. Phan Duc Hieu, a full-time National Assembly representative on the Economic and Financial Committee of the 16th National Assembly, believes that for land use rights to truly become an input resource for socio-economic development, access needs to be convenient, equal, open, and transparent. Land use rights should be allocated to entities capable of effectively utilizing this resource, based on the principles of equality, openness, transparency, and competition.
To achieve this, land information needs to be complete, clear, and accessible, thereby minimizing information discrepancies between stakeholders. This requirement is even more significant in credit activities, where land use rights are used as collateral. Transparent information provides parties with a better basis for correctly identifying assets and evaluating related transactions, thus reducing risks arising from incomplete or inconsistent information.
Actual transaction data is needed.
However, correctly identifying the asset only solves part of the problem. After knowing exactly which plot of land is being used as collateral, the bank still has to answer another crucial question: What is the actual value of that asset?
While land databases help identify what a property is, who owns it, where it's located, and its legal status, transaction data is a crucial source of information for valuing assets. This is directly relevant to the appraisal of collateral and the determination of credit limits.
You may also like
Deputy Director of the Department of Housing and Real Estate Market Management ( Ministry of Construction ) Hoang Thu Hang raised the issue that determining market price requires actual transaction data as a basis. A sharp increase in real estate prices while transaction volume is disproportionate does not necessarily fully reflect market value. Real estate prices are influenced by many factors, from investment costs, construction, land clearance, capital, financial obligations to location, supply and demand, and actual needs. Therefore, a price formed in the market does not necessarily equate to the true value of the asset.
For banks, this issue is even more noteworthy because the value of collateral is directly related to credit limits and the ability to recover debt when loan problems arise. If transaction data is incomplete, price reference can be difficult, even if the legal information of the land plot has been verified.
When land data is linked to planning information, transactions, notarization, taxes, and registration of security interests, the property verification process will have a stronger basis. This will give banks more grounds to verify collateral, and the market will have better conditions for more transparent transactions.

Accelerating the IPO process and preparing to welcome new capital inflows.
Warehouse giant BW Industrial aims for an IPO in 2027, gearing up to attract billions of dollars in funding.
Industrial real estate giant BW Industrial is accelerating preparations for its planned initial public offering (IPO) in 2027. The IPO comes amid soaring demand for factory space driven by the shift of supply chains away from China and anticipation of new international investment.
According to Nikkei Asia, BW Industrial is aiming for an initial public offering (IPO) in Vietnam in 2027. The company was established in 2018 as a joint venture between private equity fund Warburg Pincus and the Industrial Investment and Development Corporation (Becamex, ticker symbol: BCM). Although it had considered listing on the domestic stock market since 2024, sources have not yet disclosed the exact volume of shares the company plans to issue.
The impetus for the company's IPO preparations is becoming increasingly clear through its fundraising activities ahead of the listing. Nikkei Asia revealed that the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is considering a $50 million investment in BW Industrial. A final decision is expected by the bank in October of this year. Previously, in January, the company also announced a $120 million cooperation agreement with an undisclosed global institutional investor. This investment is directed towards three projects in Vietnam to serve clients operating in the electronics, automotive, and other industries. Experts believe that the recruitment of specialized personnel for the IPO, combined with the potential for a large capital inflow from the AIIB, indicates that preparations for the listing are proceeding vigorously.
If BW Industrial conducts an IPO on the Ho Chi Minh City Stock Exchange, it will have the opportunity to access a large number of foreign investors, especially after the Vietnamese stock market was officially upgraded by FTSE Russell. Commenting on this plan, Craig Martin, Chairman of Dynam Capital, believes that BW shares will be a quality addition to the industrial real estate sector, offering a direct investment opportunity in the "Made-in-Vietnam" growth story. However, the actual attractiveness of the IPO will depend heavily on the market context and available investment options. While institutional investment funds and insurance companies may value BW shares for their stability, individual investors often prefer stocks with faster growth rates.
Benefit from the wave of manufacturing relocation and supply chain diversification.
BW Industrial is currently one of the leading industrial and logistics real estate developers in Vietnam, specializing in the leasing of ready-built factory space and warehouse systems. Data published on its website shows the company manages total assets worth approximately US$3.9 billion. The company's industrial land bank exceeds 10 million square meters, distributed across 61 projects in 10 provinces and cities nationwide. Of this, approximately 4.4 million square meters of floor space has been completed, and 1.8 million square meters are under construction. The company is currently headed by Mr. Li Ting (Lance Li), who serves as its General Director.
BW Industrial's pre-built factory model is attracting significant attention from international manufacturers seeking low-cost space and tax incentives to realize their " China + 1" strategy. The boom in e-commerce and electronics manufacturing has generated substantial revenue for the company. Besides technology companies, BW also provides warehousing space for large-scale retail brands such as Shopee and 7-Eleven. Statistics from the company indicate that tenants from Greater China have an average leased area of 6,200 square meters, significantly higher than the overall customer average of 5,200 square meters.
Assessing market prospects, CEO Lance Li predicted that by 2025, manufacturing development in Vietnam would be fueled by the diversification of supply chains and a trend towards reduced reliance on transit models. As international tariffs reshape trade routes, it is predicted that more supply chains related to China will shift directly to Vietnam in the next decade. As of the end of last year, the company had successfully leased 4 million square meters of warehouse space to 470 partners, with foreign customers accounting for an overwhelming 90%. The company's shareholder profile also includes ESR, one of Asia's largest logistics management companies, which currently holds 10.4% of BW's shares and is involved in the development of several key projects.

Reaching out to the world
 The Lumi Smart Factory, spanning approximately 6,000 square meters and with a total investment of over 100 billion VND, was inaugurated in April 2024. Within the factory, small electronic circuit boards sequentially pass through the SMT production line before becoming part of smart switches, controllers, or IoT devices.
 Compared to the multi-million dollar industrial projects currently operating in Phu Tho province, Lumi Smart Factory is not a large-scale factory. However, the story behind it reveals a noteworthy approach to integration.
 Lumi started in 2012 from a group of engineers at Hanoi University of Technology. When the domestic smart home market was largely reliant on imported products, the young engineers chose to research and develop their own products. From their first products, Lumi gradually mastered hardware, software, and firmware, developed a smart home ecosystem, and expanded into IoT and smart lighting.
 According to company information, Lumi dedicates significant resources to research and development each year. 
 Lumi Smart Factory is a leading electronics manufacturing plant in Vietnam, adhering to international standards.
 According to Dam Dac Quang, Director of Lumi Smart Factory, the factory not only expands production capacity but also helps the company be more proactive in responding to the developing trend of IoT devices in Vietnam.
 Lumi not only manufactures its own-brand products but also expands into ODM, OEM, and EMS – from research and design to manufacturing complete circuit boards and devices for partners.
 According to information released by the company, Lumi has collaborated with several international partners such as Etec (Israel), Hogar Control and Eureka Forbes ( India ), and Elite (Australia); Lumi-branded products have also been introduced to many foreign markets.
 For a smart switch to enter the international market, the process behind the product is more than just assembly. It involves a chain of tasks from design, software, circuit boards, technical standards, quality control, to logistics, intellectual property protection, and after-sales service.
 According to Mr. Dam Dac Quang, the company's goal is to gradually build Lumi into a Vietnamese brand in the IoT field on the international market. To achieve this, research, design, and production capabilities must be developed synchronously.
 Locating the factory in Thang Long III Industrial Park also facilitates Lumi's connection with Noi Bai Airport, the transportation corridor to Hai Phong, and the network of electronics, components, and supporting industries in the northern region. This new production capacity not only serves Lumi's own products but also provides a foundation for the company to collaborate with partners in product development.
 According to Mr. Quang, businesses that only process orders based on existing designs will receive a different level of value compared to businesses that have the ability to research, design, test, and manufacture together with their clients. The more stages a business controls, the greater its opportunity to create and retain value.
 Lumi's story is therefore not only about the journey of bringing a Vietnamese product to the world, but also raises a challenge for businesses in Phu Tho in the process of participating more deeply in the global production network.
 Behind the billions of dollars in exports
 According to a report by the Department of Industry and Trade, in the first nine months of 2026, Phu Tho's export turnover reached over 39.3 billion USD, an increase of 48.9% compared to the same period; imports were close to 56.5 billion USD. Electronics, computers, telephones, and components accounted for approximately 80% of the total export value, concentrated in major markets such as the United States , South Korea, and Japan.
 These results demonstrate the effectiveness of attracting investment, enabling the province to increasingly participate in the global production network. However, behind these growth figures, there remains a gap in internal capacity.
 According to a survey by the Department of Industry and Trade, the majority of local businesses process orders or quotas from their parent companies abroad, thus limiting their ability to control the market.
 Notably, over 92% of the province's import turnover consists of machinery, components, and raw materials for production. Meanwhile, domestic businesses mainly supply low-value auxiliary materials such as packaging, cardboard boxes, pallets, and adhesive tape, accounting for less than 3% of the total value of raw materials. Dependence on imports for key equipment and components remains a major challenge in the integration process.
 The Department of Industry and Trade also acknowledges that the value created and retained within the locality is currently mainly concentrated in labor, logistics, construction, and support services. Higher value-added stages such as research, design, technology, component manufacturing, and input materials production remain limited.
 Returning to Lumi's story, it's clear that the value of an integrated business lies not only in exporting products abroad. Lumi invests in R&D, designs its own hardware, develops software, builds factories, and seeks international customers. Once it established its production capacity, the company expanded into ODM, OEM, and EMS, gradually moving deeper into the value chain.
 This is also the direction Phu Tho province is setting for its business community. The province has issued a Plan on international economic integration for the period 2026-2030; a program on "Reaching out to international markets"; and is implementing tasks related to trade defense, e-commerce, and developing a logistics development plan.

 In particular, the project to support the connection and linkage of the province's businesses with foreign businesses participating in global supply chains, approved by the Provincial People's Committee on April 9, 2026, aims to enhance the capacity of domestic businesses, connect supply and demand, and gradually become suppliers for the FDI sector. The province plans to encourage at least four FDI corporations to develop technical support programs and develop domestic suppliers.
 From young engineers independently researching and developing products to an IoT manufacturing plant, Lumi's journey spans over a decade. Not every step was significant, but the direction was clear: Mastering another technology, another process, another market.
 Phu Tho currently has a large-scale industrial base with significant import and export activities. The focus in the coming years will not only be on increasing export figures, but more importantly, on increasing the real value created and retained within the province; from the proportion of locally produced components and the number of domestic businesses participating in global supply chains to the emergence of high-tech "Make in Vietnam" products. From models like Lumi Smart Factory, the journey towards self-reliance and integration can be expanded, creating more opportunities for Vietnamese businesses to reach further.
